title: Warrant Clearing for Artificial Intelligence Agents: Maintaining Justified Claims Across Recursive Agentic Synthesis

detail.title: Warrant Clearing for Artificial Intelligence Agents: Maintaining Justified Claims Across Recursive Agentic Synthesis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Agentic systems recursively synthesize claims and reuse those claims as premises for further reasoning and action. In current systems, the justification supporting each claim is rarely preserved as a structured, queryable object across steps. This creates epistemic debt-reasoning chains whose total support, contradictions, and conditions of validity become progressively more difficult to inspect. The problem originates at two layers: first, at the knowledge-creation and indexing layer, where claims enter AI-accessible systems without adequate structural preparation; and second, at the agentic reasoning layer, where inadequately structured claims are synthesized and reused without justification tracking. This paper introduces Warrant Clearing as a protocol for maintaining Justified Claims across recursive agentic synthesis, and integrates the Knowledge Structuring Model (KSM™; Bowen, 2026) as the upstream architectural framework that improves the quality of knowledge entering the protocol. A Justified Claim is a signed object that carries a claim, direct evidence, explicit contradictions, action constraints, adjudication status, and justification history. The Justification Adjudication Protocol requires contradictions to be surfaced and justification history updated at each synthesis or reuse step before a claim may be reused for further reasoning or action. The framework is also complementary to the Model Context Protocol (MCP): MCP standardizes access to tools and external context, while Warrant Clearing preserves the justification of claims derived from that context as they propagate through recursive synthesis. When agents reason over self-referential histories, the protocol uses declared bounds and records residual uncertainty explicitly. Together, KSM™, MCP, and Warrant Clearing describe a layered architecture for epistemic integrity in artificial intelligence agents:

title: How AI Perceives the World: Epistemic Foundations for Measuring Entity Representation without Ground Truth
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How AI Perceives the World: Epistemic Foundations for Measuring Entity Representation without Ground Truth

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and representative director of Tech Knowledge Base, Inc. (TKBase), which develops commercial products related to AI citation measurement. The author has no other competing interests to declare.

detail.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people discover, evaluate, and trust information, the way an AI system represents and cites a given entity—a company, a website, a person—has acquired real social consequence. A rapidly growing set of industry tools now attempts to measure this representation by tracking how often, and how prominently, an entity is cited or mentioned in AI answers, and recent academic work has begun to treat AI visibility as a quantity to be estimated. We argue that these efforts share a common and consequential omission: they report a quantity without first defining the estimand. Because an LLM's response is a random variable conditioned on the query, a citation rate averaged over a set of queries is not a property intrinsic to the entity being measured but an artifact of the measurer's choice of queries. We advance a three-part position. First, existing entity-representation measurement lacks a defined estimand, leaving it unclear what the reported quantity refers to. Second, once the estimand is defined by conditioning on intent context—treating an entity's representation as a field of citation rates across intent clusters—reliability, validity, and coverage become well-posed and can be addressed with established methods. Third, this framework closes the *measurement* of an AI's representational space mathematically, but the *interpretation* of any gap between representation and reality, and the discovery of latent needs, require human judgment. We import the theory of construct validity from psychometrics and the social sciences to provide an epistemic foundation for measuring entity representation in the absence of ground truth.

title: The Cognitive Cooperative: A Coordination Primitive for Agent Economies
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Cognitive Cooperative: A Coordination Primitive for Agent Economies
detail.abstract: The infrastructure for agent-based on-chain coordination became production-grade in 2025–2026: ERC-8004 trustless agent identity, Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) with 60+ launch partners, the x402 payment protocol, EIP-7702 smart accounts, and Safe-multisig agent coordination. AI agents now account for 29% of all transactions on Gnosis Chain. Decentralised autonomous organisations (DAOs) collectively held over $35 billion in on-chain treasuries by end-2024, with 2025 measurements ranging $21-25 billion as token prices fluctuated; voter participation averaged 6.3% across DAOs studied between 2020 and 2024, and emergency response can take days. This paper introduces the Cognitive Cooperative (CogCoop), an agent-native, blockchain-native, human-overseen organisational primitive in which each participant is a human represented by AI agents that execute the participant's published policy at machine speed. Humans set values, risk tolerance, and strategic direction; agents read every proposal, evaluate every counterparty, and execute within delegated scope. Voter participation rises because the cost of being represented falls. Six design patterns are proposed: governance as policy execution, reputation-weighted voting under ERC-8004, multi-agent debate for contested decisions, real-time operational execution within policy bands, machine-to-machine cross-CogCoop negotiation, and pre-execution compliance checks. The paper distinguishes Dividend CogCoops (treasury surplus flows to token holders) from Recirculating CogCoops (treasury surplus funds public goods and protocol operations) as a governance-alignment choice with different long-horizon implications for holder behaviour and protocol sustainability. Cooperative legal lineage (Forman 1975, Subchapter T) informs the Recirculating design as historical precedent for non-distributive structures organised around a shared purpose. The paper closes with a build agenda (five gaps from policy-schema standards to circuit-breaker UX) and a values-layer framing that motivates the empirical program. Companion working papers report empirical simulation evidence on monetary policy choice (Chen 2026a) and on values-aligned agent reasoning amplifying rule-policy effect-size (Chen 2026b).

title: Digital Anthropology for Enterprise AI: Closing the Work-Reality Gap in Machine-Legible Organizations

detail.abstract:
Enterprise AI initiatives frequently struggle when moving from successful pilots to enterprise-scale deployment. Existing discussions often focus on models, agents, data platforms, and governance mechanisms. This paper argues that a significant source of failure lies elsewhere: organizations frequently understand documented processes but do not adequately represent how work is actually performed.

The paper introduces Digital Anthropology for Enterprise AI as a discipline for studying actual work, human-AI interaction, tacit knowledge, informal workflows, behavioral adaptation, and governance practices within AI-enabled enterprises. It develops the concept of the Work-Reality Gap—the divergence between human reality and machine representation—and argues that enterprise AI systems reason over representations rather than reality itself.

Building on socio-technical systems theory, human-computer interaction, automation studies, and AI governance research, the paper proposes that successful enterprise AI requires stronger capabilities for understanding human reality, maintaining representation quality, and preserving legitimacy as AI systems move from recommendation to action.

The paper contributes a conceptual framework that positions Digital Anthropology as a capability that strengthens both representation quality and governance effectiveness in machine-legible organizations. It further introduces concepts including the Human-in-the-Loop Illusion, Representation Drift, and the Synergetic Workforce, and proposes a practical operating model for observing, representing, analyzing, governing, and adapting enterprise AI systems over time.

The paper concludes that the future success of Enterprise AI will depend not only on advances in AI reasoning but also on an organization's ability to understand, represent, and govern human reality.

title: Arithmetic Pedagogy for Language Models
affiliations: Bandung Fe Institute and Bandung Fe Institute

detail.title: Arithmetic Pedagogy for Language Models
detail.abstract: We investigate whether methods of human mathematics pedagogy can guide the training of language models toward arithmetic reasoning. Building on the GASING method-an Indonesian pedagogy that solves basic arithmetic through a left-to-right procedure aligned with the causal order of token generation-we operationalize each operation as a computational procedure whose execution trace is serialized into natural-language Chain-of-Thought (CoT) supervision. A small GPT-2 decoder (86M parameters) with a syllabic-agglutinative TOBA tokenizer for Indonesian is trained from scratch on this data using only a next-token prediction objective, without reinforcement learning or reward-based optimization. Monitoring training reveals three distinct learning phases, and mechanistic analyses-attention-masking interventions on the CoT information graph, residualstream probing, and logit-lens inspection-show that the model first internalizes a procedural pathway and subsequently develops an associative, "mental-arithmetic" capacity that retrieves intermediate results without explicit step-by-step computation. The trained model reaches over 80% accuracy on held-out problems and attains competitive performance against substantially larger language models, indicating that targeted, pedagogically grounded training can yield strong and economical arithmetic capability at small scale.

detail.abstract: Digital service environments have transformed the way organizations communicate with customers. Instead of face-to-face and verbal communication, organizations now communicate with customers in writing through live chat, email, social messaging, and automated support systems. In these settings, communication behavior affects the way customers perceive the competence, attentiveness, and trustworthiness of an organization. In the existing body of research on e-service quality and customer experience, response, clarity, empathy, and interaction quality are the important factors. However, these communication elements are mostly embedded in broader constructs like customer experience or e-service quality instead of being analyzed as separate analytical variables. The purpose of this conceptual framework paper is to address this limitation by proposing a literature-based model that identifies communication behavior as a central mechanism linking digital service encounters to customer satisfaction and loyalty. In this paper, we build on existing work on customer experience theory, service quality, customer engagement theory, and digital interaction literature and theorize communication behavior as three dimensions: tone, timing, and wording. The paper argues that tone affects emotional understanding, timing affects organizational attention, and wording affects cognitive clarity of digital interactions. These dimensions together influence customers' perception of service encounters in a text-only environment with no physical and vocal cues. In the proposed framework, communication behaviors influence loyalty outcomes through customer satisfaction. Theoretical Contribution: This research advances the existing models of customer experience and e-service quality analysis to a micro-level interaction analysis and goes beyond the macro-level journey perspectives. It also contributes to practice by providing a systematic means for organizations to improve customer satisfaction and retention through purposeful communication design.

title: VISAGE: Designing AI Artifacts for Dynamic Self-Presentation in Matching Platforms
affiliations: , Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information & Systems Management

detail.title: VISAGE: Designing AI Artifacts for Dynamic Self-Presentation in Matching Platforms
detail.abstract: Online matching platforms constrain users to static profiles, producing a mismatch between the idealized self a user presents and the heterogeneous preferences of potential partners. Drawing on self-discrepancy theory, we conceptualize this mismatch as an interpersonal gap between one's presented self and what each partner desires to see, with AI serving as a mediator to help address it. Following the computational design science perspective, we propose VISAGE, an AI system comprising two artifacts grounded in distinct human-AI collaboration principles. The augmentation artifact selects optimal images from users' existing assets, whereas the assemblage artifact generates new images tailored to individual partner preferences. Using large-scale operational data from a major online dating platform, we evaluate VISAGE at both the user and platform levels. At the user level, model-predicted ratings suggest that both artifacts improve attractiveness ratings. Relative effectiveness varies with partner-preference heterogeneity and user impression management skill, consistent with theoretical predictions from the human-AI collaboration literature. At the platform level, agent-based simulations suggest that VISAGE can enhance matching efficiency and reduce inequality in matching opportunities, although optimal deployment strategies depend on the platform's recommendation algorithm. The theoretical contribution of this study is to foreground the interpersonal gap as a key source of matching inefficiency and to illustrate how AI can address it at scale. The design contribution lies in actionable design knowledge, including when to deploy augmentation versus assemblage artifacts based on user and partner characteristics and how to align user-facing AI features with backend algorithmic infrastructure.

detail.abstract: Traditional internationalization strategies for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are often hindered by high consultancy costs, information asymmetry, and steep learning curves. This paper proposes a novel computational framework based on Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate strategic market entry analysis. We introduce an architecture that orchestrates specialized agents-dedicated to Macroeconomic Intelligence, Regulatory Compliance, and Cultural Localization-integrated via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over real-time global trade datasets. By formalizing the export process into a sequence of deterministic agentic workflows, the framework demonstrates a significant reduction in latency for market-readiness assessment while maintaining high factual accuracy. Our results suggest that LLM-driven agentic reasoning can democratize access to global markets, providing SMEs with institutional-grade strategic intelligence while mitigating algorithmic hallucinations.

title: The Face of Digital Twins
affiliations: , Arison School of Business ,  and Reichman University

detail.title: The Face of Digital Twins
detail.abstract: LLM-based digital twins represent individuals through text alone, capturing what people report in surveys while leaving physical appearance unrepresented despite its central role in human identity. We introduce a validated approach for generating synthetic persona facial images from survey data alone, without real photographs. Building on the Twin-2K-500 framework of Toubia et al. (2025), we extract portrait-relevant visual cues from each respondent's survey answers and use a large image model to generate photorealistic facial images per persona. Three analyses validate that the generated faces represent the underlying persona profiles: (1) faces match their source persona above chance; (2) more similar survey profiles generate more similar faces, even after controlling for demographic similarity; and (3) survey questions unrelated to appearance predict similarity in appearance-related visual cues. An exploratory analysis indicates that depression and Big Five scales — and, less consistently, anxiety — are most associated with the personality–face link. Our contribution is representational: a visual layer can be constructed from non-visual survey data alone, providing a reusable complement to the textual twin. Because the visual layer is defined by persona-level visual-cue prompts rather than fixed images, it can be re-rendered by any current or future image model as the technology improves.

title: Remarkable Convergence: Anthropic's Safeguards and the Governance Twin
affiliations: and AiSuNe Foundation

detail.title: Remarkable Convergence: Anthropic's Safeguards and the Governance Twin

publicationDetails.detailsText: AiSuNe Foundation Research Series. Preprint archived on Zenodo (29 Jun 2026). DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21035058 — https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21035058

detail.abstract: In the second week of June 2026 a public argument broke out over whether Claude Fable 5 had been jailbroken. Anthropic disputed it. However, the dispute is not the point. The point is, what the episode exposes is where governance actually lives inside these systems, and how little of it there is. Anthropic has done something real: it built a safeguard whose heaviest layer sits outside the model, where the conversation cannot talk its way past it, a direction we have described for more than a year and set out in our Governance Twin executive brief before Fable shipped [1]. But what it built is control, not governance, and the difference carries the argument. Control is a gate, asking whether a single action is allowed. Governance is a heading, asking where the whole trajectory is going and whether the system can still get back. Anthropic has built the gate, and a good one; the governing plane, which holds an evolving standard and judges the trajectory rather than the point, is the part still missing. This paper reads the episode through that distinction, applies the two cuts of the foundation paper Structure Not Content, and Trajectory Not Point [2] to one public case, credits Anthropic for the separation, and names the steps from a very good gate to a governance plane. It also reads what even the best gate costs: built efficiently only by the model's owner, it leaves the operator, who carries the liability, inheriting control rather than governance, over a system whose runtime standard it cannot set, evolve, or own. What the public shape shows is a remarkable convergence: an architecture recognisably similar to the Governance Twin, arrived at independently and pointing toward the same conclusion.

title: Structure Not Content, and Trajectory Not Point - The Two Distinctions that Turn the Governance-is-not-Control Philosophy into an Architecture

detail.title: Structure Not Content, and Trajectory Not Point - The Two Distinctions that Turn the Governance-is-not-Control Philosophy into an Architecture
detail.abstract: The two distinctions that turn the governance-is-not-Governance is not control. Governing a system is about where its trajectory goes, and whether it can still get back, not about whether the single action in front of it happens to be allowed. That claim is argued elsewhere. On its own, though, it does not tell you what to build. This paper adds a perspective of its own, on the form runtime governance has to take, and it draws that form out in two distinctions. Together they make an ontology of governance: what it is about, and what it is made of. The first concerns what governance evaluates, the point, one action at a time, or the trajectory, across the whole sequence. The second concerns how governance is encoded, as content, which the operation can reinterpret, or as structure, which it cannot. Each rules out a familiar shortcut. Together, wherever a system must stay adaptive and the operation can reinterpret what it is told, they force one shape: a governance plane that stands apart from the operation, assesses the path rather than the step, and reaches it only through immutable infrastructure the operation cannot reframe. That shape is realised in a separate architecture; here the argument is why governance has to take this form, not how to build it. The treatment is governance-agnostic. It concerns how governance is encoded and what it watches, not which values it should hold. AI is the running illustration, for that is where the failure modes are currently live and documented. The two distinctions themselves are general.control philosophy into an architecture.

detail.abstract: Current scaling trajectories for Generative AI, typified by linear supply-side "stacks," prioritize performance density while externalizing significant thermodynamic and material costs. As the "Twin Transition" of green and digital transformation accelerates, the industry faces technology gaps-including Scope 3 emissions and e-waste recycling-that impede sustainable scaling and lead to social tensions. This study proposes a Regenerative Socio-Technical roadmap that repurposes the Sustainable Production and Consumption system map to reframe artificial intelligence infrastructure as a system-of-systems governed ultimately by planetary limits. By integrating the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IEEE IRDS) sustainability considerations for semiconductor facilities, the study proposes a metabolic circuit framework that centers "Values and Needs" within production and consumption relationship loops. This study identifies critical gaps in current Nvidia-centric roadmaps and proposes a competing reference architecture. It demonstrates how a spontaneous order of resource parsimony and planetary accountability can provide an actionable pathway for regulatory compliance and industrial resilience in the digital circular economy.

title: The Future of Human and AI Coexistence: Admissibility and Recoverability - Governance Is Not Control, and Control Is Not Governance

detail.title: The Future of Human and AI Coexistence: Admissibility and Recoverability - Governance Is Not Control, and Control Is Not Governance
detail.abstract: Across institutions, markets, and now artificial agents, one distinction is consistently underspecified and consistently expensive to ignore: governance is not control. Control preserves the consistency of what a system is doing now; governance preserves the continuity of how a system interprets itself and what futures remain open to it as it changes. The two preserve categorically different objects, and no quantity of control yields governance. This overview consolidates a multi-paper research program built on that distinction. The program proceeds in three layers: a philosophy of what governance is and preserves (continuity, recoverability, and the openness of the future); an architecture, the Governance Twin, that realizes the philosophy as a buildable system of services, data structures, and flows; and a runtime, the Governance Harness, that makes governance reach each operational action without collapsing back into control. Around this spine sits a body of applied and historical work-on labor substitution, delegation, apprenticeship, manufacturing, and the distinct cognition of AI systems-published under persistent identifiers. The document is an orientation rather than a derivation: it states the program's established results as findings and points to the sources that develop each, naming work still in preparation as direction rather than settled result.

title: The AI Trust Gap:  The Missing Link Between AI Capability and Economic Value

detail.title: The AI Trust Gap:  The Missing Link Between AI Capability and Economic Value

keywords: Artificial Intelligence (AI); AI Strategy; AI Trust; AI Trust Gap; Trust in AI; AI Adoption; Human-AI Interaction; Intelligent Decisioning; Economic Value Creation; Value Realization; Trust Calibration; AI Governance.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence systems are often evaluated through measures of technical performance such as accuracy, precision, recall, or predictive capability. Yet organizations frequently find that technically capable AI systems fail to generate the economic value anticipated from their deployment. The reason is that capability alone does not create value. AI systems create value only when their outputs influence decisions, actions, and behaviors.

This paper introduces the concept of the AI Trust Gap: the difference between the economic value an AI system could create if its outputs were fully utilized and the value actually realized in practice. The paper argues that trust functions as an economic mechanism governing the conversion of AI capability into realized value. However, this mechanism is often misaligned: both insufficient trust and excessive trust can distort economic outcomes.

Systems that are trusted are adopted, integrated into workflows, delegated authority, and allowed to learn from experience, while systems that are mistrusted remain underutilized and fail to realize their full potential. Conversely, systems that are trusted beyond their actual capability may expose organizations to operational, financial, reputational, regulatory, and safety risks. Trust therefore influences not only value realization but also risk exposure.

The paper further argues that trust must be calibrated to actual capability rather than maximized. Through illustrations including IBM Watson Health, Zillow Offers, GitHub Copilot, and Netflix, the paper demonstrates how differences in trust calibration produce dramatically different economic outcomes even among systems with comparable technical capabilities. The central conclusion is that trust calibration is a critical determinant of both AI value realization and AI risk management.

detail.abstract: Sustainable investing has developed rapidly through ESG integration, disclosure frameworks, and stewardship practices. Yet evidence of system-level impact remains limited. Most existing analysis treats these limitations as problems of implementation or scale. This article argues the failure is structural. Dominant mechanisms-secondary market capital allocation and shareholder engagement-cannot deliver system-level outcomes because they operate at the wrong level of analysis. For universal asset owners, whose portfolios approximate the global economy, system conditions determine long-term returns, making systemic risk management integral to fiduciary duty. The article introduces the primary/secondary capital allocation distinction as the operative test for impact additionality and proposes a coalition index governed by asset owners to enable coordinated action on system-level risks.

detail.abstract: State capacity is often equated with fiscal resources or institutional design, yet routine, high-coordination public services depend on a less visible input: the continuity of the local bureaucracy that delivers them. We study what happens when that continuity breaks without warning. In Brazil, electoral courts routinely remove sitting mayors for campaign irregularities, triggering an off-cycle supplementary election; while removal is not random, its timing is governed by judicial processing speed and is plausibly exogenous to local health trajectories. Using a panel of all 5,570 municipalities (2012-2019) and staggered difference-indifferences estimators (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021), we estimate the effect of this unscheduled administrative discontinuity on primary health care. Removal reduces the operational capacity of primary care-the population coverage of Family Health Strategy teams-by roughly 2 to 4 percentage points (the effect on the number of teams is negative but imprecise). The decline is consistent across controls, alternative estimators, subsamples, and stateby-year fixed effects, and survives relative-magnitude sensitivity analysis for violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth 2023), though with a moderate breakdown threshold. Childhood vaccination coverage shows a pattern consistent with this supply-side channel-declining selectively in routine vaccines and not in those administered at maternity (a negative control)-but, given its fragility, we treat this downstream outcome and the personnel-turnover mechanism as suggestive rather than identified. The findings reframe the cost of political instability from the fiscal to the operational, linking the judicialization of local elections to the delivery of decentralized public services.

title: Multi-timescale Prediction of Shallow and Deep Groundwater Levels Using a Differentially Physics-Constrained GRU Model
affiliations: Hebei GEO University, Hebei GEO University, Hebei GEO University, Hebei GEO University, Hebei GEO University, Hebei Key Laboratory of Mountain Geological Environment, Hebei GEO University and Hebei GEO University

detail.title: Multi-timescale Prediction of Shallow and Deep Groundwater Levels Using a Differentially Physics-Constrained GRU Model
detail.abstract: Groundwater-level prediction is essential for water resources management in groundwater-overexploited regions. However, conventional data-driven models often have difficulty simultaneously representing groundwater-level dynamics, pumping effects, and response differences among aquifer types. In this study, Guantao County, a typical agricultural groundwater pumping area in the North China Plain, was selected as the study area. Based on groundwater-level, meteorological, and pumping data from three shallow wells and three deep wells, a multi-timescale groundwater-level prediction model was developed using a differentially physics-constrained GRU. The results showed that, compared with the conventional GRU, the physics-constrained GRU achieved overall better predictive performance at both daily and dekadal scales. At the daily scale, the average RMSE was reduced by approximately 7.6% and 8.0% for shallow and deep wells, respectively; at the dekadal scale, the corresponding reductions were approximately 3.9% and 2.8%. For deep wells, the contribution of pumping information depended more strongly on an appropriate representation of the cumulative time window. The 60 d moving-average pumping series showed relatively stable performance in terms of overall average metrics, whereas the 30 d and 90 d windows yielded better results for some individual wells. These findings indicate that pumping information should not only be incorporated into groundwater-level prediction models, but also be represented differentially according to aquifer type and response timescale. This study provides a modeling framework that integrates data-driven learning and process constraints for differentiated prediction of shallow and deep groundwater levels in agricultural pumping areas.

title: The Calculation Problem in Capacity Markets: Constructing Price Discovery from Austrian Principles

detail.title: The Calculation Problem in Capacity Markets: Constructing Price Discovery from Austrian Principles

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by Ericsson, a telecommunications equipment manufacturer. The research concerns radio access network resource coordination mechanisms. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical economics paper involving no human subjects, patients, or participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by Ericsson.

detail.abstract: Provisioned capacity rights, including network reservations, cloud commitments, and spectrum licences, are allocated by central administration. No market exists for their multi-dimensional subdivisions. The infrastructure provider cannot calculate the most valued use of idle capacity because the prices required for that calculation are not produced by any existing process. This is the calculation problem that Mises (1920) identified for socialist planning, reproduced in a commercially significant domain. This paper presents a customer-to-customer (C2C) mechanism that creates the missing market. Owners of underutilised capacity partition unused resources along orthogonal dimensions and offer the resulting subdivisions for competitive sealed-bid lease. Derivative rights are settled on a permissioned ledger. A demand-driven variant generates price signals for resources that have not been provisioned. The mechanism is analysed as institutional design: it satisfies several of Ostrom's (1990) design principles for common-pool resource governance, reduces the transaction costs that Williamson (1985) identifies as barriers to market governance, and uses blockchain as institutional technology (Davidson, 1 De Filippi, and Potts 2018). The mechanism was derived from Austrian epistemological principles taken as engineering constraints. The paper demonstrates that these principles constitute a generative framework for constructing coordination institutions in domains where markets do not yet exist.

title: Equitable Auction Design with Provable Regret Guarantees
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Institute of Operations Research and Analytics, Universite du Luxembourg and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Industrial & Systems Engineering

detail.title: Equitable Auction Design with Provable Regret Guarantees
detail.abstract: We study a mechanism design problem where a seller aims to allocate a good to multiple bidders, each with a private value. The seller supports or favors a specific group, referred to as the minority group. Specifically, the seller requires that allocations to the minority group are at least a predetermined fraction (equity level) of those made to the rest of the bidders. Such constraints arise in various settings, including government procurement and corporate supply chain policies that prioritize small businesses, environmentally responsible suppliers, or enterprises owned by historically disadvantaged individuals. We include the equity requirements as constraints in the design of a mechanism, and our goal is to characterize equitable mechanisms with provable performance guarantees. Motivated by settings where reliable information about the bidders' values is unavailable, our main focus is a regret-based mechanism design problem, which makes no assumptions about the distribution of the bidders' values and aims to minimize the maximum (worst-case) ex-post regret in view of all possible bidders' values. Here, regret is defined as the difference between the highest revenue achievable in hindsight and the revenue generated by a mechanism. For this problem, we propose a closedform mechanism and prove that its ex-post regret is at most a constant multiple (dependent on the equity level) of the optimal worst-case regret. We find that, when bidders' value supports are identical, this factor is less than 1.31 across all possible equity levels. We also show that the proposed mechanism is asymptotically optimal as the equity level decreases and increases. Additionally, we show that this mechanism is also equipped with an additional layer of pricing protection for the minority group. As a benchmark based on distributional information, we also study a stochastic mechanism design problem, which assumes that the bidders' values are random variables following a known distribution and aims to maximize the expected revenue. We characterize the optimal mechanism in this benchmark problem under standard independence and regularity assumptions. Both mechanisms can be interpreted as set-asides, a common policy tool that reserves a fraction of goods for minority groups. Numerical results demonstrate that the stochastic mechanism performs well when the bidders' value distribution is accurately estimated, while the regret-based mechanism exhibits greater robustness under estimation errors.

title: Governance Is Not Control, and Control Is Not Governance - Recoverability and the Preservation of Meaningful Continuation

detail.title: Governance Is Not Control, and Control Is Not Governance - Recoverability and the Preservation of Meaningful Continuation
detail.abstract: This paper restores a distinction habit has let blur: control is not governance, and governance is not control. Control preserves operational-state consistency: it holds the system's present condition within acceptable bounds, admitting or rejecting each action as it arises. Governance preserves governance-state continuity: it keeps the system recognizably itself as it changes, maintaining the interpretive frame through which its direction stays legible. The two are not refinements of each other; they preserve categorically different objects, one a state and the other a trajectory through time. From that distinction the paper develops what governance alone protects: recoverability, the property by which acceptable future continuations remain reachable even as the system changes, and with it the possibility of meaningful continuation. Recoverability belongs to no single function but emerges from execution, control, and governance together, and it can be lost silently, through a run of individually acceptable steps, long before any visible failure announces it. Control without governance vanishes violently. Governance without control vanishes silently. The work is an attempt to keep both, precisely. None of this is new, and none of it is specific to any one technology: the paper sharpens principles we already rely on rather than inventing any. The blurring of control and governance stayed manageable while systems were slow and simple, because an outside hand could often correct a crossed boundary before it became irreversible. It stops being manageable as systems grow complex and fast enough for that slack to vanish, a pressure long building in tightly coupled institutions, markets, and supply chains. Artificial intelligence is only the latest and fastest occasion to expose it; the distinction was always there, and it matters wherever a system moves faster than correction can follow.

title: Dopamine Receptor Depletion and Recovery

detail.title: Dopamine Receptor Depletion and Recovery

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Behavioral addiction is increasingly understood not as a failure of willpower but as a neuroplastic process involving measurable changes to the brain's reward circuitry. This narrative review synthesizes findings from leading neuroscientific research on dopamine D2 receptor downregulation, synaptic pruning, DeltaFosB accumulation, Default Mode Network recalibration, and prefrontal cortex reactivation during abstinence. Drawing on the work of Nora Volkow (NIDA), Judson Brewer (Brown University), and others, the paper traces a week-by-week timeline of neural recovery and evaluates the empirical superiority of habit replacement over habit elimination. The review concludes that moralistic approaches to behavioral change are contradicted by current neuroscience, and that public-health frameworks for addiction and screen-time regulation should incorporate neuroplasticity-informed intervention design. This paper is a literature synthesis and proposes no new empirical data. It is written from an interdisciplinary perspective to bridge neuroscience findings with policy and educational applications.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Education purposes for the IEA
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The People vs Paternalism examines the growth of government interventions aimed at influencing individual behavior in the name of improving public health and social welfare. The paper argues that paternalistic policies including taxes on unhealthy products, advertising restrictions, and regulatory measures intended to shape consumer choices often rest on the assumption that individuals are unable to make decisions in their own best interests. Drawing on economic theory and empirical evidence, the authors contend that such interventions can undermine personal autonomy, distort markets, and produce unintended consequences. The paper advocates a policy framework grounded in individual responsibility, informed choice, and voluntary mechanisms rather than coercive regulation. It concludes that limiting paternalistic interventions would better preserve individual freedom while allowing consumers to make decisions according to their own preferences and circumstances.

title: Not Invented Here
affiliations: Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) and Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)

detail.title: Not Invented Here
detail.abstract: Not Invented Here: Institutional Resistance to Practical Solutions examines how ideological commitments can prevent campaign groups and policymakers from embracing effective solutions to social and environmental problems. The authors argue that many organizations, while presenting themselves as focused on issues such as obesity, climate change, smoking, housing, and food security, often reject market-based or technological innovations because these solutions conflict with broader anti-capitalist or interventionist beliefs. Through a series of case studies, including weight-loss drugs, nuclear energy, safer nicotine products, and housing reform, the paper demonstrates how practical and evidence-based approaches are frequently opposed simply because they originate outside preferred ideological frameworks. The authors conclude that policymakers should prioritise outcomes and empirical evidence over political or institutional biases, allowing innovation and consumer choice to play a greater role in addressing major societal challenges.

title: Volatility Psychophysics in Gold Futures: Weber-Fechner Perception Laws, COT Positioning and HMM Regime Detection in COMEX Gold (2006-2026)

detail.title: Volatility Psychophysics in Gold Futures: Weber-Fechner Perception Laws, COT Positioning and HMM Regime Detection in COMEX Gold (2006-2026)
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether human perception of financial volatility obeys logarithmic (Weber-Fechner) scaling laws, and whether psychophysical transformations of CFTC Commitment of Traders (COT) positioning data improve out-of-sample gold volatility forecasting. Using 1,032 weekly observations of COMEX Gold futures (September 2006-June 2026), we construct three theory-grounded features; Perceived Volatility (PV), Psychophysical Positioning (PP), and Position Shock and embed them within a Random Forest framework augmented by three-state Hidden Markov Model (HMM) regime detection and TreeSHAP explainability. The HAR-RV linear benchmark achieves R² = 0.313, substantially outperforming both the RF Baseline (R² = 0.079) and the full psychophysical RF model (R² = 0.125) on the 2022-2026 post COVID test window. This regime mismatch, where linear autoregression dominates tree-based models on structurally novel data, is itself an astonishing finding. Psychophysical features (CrisisProb, RegimeDuration, ProdPressure) contribute approximately 13% of total feature importance, providing evidence of partial support for Hypotheses H1-H3. H4 (psychophysical augmentation outperforming HAR-RV) is not supported.

title: Transformational Wellbeing: Conscious Leadership and Digital Mental Health Ecosystems in Hybrid South African Workplaces

detail.title: Transformational Wellbeing: Conscious Leadership and Digital Mental Health Ecosystems in Hybrid South African Workplaces
detail.abstract: South African workplaces are changing rapidly due to digital technology and the shift to hybrid work. This study explores four key concepts: conscious leadership, psychosocial safety climate, digital mental health, and organisational development, interact to shape employee wellbeing in this environment. A mixed-methods approach combined quantitative surveys from 56 employees with qualitative interviews from 15 leaders across HR, IT, technical, and administrative sectors. Findings reveal that leaders exhibiting integrity, emotional intelligence, and cultural awareness foster greater employee engagement and resilience. However, technical and administrative teams often lack support and digital wellbeing programs, particularly in areas with poor infrastructure or limited resources. Digital mental health tools (e.g., apps and online support) prove effective when localised for languages and communities, with active leadership endorsement. Challenges include unequal technology access, policy gaps, and funding shortages, disproportionately affecting rural employees. Coaching, feedback, and professional development aid adaptation but must extend beyond management and HR. Recommendations urge organisations to improve internet/power infrastructure, create inclusive policies, and co-design well-being initiatives with staff. This research offers South African organisations a practical roadmap for resilient workplaces through conscious leadership, strong psychosocial climates, tailored digital tools, and equitable development.

title: The Fear of Being Seen: Local Media as a Constraint on Labor Adaptation
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Management

detail.title: The Fear of Being Seen: Local Media as a Constraint on Labor Adaptation
detail.abstract: Firms often respond to competitive pressure through adaptive decisions that displace and harm stakeholders. When can affected stakeholders constrain such adaptation? In this paper, I argue that local media, by acting as an information intermediary for disenfranchised stakeholders, increases the visibility of labor-displacing decisions and raises their expected reputational costs. As a result, firms in stronger local media environments become less willing to undertake adaptive actions that impose concentrated harm on workers and communities. I test this argument using a shift-sharestyle research design that exploits variation in Chinese import competition across U.S. industries. I find that firms headquartered in regions with greater local media intensity are less likely to lay off workers in response to industry downturns and are less likely to close establishments located in high-media regions. These results are robust to a range of empirical checks. Mechanism tests show that local media amplifies the reputational costs associated with layoffs and induces more stakeholderinclusive executive discourse during industry downturns. The effects are attenuated in industries with strong union presence and concentrated among firms with greater monopsonistic power in labor markets. These constraints also propagate downstream, slowing workforce skill reconfiguration and shaping AI adoption. The findings suggest that informational transparency, while protecting stakeholder claims, can impose real strategic costs by constraining organizationally necessary adaptation.

title: A Data-Driven Food Redistribution Decision-Support Model for Food Banks: Equity-Based Targeting and Social Impact Measurement

detail.title: A Data-Driven Food Redistribution Decision-Support Model for Food Banks: Equity-Based Targeting and Social Impact Measurement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual, non-empirical study based on previously published literature; it did not involve any new data collection from human participants, patients, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Large quantities of edible food are lost or discarded before reaching people who could use them, and food redistribution recovers part of this surplus as social value. Food banks carry out much of this work, yet their reliance on variable donations of food, money and labor leaves them supply-driven, resource-scarce and unstable, while the volume-based metrics they conventionally report obscure the depth of food insecurity. This paper develops a conceptual, data-driven decision-support model that aims to help food banks allocate limited resources more fairly and transparently. The model is a managerial framework rather than an implemented or validated system. It is organized as a layered structure combining equitybased targeting grounded in food access and food acquirability, stakeholder-informed resource allocation, AI-enabled decision-support, fresh food logistics, and multidimensional social impact measurement under explicit governance. Its contribution is integrative: by connecting techniques the literature has developed separately, it offers food banks a fairer and more accountable basis for redistribution than quantity-based reporting allows.

title: Bringing Food Closer: A Stochastic Programming Approach to Analyze the Role of Pop-up Markets in a Food Bank Network to Improve Accessibility
affiliations: , University of Michigan and North Carolina State University

detail.title: Bringing Food Closer: A Stochastic Programming Approach to Analyze the Role of Pop-up Markets in a Food Bank Network to Improve Accessibility

declarations.funderStatement: This work is supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (Grant#2125600 and #2234598).

detail.abstract: Food banks and their partner food agencies play a vital role in alleviating community food insecurity by distributing surplus food to those in need. In the United States, food bank networks are committed to ensuring fairness in allocating donated food to all service regions within their network. While it is possible to ensure equitable allocation of supplies, disparities in accessibility persist due to insufficient food assistance sites in some service regions. To serve communities with limited access to existing facilities, food banks operate pop-up markets (PUMs), walk-up and mobile operations, to ensure consistent and reliable access to food. This study develops a systematic decision-making tool using a two-stage stochastic model to optimize PUM locations under uncertainty in the network's donation supply. Our model develops a multi-period problem that accounts for the availability of existing facilities across periods and proposes optimal locations for PUMs to minimize the expected distance to facilities from food-insecure communities at the census tract level. We perform a case study with 66 census tracts in five rural counties served by the Food bank of Central and Eastern North Carolina (FBCENC) to examine the impact of optimal PUM locations on accessibility. We perform accessibility analysis with a varying number of PUMs available analyze the trade-off between PUM opening cost and improvement in accessibility to provide important managerial insights.

title: Socially Informed Supply Chain Design and Planning: Integrating Optimization and Social Life Cycle Assessment
affiliations: CEG-IST, Instituto Superior Técnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Centre for Management Studies of Instituto Superior Técnico (CEGIST), CEG - IST, University of Lisbon and University of Lisbon - Instituto Superior Técnico

detail.title: Socially Informed Supply Chain Design and Planning: Integrating Optimization and Social Life Cycle Assessment
detail.abstract: Supply chain design requires decision-support approaches that account not only for economic performance but also for social outcomes across the network. However, social considerations remain difficult to implement in strategic design decisions, particularly when both downstream equity concerns and upstream social risk exposure must be considered. This paper proposes a decision-support framework that integrates multi-objective supply chain optimization with social life cycle assessment to support socially informed supply chain design and planning. The framework jointly considers economic performance and equity in access, while evaluating social risk exposure under two complementary scopes: direct and global. The approach is illustrated through a meningitis vaccine supply chain case study. Results show that prioritizing equity in access relocates production closer to high-burden disease regions and substantially improves equity with only a limited reduction in economic performance, but also increases upstream social risk exposure. The dual-scope assessment further reveals that direct and global analyses identify different social issues and hotspots, leading to different supply chain mitigation and redesign priorities. These findings show the value of integrating optimization and social assessment in a common decision-support structure for supply chains.

title: AI-Enabled Quantum Acceleration: Distinguishing Co-Location from a Development-Rate Effect

detail.title: AI-Enabled Quantum Acceleration: Distinguishing Co-Location from a Development-Rate Effect

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Most assessments treat artificial intelligence and quantum computing as separate technology trajectories. This paper proposes a sharper, more testable proposition: that artificial intelligence is already acting on the rate at which quantum computing advances. It introduces the AI-Enabled Quantum Acceleration framework, a method for assessing whether artificial intelligence is compressing the quantum computing timeline rather than merely developing alongside it. The framework's central device is the distinction between co-location, in which two technologies advance independently, and acceleration, in which one measurably influences the development rate of the other. It identifies three channels through which acceleration would operate-hardware operation, algorithm optimization, and research acceleration-and specifies, for each, the evidence that would confirm it and the evidence that would disconfirm it. The framework is presented as a measurement structure populated with indicative evidence, not a claim of established causation. Applied to developments through mid-2026, it finds confirmed, baseline-relative evidence in hardware operation and algorithm optimization, while the research-acceleration channel shows no publicly attributable artificial-intelligence effect-a finding reached by refusing to count a rapid but conventionally attributed research result as acceleration. The contribution is a reusable diagnostic that separates genuine development-rate effects from coincidental simultaneity, giving analysts, investors, and policymakers a disciplined way to judge whether prevailing quantum timelines understate the influence of an adjacent, faster-moving technology.

reference: Euricse Working Papers No. 139|26
title: ESG Implementation and Governance Boundaries in Cooperatives: A Cross-Sector Managerial Perspective
affiliations: and Centre for Socio-Eco-Nomic Development

detail.title: ESG Implementation and Governance Boundaries in Cooperatives: A Cross-Sector Managerial Perspective

publicationDetails.journalName: Euricse Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Cooperatives are frequently presumed to align with sustainability due to their democratic governance and community focus, yet empirical evidence on their implementation of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) standards remains fragmented. This article analyzes ESG practices across six cooperative sectors—agriculture, finance, housing, consumer/retail, utilities, and worker/platform cooperatives—using comparative document analysis, sectoral case studies, and emerging federation guidelines. We introduce the cooperative boundary of responsibility to examine how ESG and Decent Work obligations extend beyond member-owners to employees, contractors, seasonal laborers, and platform workers. Findings reveal that while cooperatives excel in democratic governance and community-oriented social metrics, ESG adoption varies significantly by sector. Performance weakens where labor relations diverge from membership structures, particularly in outsourced, seasonal, or digitally mediated work. Environmental reporting is inconsistent, with gaps in accountability for non-member workers. For example, agricultural cooperatives often lack robust environmental metrics, while platform cooperatives struggle to ensure fair wages and protections for gig workers.

By synthesizing cross-sector evidence, this study advances debates on cooperative governance by demonstrating how institutional design, labor models, and sectoral constraints shape ESG outcomes. It highlights the tension between cooperatives’ member-centric ethos and the broader sustainability expectations of global supply chains, regulatory frameworks, and consumer demands. The article concludes with actionable recommendations: (i) strengthening ESG capabilities through federation-led training and capacity-building initiatives; (ii) standardizing reporting frameworks to address sectoral disparities and improve transparency, and (iii) reconciling cooperative identity with global sustainability expectations, particularly for non-member labor. The analysis underscores the need for policy and managerial interventions to close responsibility gaps and uphold ESG commitments across cooperative ecosystems. By addressing these challenges, cooperatives can better align their operations with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and reinforce their role as drivers of inclusive, sustainable development.

title: Last-Mile Advisory Services and Smallholder Productivity: Evidence from the Philippines
affiliations: and Emory University - Goizueta Business School

detail.title: Last-Mile Advisory Services and Smallholder Productivity: Evidence from the Philippines
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Smallholder farms in developing countries provide livelihoods to millions of the world's poorest and persistently operate below their potential productivity levels. Governments and supply chain firms have invested heavily in research, training, and advisory programs to improve smallholder productivity, yet these efforts often face severe operational challenges related to geographic dispersion, limited agent capacity, travel costs, and uneven service access. We study agricultural extension systems as a service delivery and operations problem, examining whether physical access to local extension facilities improves farm productivity and practice adoption, and exploring the mechanisms through which proximity affects advisory effectiveness. 

Methodology/results: We combine proprietary survey data from 1,480 Philippine smallholder coconut farms with environmental and institutional data, and exploit plausibly exogenous variation in extension office locations. Farms located within 10 kilometers of an extension office exhibit 20–26\% higher yields, with estimates remaining stable across extensive controls, robustness checks and  adjustments for office placement propensity. Surprisingly, proximity is not associated with broad increases in adoption of recommended practices. Instead, exploratory analyses suggest that nearby farms disproportionately adopt a small subset of higher-return practices and implement them more effectively. This suggests that extension agents translate generalized recommendations into locally feasible practices under resource and implementation constraints. 

Managerial implications: Our findings highlight physical access as an important operational lever in agricultural advisory systems. Despite substantial investment in extension and advisory programs, facility allocation decisions are often driven by administrative or institutional considerations rather than service accessibility. Projections based on our data suggest that simple data-driven facility reallocation rules can substantially expand service coverage and generate productivity gains comparable to costly capacity expansion. More broadly, our results suggest that advisory effectiveness depends not only on transmitting codified recommendations, but also on enabling repeated, context-specific interactions involving tacit implementation support, with implications for the design of advisory systems, digital substitutes, and technology dissemination programs for small, under-resourced firms.

title: Bridging the Commercialization Gap in 3D-Printed Lower-Limb Prosthetics: A Lab-to-Market Framework

detail.title: Bridging the Commercialization Gap in 3D-Printed Lower-Limb Prosthetics: A Lab-to-Market Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a systematic literature review and does not involve human participants or animal research; therefore, ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) has significantly reduced costs and lead times in upper-limb prosthetics; however, load-bearing lower-limb prostheses face ongoing challenges in clinical adoption. The widespread use of 3Dprinted transtibial and transfemoral sockets is hindered by two primary factors: the structural limitations of single-material polymers under dynamic ground reaction forces and the reliance on traditional, labor-intensive plaster-casting workflows. This paper systematically reviews the mechanical and operational limitations of current 3D-printed prosthetic interfaces and proposes an integrated digital manufacturing framework. Mechanical evaluations from the literature demonstrate that while standard fused deposition modeling (FDM) polymers frequently fail below the ISO 10328 ultimate load standard of 3840 N [11], structural parity with traditional laminated composites can be achieved through finite element analysis (FEA) guided topology optimization, hybrid multimaterial architectures (PA12/TPU) [10], and cement-based post-processing reinforcements [1]. Furthermore, to reduce the subjectivity of manual fabrication, this paper outlines a digital pipeline. By combining artificial intelligence (AI) optical scanning for automated geometric design [13] with dynamic pressure mapping [12] to generate zero Poisson's ratio metamaterial lattices, studies indicate that peak interface pressures can be significantly reduced [3]. Ultimately, scaling advanced prosthetics in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) [15] requires transitioning from decentralized standalone hardware to a closed-loop digital supply chain.

reference: Euricse Working Papers No. 141|26
title: Cooperatives in the Twin Transition: Multistakeholder Governance, Technology Adoption and Risk of Strategic Failure
affiliations: European Research Institute on Cooperative & Social Enterprises (EURICSE), European Research Institute on Cooperative & Social Enterprises (EURICSE) and Universitas Mercatorum

detail.title: Cooperatives in the Twin Transition: Multistakeholder Governance, Technology Adoption and Risk of Strategic Failure

publicationDetails.journalName: Euricse Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the adoption of digital and green technologies among industrial cooperatives in the context of the twin transition. Despite growing policy attention, limited empirical evidence exists on how cooperatives are facing the twin transition. We analyse the determinants of adoption of 15 core technologies identified by the European Union, focusing on multistakeholder governance, managerial perceptions, and structural characteristics. Using original survey data from 61 cooperatives in North-Eastern Italy, we estimate a logit model with cross-sectional data. Results indicate that multistakeholder governance increases the probability of technology adoption and moderates the effect of managerial perceptions, mitigating the risk of strategic failure. Managerial perceptions are also found to be significant predictors of adoption. These findings highlight the role of governance openness and provide new empirical evidence on how governance models shape the implementation of the twin transition within cooperatives.

title: Wealth Inequality and Health Inequality among Older Adults in Luxembourg

detail.title: Wealth Inequality and Health Inequality among Older Adults in Luxembourg

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on a secondary analysis of de-identified data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Ethical approval for SHARE was obtained by the SHARE project in accordance with applicable national and international ethical standards, and all participants provided informed consent. No additional ethical approval was required for this secondary analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This study is not a clinical trial.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between wealth inequality and health inequality among adults aged 50 and over in Luxembourg using longitudinal data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), Waves 5-9 (2013-2022). Drawing on the social determinants of health perspective and cumulative disadvantage theory, the analysis investigates whether differences in accumulated wealth are associated with variations in self-rated health, chronic conditions, and depressive symptoms. Using descriptive analyses, wealth-group trend analysis, and panel fixed-effects models, the study examines the persistence and evolution of health disparities across wealth groups over time. By focusing on Luxembourg, a highly developed welfare state, the study contributes to the literature on healthy ageing and highlights the continued relevance of socioeconomic inequalities for health and well-being in later life. The results provide evidence of a significant wealth-related disparity in self-rated health, while evidence for chronic conditions and depressive symptoms is comparatively weaker.

title: The Betul Anomaly: Weaving Nutrition Security Through Agro-forestry in Madhya Pradesh

detail.title: The Betul Anomaly: Weaving Nutrition Security Through Agro-forestry in Madhya Pradesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The work acknowledges the support of IIFM Bhopal. The paper is presented at IIM Raipur conference. The inputs and discussion were useful.

detail.abstract: This case study addresses the persistent public health crisis of malnutrition in Madhya Pradesh , where high rates of childhood stunting (35.7%) , wasting (19%) , and rampant anemia (67.2% in children) persist despite decades of interventions. It identifies a core "convergence conundrum" where existing programs, like the Public Distribution System (PDS) and Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) , successfully provide food security (calories via cereals) but fail to ensure nutrition security (access to a diverse diet). This leaves families trapped in a cycle of monotonous, nutrient-poor meals. To break this impasse, the case explores a solution proposed by NABARD, aligned with NITI Aayog's G.R.O.W. initiative : empowering small farmers to cultivate diverse, nutrient-rich foods on their own land through integrated agro-forestry. It details specific strategies, such as the "Homestead Agri-Horti-Forestry Model" ('Poshan Vatika Plus') , which combines millets , fruit trees , kitchen gardens, and small livestock like poultry to directly improve household diets. The case follows the implementation of the "Sampoorn Poshan" pilot in Betul district , detailing its on-ground challenges (e.g., farmer skepticism, regulatory permits) and solutions, like reimagining Anganwadi workers as 'Poshan Preraks'. After two years, the pilot demonstrated success, significantly increasing household dietary diversity and reducing anemia. The case concludes with the central dilemma: how to scale this resource-intensive pilot into a sustainable, financially viable, and administratively feasible statewide program for Madhya Pradesh's remaining 51 districts.

reference: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2604
title: Macroprudential FX Regulations and Small Firms: Unintended Consequences for Credit Growth
affiliations: Banco de España

detail.title: Macroprudential FX Regulations and Small Firms: Unintended Consequences for Credit Growth

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2604
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Macroprudential FX regulations aim to reduce systemic currency-mismatch risks, yet their distributional effects on firms’ access to credit remain poorly understood. This paper studies Peru’s 2014 dedollarization policy, which sharply increased reserve requirements on banks’ foreign-currency liabilities in proportion to their dollar lending to nontradable firms. Exploiting cross-sectional variation in banks’ exposure and using administrative loan-level data covering the universe of firms, I find that moving from the median to the 75th percentile of exposure reduces growth in total new loans by roughly 10 percentage points for micro and small firms, with no significant effects for medium or large firms. Larger firms absorb the shock by reallocating borrowing across banks and into local currency credit, whereas micro firms experience sharp declines in both dollar and total credit, higher borrowing costs, and modest employment losses. The results highlight a trade-off between macroprudential objectives and credit access for small firms.

reference: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper No. 861
title: Monetary Policy in the Euro Area, when Philips Curves ... Are Curves
affiliations: University of Oxford, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Vienna University of Technology, Oesterreichische Nationalbank (OeNB) and CMAP, Ecole polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris

detail.title: Monetary Policy in the Euro Area, when Philips Curves ... Are Curves

publicationDetails.detailsText: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper No. 861
publicationDetails.journalName: De Nederlandsche Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We study monetary policy in an environment where price and wage Phillips curves exhibit true curvature. To this end, we propose a New Keynesian model with endogenous adjustment of price and wage setting frequencies, moving beyond the quasi-linear structure of standard nonlinear NK Phillips curves. Using euro area data from 1999Q1 to 2024Q4, we estimate and simulate the non-linear model, analyzing the recent inflation surge and the implications of state-dependent prices and wages for monetary policy. Unlike conventional models, our framework does not attribute inflation dynamics primarily to exogenous supply shocks. Instead, the impact of shocks is asymmetric and depends on their timing, size, and the business cycle. Consequently, the inflation–output stabilization trade-off is state-dependent: monetary policy is more effective in curbing inflation, and supply shocks have larger effects during periods of high inflation.

title: Thou Shalt Question: What Judaism Has Always Known About Critical Thinking Before It Became a Crisis
affiliations: City University of New York (CUNY) - Koppelman School of Business

detail.title: Thou Shalt Question: What Judaism Has Always Known About Critical Thinking Before It Became a Crisis
detail.abstract: The Talmud records a teaching in which six questions await every soul before the Heavenly Court after death, spanning honest business conduct, dedicated Torah study, sharp dialectical reasoning, and the capacity to generate original understanding from accumulated knowledge. This paper argues that critical thinking occupies a privileged and non-negotiable place within that framework, appearing not as a modern virtue retrofitted onto ancient texts but as an explicit divine expectation embedded in the tradition itself. The paper traces this commitment across the full arc of the Jewish intellectual tradition. Biblical narrative models it through the deliberate moral fallibility of its greatest leaders. The prophetic tradition extends it by vindicating figures who confront divine justice directly while rebuking those who defend received certainty without honest inquiry. Talmudic discourse institutionalizes it through the bar plugta relationship, the preservation of minority opinions, and narratives such as the Oven of Akhnai in which God Himself is overruled and responds with laughter. In an era that systematically punishes dissent, this tradition offers an enduring countermodel: one in which disagreement is sacred, intellectual adversaries are valued, and the courage to ask difficult questions is treated not as a threat to faith but as its fullest expression.

title: Education is Health: An Integrated Cross-Sectoral Cost-Effectiveness Framework for Education Interventions Targeting Vulnerable Adolescent Girls in LMICs

detail.abstract: Applying a novel cross-sectoral cost-effectiveness analysis of education-related interventions on adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs), we find traditional methods focused narrowly on economic benefits dramatically underestimate social returns, with health and social outcomes accounting for approximately 59% of total impacts. This siloed perspective mirrors the fragmented approach to budgeting and investment common across line ministries and donor strategies organized by sector, and may be particularly ill-suited to the lived experience of AGYW, for whom education and life choices-including marriage and sexual partnership-carry simultaneously economic, health, and social consequences. This study develops and applies an integrated cross-sectoral cost-effectiveness framework that captures the full range of returns to education-linked interventions for AGYW in LMICs, channeling the perspective of an archetypical ministry of finance and planning. Drawing on a structured evidence review, we model health, social, and economic outcomes using a welfare-based valuation approach that applies explicit moral weights to enable comparison across outcome domains. Using a cash benchmarking approach, we estimate the median cost-effectiveness of interventions analyzed was approximately 50% above a benchmark for high-performing unconditional cash transfers. These findings demonstrate the importance of integrating outcome measures and investment strategies across sectors for effective policy prioritization. The framework presented can be adapted beyond the specific use case shown, using local risk profiles, costs, and valuation assumptions, to support cross-sectoral planning across health, education, and finance ministries.

title: An Extended Score-Driven Dynamic Factor Model: Constructing Composite Indices in Turbulent Times
affiliations: , Erasmus University Rotterdam - Erasmus School of Economics - Econometric Institute and Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE)

detail.title: An Extended Score-Driven Dynamic Factor Model: Constructing Composite Indices in Turbulent Times
detail.abstract: We propose an extended score-driven (ESD) dynamic factor model (DFM) that can accommodate non-Gaussian innovations, nonlinear factor dynamics, and timevarying volatility. The main novelty of our model is a state equation that includes both lagged and contemporaneous scores, implying that factors are not predetermined. We show that this novel model nests both the classic (parameter-driven) state-space DFM as well as the more recent score-driven DFM, bridging the gap between these two model classes. Empirically, our ESD-DFM proves useful for working with (post-)COVID-19-era observations, which have posed substantial challenges for macroeconomic modeling. For instance, while the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia suspended publication of its leading index due to pandemic-related anomalies, our model remains robust to such extreme observations and enables reliable computation of the index. We further apply the ESD-DFM to The Conference Board's (TCB's) Coincident and Leading Economic Indices (CEI and LEI). When indices are constructed from the estimated factors, the unprecedented divergence between TCB's CEI and LEI observed during the post-pandemic period disappears: although the reconstructed LEI declines in 2022, it resumes an upward trajectory from the second half of 2023 through the end of 2025.

title: Optimal Pay-for-Performance Contracts in Healthcare Co-Production under Asymmetric Information
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management and

detail.title: Optimal Pay-for-Performance Contracts in Healthcare Co-Production under Asymmetric Information
