detail.abstract: This paper argues that any long-term analysis of Israel's future political economy must distinguish between diplomatic normalization, commercial cooperation, and social legitimacy. Stephen I. Ternyik's proposal usefully connects Israeli domestic polarization, regional geoeconomics, and global power transition, but its "Regional Integration and Inclusive Growth" scenario risks overestimating elite-level normalization while underestimating durable cultural, political, religious, historical, and moral resistance to Israel among surrounding societies. The central claim is not that Israel cannot sign agreements or build selective economic corridors. It is that integration without popular legitimacy remains structurally fragile. Saudi Arabia is the decisive Gulf actor, and its normalization position is constrained not only by diplomacy but also by Arab public opinion, the Palestinian question, and the post-Gaza legitimacy crisis. The paper proposes a fourth scenario: "Transactional Integration Under Legitimacy Deficit," in which technology, energy, and Gulf investment proceed selectively but remain vulnerable to shocks from Palestine, Gaza, Jerusalem, Western youth politics, and Israel's declining moral image.

title: Beyond One Shot: Contracting for Sequential Trials
affiliations: Imperial College Business School,  and NYU Shanghai

detail.title: Beyond One Shot: Contracting for Sequential Trials
detail.abstract: We study contract design in a setting where an agent can adaptively choose among several costly actions and resample the same action, while the principal observes only the final reported outcome. Given a contract, the agent's best response has a reservation-value structure. Unlike Weitzman's classic search problem, however, these reservation values are stage-dependent because the agent's willingness to continue depends on how many trials remain. Our main result is that a calibrated debt contract, which pays the agent only for outcomes above a face value set at the highest Weitzman index, nearly solves this dynamic incentive problem. Its payoff loss relative to the second best decays exponentially in the trial cap. In the infinite-trial benchmark, the same contract is exactly optimal: it implements the first-best value and leaves the agent with zero expected rent. We also show that more experimentation opportunities need not benefit either party. Increasing the trial cap can expand the agent's hidden continuation opportunities enough that the re-optimized second-best contract may simultaneously lower both the principal's and the agent's equilibrium payoffs. Finally, we extend the analysis to time-contingent payments, correlated sampling, and multiple agents, where our main insight about the asymptotic optimality of a calibrated debt contract still holds.

title: Tail Risk Analysis of NIFTY50 Stocks Using the Bates Jump-Diffusion Model

detail.title: Tail Risk Analysis of NIFTY50 Stocks Using the Bates Jump-Diffusion Model
detail.abstract: This paper provides an exhaustive analysis of tail risk using the Bates stochastic volatility with jumps model across all NIFTY50 index constituents. We calibrate the Bates parameters to option chains via the Carr-Madan FFT method, quantify the volatility smirk, and stress-test a pairs-trading strategy under jump-diffusion scenarios. An adaptive risk management mechanism based on latent variance is shown to mitigate losses. Results are homogeneous across the index: mean reversion speed κ = 2.5, jump intensity λ = 0.12, base Sharpe ratio of 1.45, stress drawdown of-8.2%, and a recovery period of 12 days. The study proves that Bates-based stress testing is critical for surviving tail events in the Indian equity market.

title: Coaching Leadership Theory (CLT): A Generative Mechanism Framework for Navigating the Evaluation-Development Paradox in Managerial Coaching

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Managerial coaching occupies a structurally contradictory position in contemporary organizations: managers are simultaneously responsible for evaluating and developing the same employees, creating conditions under which developmental authenticity is systematically threatened. Existing theoretical frameworksincluding Leader-Member Exchange, empowering leadership, and psychological safety modelsaddress adjacent concerns but do not theorize this dual-role paradox at the level of causal mechanism. This article introduces Coaching Leadership Theory (CLT), a Critical Realist, meso-level theoretical framework that reframes managerial coaching as a structural practice rather than a behavioral skill repertoire. CLT identifies Ethical Role Boundaries (ERB) as the central generative mechanism through which Coaching Mindset becomes capable of enabling genuine developmental dialogue and collaborative performance management, ultimately producing Human Capability Development in Sen's capability terms. Rather than claiming to resolve the evaluation-development paradox which would be theoretically indefensible given its structural roots-CLT offers a framework for navigating and partially containing it through explicitly theorized mechanisms, failure modes, and boundary conditions. A distinctive contribution of CLT is the construct of Boundary Performance: the enacted appearance of ethical boundary maintenance without genuine developmental intent. This failure mode is more consequential than outright boundary collapse because it operates through coaching competence, resists detection, and produces retroactive recontextualization of prior disclosures as potentially exploitative. Five theoretically grounded propositions are advanced, each with explicit falsification conditions and boundary specifications consistent with Critical Realist methodology.

title: Voting Rules and the Price of Peace
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Faculty of Law

detail.title: Voting Rules and the Price of Peace
detail.abstract: In a conflicted controlling-shareholder transaction (e.g., a freeze-out merger), the controller sits on both sides, and corporate law often relies on a vote of the minority to screen out value-destroying deals. The conventional view holds that a tougher vote screens better. This intuition is incomplete. Raising the required margin works like raising the 'passing mark' on an exam: it relocates who games the threshold, since controllers just below the higher bar exaggerate to clear it. Nor does the vote settle the matter. A controller who over-sells a deal to win approval may have to pay again, later, to settle the litigation that over-selling invites. When the same threshold that approves a deal also governs its later ratification, a stricter rule raises two prices at once, the price of persuasion before the vote, and the price of peace after it. Our central result is that this second price can dominate, so that a tougher vote can lower misrepresentation, which can reverse the conventional prediction. Whether that helps minority investors then depends on how wasteful the litigation is and on the quality of the deterred deals, which clarifies when allowing a controller to satisfy one procedure instead of both leaves investors underprotected.

title: Judicial Decisions under Pressure: Evidence from the Chinese Judiciary

detail.title: Judicial Decisions under Pressure: Evidence from the Chinese Judiciary
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether caseload pressure changes appellate decision-making. Using 3.3 million Chinese civil appellate decisions from 2013 to 2021, I link appellate outcomes to judge-level workload and written reasoning. I instrument a presiding judge's caseload with the leave-one-out workload of other presiding judges in the same court and month. A doubling of appellate caseload increases the probability that the appellate court upholds the first-instance judgment by about 0.7 percentage points. Heavier caseloads also reduce legal citations and increase textual similarity between first-and second-instance reasoning. The results show that court congestion changes not only how quickly courts process disputes, but also how intensively appellate judges review lower-court decisions.

title: Analyst Labor Market Allocation and Price Efficiency: A Structural Approach
affiliations: Saïd Business School, University of Oxford and University of Oxford - Said Business School

detail.title: Analyst Labor Market Allocation and Price Efficiency: A Structural Approach
detail.abstract: We study how the labor-market allocation of financial analysts affects stock price efficiency. Using brokerage mergers and senior analyst retirements as quasi-natural experiments, we document causal effects of brokerage platform matching and team composition on analyst forecast informativeness. However, analyst job mobility remains low and is declining over time, which may undermine the quality of matching. To quantify the impact of the analyst labor market on price efficiency, we develop and estimate a structural model that unifies forward-looking broker choice subject to idiosyncratic preferences and mobility costs, Nash-in-Nash bargaining under oligopolistic competition, and heterogeneous analyst-broker matching. Our results suggest that labor-market frictions limit price efficiency primarily by impeding analyst mobility toward mid- and lower-tier brokers that rely more heavily on high-quality analyst teams. Reducing job-switching costs to one tenth of their estimated level, for example, raises analysts' aggregate price impact by 8.25%.

title: Measuring Long-Term Program Impacts with Administrative Data: Evidence from Big Brothers Big Sisters
affiliations: Georgia State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Measuring Long-Term Program Impacts with Administrative Data: Evidence from Big Brothers Big Sisters
detail.abstract: Thousands of youth-serving nonprofits maintain detailed records on program applicants, participants, and those who applied but did not receive services-yet these data are rarely linked to long-run outcomes or used for rigorous performance measurement. This paper demonstrates how such records can be transformed into a practical evaluation infrastructure. Drawing on administrative data from a large Big Brothers Big Sisters affiliate linked to U.S. tax records, I compare long-run outcomes for youth matched with a mentor to those who applied but were not matched. The resulting estimates are observational and should be interpreted with appropriate caution, but they offer suggestive evidence that mentored youth are approximately 7 percentage points more likely to attend college and earn roughly 19% more in early adulthood. A unique feature of this setting is that long-run experimental evidence is also available from a companion randomized evaluation of the same program, allowing the observational approach to be benchmarked against randomized evidence; the two sets of estimates broadly align. More broadly, the paper illustrates a path from episodic program evaluations toward ongoing, data-driven performance measurement.

title: TikTok, Instagram, and the "Fourth Party": The Impact of Technical Design on Personal Content Moderation
affiliations: Stanford University, Law School

detail.title: TikTok, Instagram, and the "Fourth Party": The Impact of Technical Design on Personal Content Moderation

publicationDetails.journalName: Stanford Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ohio State Journal On Dispute Resolution 2025

detail.abstract: As policymakers debate Section 230, children's online safety, and social media regulation, increasing attention has shifted from online content to the design of digital platforms. This article examines how the personal content moderation systems of TikTok and Instagram shape user experiences through interface design, reporting tools, appeals processes, and platform governance. Drawing on dispute system design, it introduces the concept of the "fourth party" to explain how technical design influences online disputes and redistributes power between platforms and users. The article argues that platform design is analytically distinct from protected speech and should therefore be evaluated separately from content moderation under the First Amendment. By reframing content moderation as a problem of product and interface design rather than speech alone, the article offers a framework for platform accountability, consumer protection, and online safety that preserves free expression while addressing the harms of modern social media.

title: Digital Asset Market Structure at a Regulatory Crossroads: Three Post-CLARITY Act Scenarios
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Digital Asset Market Structure at a Regulatory Crossroads: Three Post-CLARITY Act Scenarios
detail.abstract: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act (CLARITY Act) represents one of the most consequential U.S. legislative efforts to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework for digital assets. As the bill advances through the legislative process, uncertainty surrounding its ultimate enactment remains significant. Rather than focusing on a binary prediction of passage or failure, this paper examines the market-structure implications of three plausible regulatory outcomes. Using a scenario-planning framework, the analysis explores how stablecoins, tokenized commercial bank deposits, decentralized finance (DeFi), and base-layer crypto commodities may evolve under alternative legislative and regulatory paths. The scenarios recognize that federal agencies, courts, financial institutions, and digital asset firms are already adapting their strategies in anticipation of divergent policy environments. Drawing on legislative records, regulatory filings, industry announcements, and legal scholarship, the paper identifies the principal opportunities, risks, and structural shifts associated with each scenario and assesses their implications for the future development of U.S. digital asset markets.

title: Market Reactions to Complex Language in Corporate News
affiliations: , University of East Anglia (UEA) - Norwich Business School, University of Notre Dame  and University of East Anglia (UEA) - Norwich Business School

detail.title: Market Reactions to Complex Language in Corporate News
detail.abstract: We investigate how language complexity of firm-specific news affects financial markets. We assess complexity in a new way using dependency distance, a widely-used psycholinguistic measure of cognitive load based on average syntactic distance between related words. An increase in language complexity is associated with significant shifts in volatility and trading volume. Using theories of disagreement, we argue that complex language fosters opposing views among investors, who trade more. Positive news written in complex language is incorporated into prices more slowly, producing short-run return continuation and significant risk-adjusted returns. Our paper shows that linguistic complexity reflects information density, not deliberate obfuscation.

title: The Asymmetric Entropy of Fiat Reserve Accumulation: Sovereign Vulnerability, Algorithmic Monopolies, and the Case for Real-Asset-Backed Settlement (SVWORLD Standard 73.5 v2

detail.title: The Asymmetric Entropy of Fiat Reserve Accumulation: Sovereign Vulnerability, Algorithmic Monopolies, and the Case for Real-Asset-Backed Settlement (SVWORLD Standard 73.5 v2
detail.abstract: This paper exposes two interlocking structural pathologies in the modern financial architecture: the accumulation of unbacked foreign fiat reserves by sovereign nations, and the outsourcing of central bank risk management to proprietary algorithmic monopolies. Using the SVWORLD STANDARD 73.5 v2.0 methodology, we demonstrate that major reserve currencies are backed by less than 1.5% real assets, while all G7 reserve issuers operate in a state of deep thermodynamic insolvency. We introduce the concept of "implicit seigniorage" to quantify the hidden tax levied on the Global South, and apply the Foreign Exchange Risk (FXR) multiplier to prove that emerging markets in Africa, Asia, and Latin America suffer a 22% to 66% structural penalty simply for holding foreign-currency debt. Furthermore, we show that central banks relying on platforms like BlackRock's Aladdin face a systemic erosion of monetary sovereignty due to algorithmic herding and concentration risk. The methodology presented here has been empirically validated in 14 peer-reviewed SSRN papers (Author ID: 10594317) with over 1,400 abstract views and 258 downloads, constituting a comprehensive forensic audit of the global financial system. We propose Sovereign Digital Assets (SDA) as the only mathematically sound alternative to restore global financial stability. The full 13-step calculation protocol is available to qualified institutional counterparties under mutual NDA.

title: Fatherhood Engagement Capacity: A Public Health Infrastructure Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Fatherhood Engagement Capacity: A Public Health Infrastructure Framework

The author is employed as a Community Health Worker and Fatherhood Engagement Specialist at Healthy Start Inc. in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and serves in a voluntary capacity with the Fatherhood Collaborative Council of Western Pennsylvania. All work was conducted as part of the author's independent scholarly development alongside his professional practice in community health and fatherhood engagement.

detail.abstract:
Public health has spent decades proving that fathers matter. It has not yet built systems that act like they do.

This paper argues that the gap between what the evidence shows and what systems are designed to do is not an awareness problem; it is a design problem. Maternal and child health was built around a maternal-infant dyad, and fathers were added to that architecture as optional participants rather than as structurally integrated contributors to health production. The result is fatherhood work that depends on individual champions, episodic funding, and program-by-program discretion rather than on durable organizational capacity.

To address this, the paper introduces the concept of fatherhood engagement capacity — the organized ability of a public health system to identify, engage, support, document, refer, measure, and sustain fathers and father figures as contributors to maternal, infant, family, and community health. Drawing on a cross-disciplinary synthesis spanning public health, developmental psychology, family science, epidemiology, men's health, and sociology, the paper identifies seven fatherhood health pathways and proposes a ten-domain framework for building this capacity as a core public health function.

The central argument is that when fatherhood engagement capacity is deliberately designed, resourced, and maintained, it constitutes public health infrastructure — the foundational, organized conditions without which a health-producing function cannot reliably operate at scale. The paper distinguishes this infrastructure claim from prior advocacy for father inclusion and proposes that closing the gap requires a fundamental shift in how fatherhood engagement is conceptualized, measured, and financed within maternal and child health systems.

title: Flipping Out: Changing the Governing Law of Sovereign Debt Instruments
affiliations: Center for Contract and Economic Organization and University of Virginia School of Law

detail.title: Flipping Out: Changing the Governing Law of Sovereign Debt Instruments

publicationDetails.detailsText: Virginia Public Law and Legal Theory Research Paper (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: Lenders have begun to insist on the inclusion of provisions in sovereign debt contracts — Flip Clauses — that permit the lenders to change the governing law of the contract if they become alarmed at some future change in the chosen legal regime. Flip Clauses are not necessary to ensure that the parties choice of the governing law as it exists on the day the contract is signed will be respected. There is a more conventional contractual technique to achieve that objective — a so-called Freezing Clause. Jettisoning the choice of the law of New York or England for sovereign debt instruments exposes all parties to unnecessary risks.

title: Beetles with Ballooning Burdens: Pushing out Pre-IPO Compensation Costs until the RSU Reckoning
affiliations: Yale University - Law School

detail.title: Beetles with Ballooning Burdens: Pushing out Pre-IPO Compensation Costs until the RSU Reckoning

declarations.funderStatement: This research has been supported by the Oscar M. Ruebhausen Fund at Yale Law School.

detail.abstract:
This paper scrutinizes the stock-based compensation practices of pre-IPO unicorn firms in the United States - privately held firms that achieved a valuation of $1 billion or more in a venture capital-backed financing round. Using a hand-collected dataset of 91 unicorns that went public in the United States via an initial public offering (IPO) between 2014 and 2024, I find that unicorns often exploit accounting rules to omit sizable compensation expenses associated with their pre-IPO equity award activity from the financial performance reported in their IPO prospectus by deferring recognition of these expenses until their IPO.

When they went public, 60 out of the 91 unicorn firms in this study recognized, on average, $358 million in accumulated but deferred stock-based compensation expenses (inflation-adjusted) from pre-IPO equity award activity. Eight of these unicorns had deferred more than $1 billion in such stock-based compensation expenses until their IPO.

Accumulating but deferring stock-based compensation expenses of at least $107 million (adjusted for inflation) until the IPO is associated with a high risk of post-IPO stock price decline. I find that accumulated but deferred stock-based compensation expenses at or above this threshold are statistically associated with an 83% probability of decline following the release of financial results for the quarter in which the IPO occurred.

The stock market reacts negatively when these sizable stock-based compensation costs are first reported as part of operating expenses in the quarter of IPO occurrence. These expense deferral practices pose material risks for secondary market investors contemplating an investment in the now-public unicorn ahead of its earnings release for the IPO quarter, such as retail investors attracted to the perceived high-quality firm status associated with the unicorn label.

These concerning practices by pre-IPO unicorns, which typically involve the use of equity awards in the form of so-called double-trigger restricted stock units (RSUs), have proliferated over the study period and may implicate many more unicorns going public in the future. I find that these practices were routinely associated with unicorns that achieved high pre-money valuations when they went public. At their IPO, these unicorns commanded a median pre-money valuation of $11.4 billion (inflation-adjusted). There are currently at least 30 unicorns in the United States with post-money valuations in recent venture capital-backed financing rounds that equal or exceed $11 billion.

Nothing in my research indicates that future IPO candidates will, absent regulatory intervention, refrain from engaging in these expense deferral practices. I recommend significant improvements to often incomplete prospectus disclosures regarding these practices, which arguably do not comply with federal securities laws. Moreover, I recommend reform of the accounting rules that currently require private firms to defer the stock-based compensation expenses associated with their double-trigger equity award activity so as to address the RSU reckoning that typically follows the IPO.

title: Price Formation Without Communication: A Constructive Illustration of Mises and Hayek

detail.title: Price Formation Without Communication: A Constructive Illustration of Mises and Hayek

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by Ericsson, a telecommunications equipment manufacturer. The research concerns radio access network resource coordination mechanisms. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical economics paper involving no human subjects, patients, or participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by Ericsson.

detail.abstract: Mises (1920, 1949) established that monetary prices are the necessary instrument of economic calculation: they must be produced by a process, not collected from a register. Hayek (1945) argued that the price system achieves coordination among agents who need not possess each other's knowledge. This paper presents a formal mechanism that constructively illustrates both claims. In a hierarchy of autonomous components, where each component's quality is private, each selector observes only the outcome of its chosen path, and no explicit feedback crosses organisational boundaries, prices nonetheless form. The price signal is one bit per interaction: did my market share increase or decrease? This binary signal propagates without degradation through arbitrarily many levels of hierarchy. Under proportional redistribution of market share, prices converge to a unique interior equilibrium reflecting the quality differential between competing components. Each level of the hierarchy operates as an independent market on a thinned clock, producing correct aggregate allocation without any level possessing knowledge of any other. The mechanism uniformly dominates uninformed selection at every equilibrium: majority market share always flows to the better component. The mechanism's information constraints formalise claims familiar from Austrian price theory: the 1 necessity of a price-forming process for calculation, the subjectivity of value, and the dispersion of knowledge. The paper shows how these claims can be rendered in mechanism form, illustrating one institutional logic consistent with Austrian price theory.

title: Bayesian Stories: Turning Narratives into Evidence A Weight-of-Evidence Theory, with the Murder of Meredith Kercher
affiliations: Chess Ed and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Bayesian Stories: Turning Narratives into Evidence A Weight-of-Evidence Theory, with the Murder of Meredith Kercher
detail.abstract:
We develop a Bayesian theory of stories, a calculus for turning narratives into evidence. A story is a complete causal-temporal account of how events unfolded: formally, a root-tosink path through an event tree, the object a chain event graph compresses. A story earns evidential weight not from its internal coherence but from the probability it confers on what was actually found, weighed against its rivals; the weight of evidence for one story against a rival is the log-likelihood-ratio log P(E ⋆ | s 1)/P(E ⋆ | s 2) into the observed evidence E ⋆ , with their prior path-probabilities attached by Bayes. Coherence is not probability, and mistaking a vivid story for a likely one is the prosecutor's fallacy at the level of narrative. The grammar of stories is the chain event graph (Smith); the scoring rule is Good's weight of evidence; and the causal status of a story, a counterfactual claim, is read through Pearl's hierarchy and bounded by Tian-Pearl probabilities of causation. 
We stress-test the theory on the 2007 murder of Meredith Kercher and the exoneration of Amanda Knox and Raffaele Sollecito, a case that stacks three probabilistic errors: the prosecutor's fallacy on the DNA, neglect of the base rate, and a conditional-independence error in the much-cited "re-test the knife" argument. Grading the evidence in Good's decibans, modelling contamination as a latent common cause (a d-separation failure in Pearl's semantics, under which the act cannot be shown necessary), relating the construction to the Wigmore-chart, Bayesian-network and chain-event-graph comparison of Dawid et al. (2025), and quantifying the spurious weight a non-probative attribute such as race can inject, we weigh the burglary and sex-crime accounts as competing stories. The posterior never leaves the neighbourhood of its prior, where the Court of Cassation also landed, citing an "absolute lack of biological traces." The likelihood ratios are illustrative; the conclusion is structural and robust, and it is the theory's first demonstration: the story that earns the evidence is not the one that assigns high probability to the observations but the one of greatest relative weight (the largest Bayes factor against its rivals); that story is the lone intruder's. The quantity we report is that relative weight, a likelihood ratio and not a posterior: the corrected evidence favours the lone-intruder story over the group sex-crime story by roughly 30 to 50 decibans, a Bayes factor near 10 3 to 10 5 : 1. Whoever holds a strong prior on the sex-crime account keeps it; the decibans report only how far the evidence moves a prior, and they are illustrative, robust in sign and order of magnitude rather than exact.

title: Sunshades in Space Undertaking. A Cash-Flow-Contingent Framework for Financing a Global Public-Good Projects
affiliations: , Stiftelsen Fuglesang Space Center, HSA Söderqvist, Hexicon AB, Östra Järnvägsgatan and Stockholm School of Economics

detail.title: Sunshades in Space Undertaking. A Cash-Flow-Contingent Framework for Financing a Global Public-Good Projects
detail.abstract:
A liquidity flow (cash-flow) based method to finance and govern long-term development projects, FiGo, is suggested. FiGo is applied to a space-based SRM (Solar Radiation Modification) method for climate stabilization purposes, Planetary Sunshades at L1*.

This application of the method is a long-term undertaking and is referred to as SiSU (Sunshades in Space Undertaking). The SiSU objective is to develop the capability to reduce up to 1% of the infrared light from the Sun to Earth in order to, as part of a broader climate stabilization effort, stabilize the global temperature in line with the goals of the COP21 “Paris Agreement” (2015).

The global space economy has been forecasted to annually grow by 9 percent to $1.8 Trillion by 2035 [1] WEF and McKinsey & Company. Space: The $1.8 Trillion Opportunity for Global Economic Growth; 2024.

Space investments are typically long-term, and SiSU is based on active engagement in capturing, integrating and optimizing IP (Intellectual Property) returns from the space economy over approximately a 50-year time period. This makes it possible to repay non-public investments with returns, as well as to finance the undertaking as such.

The control structure separates strategic governance by an industrial foundation, financing by a holding company fully owned by the foundation, and operations in subsidiaries of the holding company of two types, IP generating and IP sales returns optimizing.

The financing returns are not reliant on actual deployment of the Sunshades, which removes the risk of profit-driven reasons for deployment overtaking the maturity of strategic, legal, ethical and multilateral approvals.

title: India’s Economic Crossroads: Growth, Inequality, Dependency, and the Road Ahead

detail.title: India’s Economic Crossroads: Growth, Inequality, Dependency, and the Road Ahead
detail.abstract:
India has re‑emerged as one of the world’s fastest‑growing large economies, yet persistent concerns about job quality, inequality, and strategic dependence raise doubts about how far headline growth translates into durable development.

This paper asks whether India can convert high growth into inclusive, job‑rich, and strategically resilient development in a frontier‑technology era defined by AI, semiconductors, digital public infrastructure, and advanced defence and data‑centre technologies.

The analysis documents that while real output and fiscal‑backed investment have risen strongly, labour reallocation into high‑productivity manufacturing and modern services remains incomplete, so growth has been output‑rich but only partially employment‑rich across most states.

Official consumption data show substantial poverty reduction, but inequality remains high and multi‑dimensional, with rising top‑end concentration and enduring gaps by state, caste, gender, and employment type.

External vulnerability is concentrated in oil, electronics, and advanced hardware and software inputs, even as digital public infrastructure and frontier‑tech sectors deepen.

The paper argues that India’s long‑run challenge is not growth per se but the political‑economy task of aligning structural transformation, capability‑building, and technology‑era industrial and social policy so that high growth yields broad‑based mobility, lower strategic dependence, and stronger, more even state capacity.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35386
title: Openness, Integration, and the International Monetary Order
affiliations: Boston University, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Renmin University of China and

detail.title: Openness, Integration, and the International Monetary Order

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper develops a calibrated general-equilibrium model to study how different configurations of trade and financial policy reshape the hierarchy of global currencies—and the U.S. dollar's position at its anchor. Currency safety and anchor status arise endogenously from each economy's 'effective size'—the weight its domestic shocks carry in setting world prices. Tariffs reduce this effective size on the goods side; capital controls do the same on the financial side. A unifying result emerges: The economy that maintains the deepest integration with the global trading network retains the largest safety premium and gains anchor status. We use this framework to evaluate the effects of three policy levers for Europe that affect the effective size of the euro: internal harmonization and enlargement, trade openness, and capital-account openness. The stakes are large: In our model, shifts in currencies' safety can redirect global capital flows and alter sovereign borrowing costs by hundreds of billions of dollars annually.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35387
title: GLP-1–Induced Weight Loss and the Female Obesity Penalty
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: GLP-1–Induced Weight Loss and the Female Obesity Penalty

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
GLP-1 medications generate large weight loss and may also alter social and economic outcomes. Using the Understanding America Study, I compare women starting GLP-1s for weight loss with matched women who would like to start a GLP-1 but have not. Single women’s marriage/cohabitation rates rise by 29 percentage points and employment among baseline non-employed women rises 27 percentage points after six or more quarters. Existing partnerships do not dissolve, and already-employed women show no upward job mobility. The pattern suggests that part of the female obesity penalty operates at new-match formation rather than only through health or incumbent productivity.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35383
title: Unilateral-Veto Mechanisms
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, Duke University and Harvard University

detail.title: Unilateral-Veto Mechanisms

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Unilateral vetoes, in which an agent takes an action that restricts the set of possible outcomes for themselves independent of what other agents do, are a frequently used tool in real-world approaches to multi-dimensional screening. We study how this tool works in a class of task-allocation problems. We characterize obvious strategy-proofness of unilateral-veto mechanisms, yielding structural insights into how veto rights shape incentives: obviously strategy-proof mechanisms consist of diverse menus of narrowly defined rights. We then examine the potential of this simple class of mechanisms as a practical market-design tool and provide empirical evidence of their efficacy in two applications.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35385
title: The Fragility of Semi-Liquid Private Credit Funds
affiliations: Drexel University, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School - Finance Department  and

detail.title: The Fragility of Semi-Liquid Private Credit Funds

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study fragility in semi-liquid private credit funds, which have expanded rapidly and now manage over $300 billion in assets. These funds perform liquidity transformation by holding far more illiquid loans than traditional loan mutual funds while allowing investors to redeem at NAV through quarterly repurchase offers, typically capped at 5% of shares outstanding. We show that cash buffers and contractual loan repayments are insufficient to fund repeated 5% quarterly redemptions; inflows decline precisely when outflows rise; and net outflows are met with sales of illiquid loans, external borrowing, and delayed payments through repurchases payable. As a result, strategic complementarity arises, because redemptions impose liquidation and leverage costs on the remaining investors. We show that loan liquidation, leverage increase, and NAV inflation play an important role in amplifying the current episodes of run-like redemptions. Overall, our evidence suggests that quarterly gates and redemption caps do not eliminate run-like fragility in semi-liquid private credit funds, raising cautions about expanding retail access to private credit markets.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35389
title: International Risk-Sharing in a Fragmented World
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, Kiel Institute for the World Economy, University of Oxford and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: International Risk-Sharing in a Fragmented World

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper studies how geopolitical risk shapes financial fragmentation and international risk-sharing, using bilateral official lending data from 1910 to 2024. We document that when geopolitical risk is high, bilateral lending increasingly follows geopolitical alignment. Because geopolitically aligned countries experience more synchronized shocks, this fragmentation limits the effectiveness of international risk-sharing. To rationalize these patterns, we introduce geopolitical considerations into a limited-commitment model of sovereign borrowing. The model shows that, even with non-discriminatory default, higher geopolitical tensions redirect international lending toward allied countries and weaken risk-sharing.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35390
title: Pricing and Production Without the Invisible Hand
affiliations: Yale University,  and Princeton University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Pricing and Production Without the Invisible Hand

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Modern theories of the business cycle do not allow for the simultaneous rational choice of both prices and quantities, instead assuming that an “invisible hand” determines one of these variables to clear markets. In this paper, we develop a macroeconomic model in which both prices and quantities are chosen optimally by firms and exchange is both voluntary and efficient. As a consequence, individual markets will generically be in Walrasian disequilibrium: either slack (over-supplied) or rationed (under-supplied). The absence of market clearing changes pricing and production in qualitatively important ways: markups are governed by the probability of rationing rather than the elasticity of demand, and higher uncertainty reduces production and increases markups. Marrying the Old and New Keynesian traditions, we study general Walrasian disequilibrium with rational expectations and optimal firm decisions. On a technical level, we characterize cross-market spillovers arising from rationed demand with differentiated goods, overcoming the standard combinatorial problem that arises when studying multi-market disequilibrium. Unlike in New Keynesian economies, monetary shocks propagate by reducing product-market slack, raising aggregate labor productivity and consumption with muted effects on employment, while uncertainty shocks act as stagflationary cost-push shocks.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35391
title: Government Funding Costs Under Financial Repression
affiliations: London Business School, London Business School, Stanford University and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Government Funding Costs Under Financial Repression

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study the equilibrium effects of financial repression on government funding costs in an endowment economy with limited asset market participation. We show how a broad set of repression policies operates through a wedge in the Euler equation responsive to government size or by affecting fiscal redistribution between agents. Repression intensity is captured by a policy feedback rule that depends positively on net government spending. When fiscal policy is profligate and monetary policy accommodates, we show that such a repression policy raises bond values, reduces the inflationary cost of unfunded fiscal expansions, and lowers bond risk premia. Repression is not a free lunch for bondholders---they pay a lower inflation tax but also earn lower future real returns. When monetary policy does not accommodate fiscal policy, repression can provide stopgap funding for deficits, allowing the central bank to retain control over inflation while making government debt a hedge for fiscal inflation.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35392
title: Immigration, Innovation, and the Geography of Growth
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics,  and Yale University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Immigration, Innovation, and the Geography of Growth

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Between 1880 and 1920, more than 20 million immigrants settled in the United States. We study how this migration wave affected innovation and growth. Using a newly constructed dataset linking individual census records to historical immigration records and the universe of US patents, we highlight a new channel through which immigrants contributed to growth: they disproportionately settled in urban innovation hubs. To quantify the aggregate and regional effects of this mass migration episode, we develop a new spatial growth model in which skilled workers have a comparative advantage in innovation and sort endogenously across space. We find that international arrivals after 1880 raised US income per capita by 8.2% by 1940. Removing the subsequent immigration restrictions of the 1920s would have raised income per capita by a further 1.7% by 2000. Immigrants' skill composition and their concentration in urban hubs are key drivers of these effects.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35393
title: Wealth Inequality and Safe Asset Demand
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business and

detail.title: Wealth Inequality and Safe Asset Demand

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study how wealth inequality shapes safe-asset demand in heterogeneous-agent economies. Asset bubbles arise when agents face sufficiently high probabilities of falling into extreme poverty. In such cases, assets insulated from idiosyncratic risk become infinitely large relative to agents' wealth ex-post, which makes them infinitely valuable ex-ante. This mechanism is fundamentally different from classic rational bubbles, generates bubbles even under stationary wealth distributions, and requires no aggregate uncertainty or growth. Using this insight, we revisit the pricing of aggregate assets in standard heterogeneous-agent economies, and show that prior analyses may be incomplete due to overlooked possibility of transversality condition violation.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35388
title: Fragmentation of Shareholder Power
affiliations: Boston College, Boston College, Carroll School of Management and University of Toronto - Department of Economics

detail.title: Fragmentation of Shareholder Power

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The asset management industry is increasingly shifting toward tailored portfolios, fund proliferation, and decentralization of stewardship—trends partly driven by growing heterogeneity in investor preferences. While these developments better align investment products with investor demands, they also reshape ownership structures, potentially leading to more fragmented ownership and weaker managerial oversight. We develop a framework to evaluate these trade-offs and show that fund proliferation does not necessarily weaken governance: Stronger incentives for asset managers and concentrated portfolios of specialized funds can offset these effects, especially when investor preferences are intense. However, strong investor preferences can also induce asset managers to compete on a new margin—granting investors control by decentralizing stewardship and adopting pass-through voting—without internalizing the associated governance costs.

title: Robust Social Learning on Networks
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill and University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

detail.title: Robust Social Learning on Networks
detail.abstract: This paper studies social learning on networks in which agents face ambiguity about others' private signals and the network structure. We show that belief dynamics admit a tractable characterization via a simple rule-local geometric updating-under which agents treat the local network as the global network and aggregate observed actions with geometrically declining weights. Using this characterization, we derive sharp conditions for learning outcomes. Herding occurs with positive probability if and only if the network satisfies a log-expansion property. Long-run behavior is governed by two forces: expansion, which allows social information to outweigh private signals, and forgetting, which determines whether disagreement persists and hence whether almost-sure herding and asymptotic learning obtain.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35394
title: Safer Driving for a Price: Evidence on Behavior and Habits in Kenyan Minibuses
affiliations: University of Southern California, University of Chicago and University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy

detail.title: Safer Driving for a Price: Evidence on Behavior and Habits in Kenyan Minibuses

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Road traffic injuries are the leading cause of death among people aged 5–29. Where traffic laws are weakly enforced, it is unclear whether road safety interventions can change behavior. We run a randomized controlled trial among 203 Kenyan minibuses, testing whether an incentive scheme improves safety overall or merely shifts unsafe driving to unmonitored times. Drivers reduce speeding by 29 percent and harsh braking by 13 percent, improving a safety index by 0.096 standard deviations. Labor-supply and earnings effects are modest, with little displacement across times or places. Improvements fade quickly, suggesting lasting change requires sustained enforcement or stronger incentives.

title: Berlin Pulse: A Case Study of AI, Urban Mobility, and Energy-Aware Transport Policy

detail.title: Berlin Pulse: A Case Study of AI, Urban Mobility, and Energy-Aware Transport Policy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only publicly available secondary data and does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted as an independent study.

detail.abstract: Berlin's urban mobility system faces intersecting pressures from aging public-transport assets, fiscal constraints, persistent congestion, and the need to coordinate transport demand with an increasingly renewable but volatile electricity system. This paper develops and assesses Berlin Pulse, a conceptual design for an AI-enabled platform that uses targeted microincentives and carbon-aware scheduling to shift flexible mobility demand and mobility-related electricity loads such as electric-bus depot charging toward off-peak and low-carbon hours. The study is positioned explicitly as a conceptual design and ex-ante feasibility assessment rather than an empirical evaluation. Using a qualitative single-case design grounded in document analysis and literature synthesis, it specifies the platform architecture, incentive logic, and governance safeguards; situates the proposal against Berlin's existing Jelbi platform, the flat-rate Deutschlandticket fare environment, and the BVG's fleet-electrification program; and examines plausible effects through three transparent, parameterized uptake scenarios. Illustrative calculations suggest network-wide peak-trip reductions well below one percent under conservative assumptions and a few percent on targeted corridors under supportive policy, while operator-controlled depot charging emerges as the most credible near-term source of demand-side flexibility. A small empirical sub-study using 2025 SMARD data quantifies the depot-charging case, finding roughly 2.4 percent avoided CO2 and 4.8 percent avoided wholesale cost at the current 277-bus BVG fleet, rising to about 6 percent and 14 percent, respectively, under an extended charging window. The paper concludes with implementation sequencing, fiscal and governance conditions, and a research agenda for empirical validation. An appendix bounds the central peak-shift parameter against the rewardtype peak-shifting effects already cited in the literature, placing the medium-scenario assumption on the cleanest measured effect and the high scenario explicitly above that reward-type envelope rather than on a single anchor.

title: Supplementary Material for "If You're NOT So Smart, Why Are You Rich? Robust Market Selection with General Recursive Preferences"

detail.title: Supplementary Material for "If You're NOT So Smart, Why Are You Rich? Robust Market Selection with General Recursive Preferences"
detail.abstract: This supplement collects material moved out of the main article to meet the target submission length. Section S.1 gives proofs of intermediate lemmas and facts whose statements remain in the main appendix. Section S.2 discusses Assumption 6. Section S.3 proves Theorem 3. Section S.4 constructs \epsilon-perfected economies. Section S.5 contains the DAUA/IAUA robustness results. Section S.6 gives the equilibrium-existence result and proof. title: Genetic Resources, Biotech Patents and Gene Ownership
affiliations: Universitat Pompeu Fabra - Department of Law

detail.title: Genetic Resources, Biotech Patents and Gene Ownership
detail.abstract: Human genetic resources are increasingly considered as ordinary commercial goods, but their value and utility go beyond the simple and immediate private profit. In contrast to other biological resources, commercial use does not focus upon the material itself but rather upon the genetic information it contains. Information goods are then usually subject to intellectual property rights, but in the biological and life science domains, property rights can have a negative influence upon the proper allocation of several goods, including genetic material or goods that are related to it. This scenario reflects the facts of recent litigations in the United States and Europe. In particular, these lawsuits have revived the debate over private ownership and control over genes. Within this context, the objective of the paper is to discuss how to recast the traditional right to access to and use of biochemical and human genetic material currently considered as part of the market framework. Looking beyond the protection of traditional public goods, the paper emphasizes the debate around the progressive commodification of human genetic resources facilitated by an improper use of intellectual property rights. Different scenarios are analyzed to evaluate alternative instruments and new regulatory approaches to avoid the private appropriation of human genetic resources and other natural assets.

title: The Second Displacement AI, Knowledge Work, and the Collapse of the Professional Bargain

detail.title: The Second Displacement AI, Knowledge Work, and the Collapse of the Professional Bargain
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence may unsettle educated work before it produces visible mass unemployment. This paper argues that the first modern labor displacement weakened the bread-and-meaning bargain of industrial and special-skill labor, while AI now puts pressure on a second bargain: the professional status once attached to higher education, symbolic production, and trained judgment. The central claim is that AI can generate a meaning shock before an income shock. By lowering the scarcity value of first-pass symbolic output, improving employers' outside options, and compressing junior career ladders, AI can weaken the social meaning of professional work even where employment remains intact, especially if institutions automate junior work faster than they redesign apprenticeship. The paper develops a bottleneck account of personal satisfaction, three propositions, an occupational taxonomy, and a theory of discursive overheating. It also clarifies the institutional conditions under which a successor bargain might preserve judgment formation without becoming a rescue program for the already credentialed.

title: Anti-Authoritarianism Without Civilizational Weaponization
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Anti-Authoritarianism Without Civilizational Weaponization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, institutional, or personal conflicts of interest that influenced the preparation of this paper. The paper represents an independent scholarly and ethical critique based on publicly available materials, comparative political analysis, and the author’s own academic framework.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve human participants, patients, interviews, experiments, confidential data, or private personal information. It is based on publicly available academic, political, and historical materials. Therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was independently prepared and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper accepts that authoritarianism, religious instrumentalization, nationalism and militarized populism require serious criticism wherever they appear. It also argues that anti-authoritarian discourse becomes ethically dangerous when it is absorbed into external security narratives that treat whole societies as legitimate targets of coercive pressure, military punishment, sanctions, fragmentation or externally designed regime change. 1 The immediate point of departure is Parchizadeh and Emami's 2026 article on Turkey's post-Islamist authoritarian turn. Their analysis is useful in identifying the fusion of Islamic conservatism, Pan-Turkist nationalism and authoritarian governance under Erdogan, especially in relation to Syria, Libya and Central Asia. Yet the same discussion raises a broader methodological problem: when a scholar writes across national, civilizational and cultural boundaries, critique must be disciplined by contextual humility, proportionality and respect for the agency of the people being discussed. 2 The paper therefore rejects both authoritarian apologetics and civilizational weaponization. It criticizes the Iranian regime, Turkish authoritarianism, Arab dictatorships, Western double standards and Trumpian populist recklessness, while refusing to endorse the bombing, collapse or humiliation of societies as a path to democracy. Its central contribution is a civic, ethical and third-generation framework for antiauthoritarian critique: one that protects human dignity, historical memory, cultural plurality and the right of peoples to transform their own political futures. Key thesis: The problem is not that an Iranian scholar writes about Turkey, or that a Libyan-British researcher writes about Iran. The problem begins when cross-cultural analysis becomes detached from local histories, local voices, civilian protection and the moral limits of external coercion.

reference: Financial Review, 0[10.1111/fire.70043]
title: Exposure to Left-tail Risk, Risk Appetite and Mutual Fund Flows
affiliations: University of Leicester - School of Business

detail.title: Exposure to Left-tail Risk, Risk Appetite and Mutual Fund Flows
detail.abstract: Using a measure of aggregate tail risk, we show that a fund's sensitivity (exposure) to tail risk negatively affects the fund flows and the fund's performance. Further, a fund's tail risk sensitivity relates positively to the left-tail risk measures of the fund. We estimate the left-tail risk measures non-parametrically using daily fund returns and find that the measures also relate negatively to the funds' future cross-sectional investor flows and (cumulative) risk-adjusted performance. We further find that funds, on average, are slow at changing their left-tail risk. On examining the portfolio holdings of funds, we find that a fund's left-tail risk is positively related to the left-tail risk of individual stocks in its portfolio. Additionally, funds with higher left-tail risk also hold stocks with higher idiosyncratic risk and skewness. The poor performance of funds with higher left-tail risk appears to be due to the over-valuation of stocks in their portfolios. Given the recent finding of a left-tail return momentum for stocks with high left-tail risk, mutual funds which continue to hold stocks with exposure to left-tail risk, underestimate the persistence in left-tail risk and the associated overpricing.

title: FOMC Meetings, Monetary Policy Uncertainty, and Mutual Fund Alpha
affiliations: University of Leicester - School of Business and University of Sussex

detail.title: FOMC Meetings, Monetary Policy Uncertainty, and Mutual Fund Alpha
detail.abstract: We examine the ability of mutual fund managers to generate a positive alpha in a consistent manner around the uncertainty-generating Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings. The consistency of active equity mutual funds in generating a positive alpha over the successive FOMC announcements is positively related to future fund flows. This consistency is linked to the sensitivity of fund holdings (average uncertainty beta) to the monetary policy uncertainty related to the FED decisions. The uncertainty beta of mutual funds with respect to monetary policy uncertainty can predict both the investor flows and the future performance of the fund. Thus, the monetary policy uncertainty appears to be an important risk factor for funds, as investors redirect their capital to funds with the ability to hedge this risk and provide a positive risk-adjusted return over the FOMC announcements.

title: Sowing The Seed of Cooperation: Influence of DRD4 Exon-III Polymorphism on Cooperativeness in China
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, , Southwestern University of Finance and Economics (SWUFE) - China Center for Behavior Economics and Finance and Nanjing University

detail.title: Sowing The Seed of Cooperation: Influence of DRD4 Exon-III Polymorphism on Cooperativeness in China
detail.abstract: We pair a large-scale behavioural-genetic laboratory experiment with China's nationally representative China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) survey to study how the DRD4 exon-III 2-repeat shapes cooperation. In a one-shot Public Goods Game with 1,175 Han-Chinese students, 2-repeat carriers contribute significantly more than non-carriers---the gap is robust to robustness checks for (i) genome-wide principal components, (ii) polygenic scores for risk tolerance and trust, (iii) seven well-known social-behaviour loci, (iv) controls for trust, altruism, reciprocity, and inequity aversion elicited in other games, and (v) province-stratified permutation tests. For external validity, we link our province-level DRD4 2-repeat prevalence to the CFPS. Our DRD4 genetic proxy predicts higher charitable giving, unsolicited help, and interviewerrated cooperativeness---yet only in provinces where paddy rice dominates---further validating the role of DRD4 2-repeat allele in promoting cooperation. Finally, we report suggestive evidence of gene × culture co-evolution between DRD4 exon-III polymorphism and rice farming culture in fostering social efficiency through cooperativeness.

title:
Empirical Verification of an Asset Dynamics Model in Open Economies: 
An Equilibrium Theory Endogenizing Imbalances Bridging Steady-state Conditions and Social Adaptation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Empirical Verification of an Asset Dynamics Model in Open Economies: 
An Equilibrium Theory Endogenizing Imbalances Bridging Steady-state Conditions and Social Adaptation
detail.abstract:
The general equilibrium theory, upon which mainstream modern macroeconomics relies, fails to adequately explain the realities enveloping the contemporary economy, including persistent global imbalances. In contrast, our previous studies (Kitamura, 2025, 2026) have proposed a theoretical model based on "asset dynamics" that conceptualizes the global economy as a dissipative structure woven by the concentration and diffusion of funds, understanding it as an "equilibrium theory endogenizing imbalances" where economies, each harboring its own imbalances, maintain a balance by compensating for each other's surpluses and deficits. 
This paper statistically verifies the empirical validity of this theoretical framework using multi-source macroeconomic data and socio-psychological indicators. Targeting approximately 80 countries for which data are available, we redefine a socio-psychological indicator based on a large-scale international survey regarding time value, patience, and other attributes, as a proxy for the divergence between the real interest rate and the time preference rate-which constitutes one side of the steady-state condition derived from the theoretical model. Conducting a regression analysis using the structural terms that constitute the right-hand side of the conditional equation, namely population changes, capital movement, and asset preference, we obtained statistically significant results, including the sign conditions. Furthermore, by utilizing these estimation results, we visualized the dissipative structure that weaves the global economy, rendering the contrasting positions and interdependence of the two major economic superpowers as data-driven facts, such as the United States as a self-organizing economy and China as a dissipative economy. 
The contributions of this paper provide an empirical foundation for a new macroeconomic paradigm that reframes imbalances not as an undesirable state to be eliminated, but endogenously explains them as the energy required for the global economic system to maintain its vitality.

title: Lead Time and Innovation
affiliations: , Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and Union College - Department of Economics

detail.title: Lead Time and Innovation
detail.abstract: Using data from the Chinese Patent Survey, we document that the perceived importance of lead time advantages over competitors varies substantially across firms and is negatively associated with firms' preferences for patents relative to trade secrecy. We study this relationship formally in an endogenous growth model in which innovation-specific lead time influences firms' decision to patent their innovation or to keep it secret. We find that innovators with sufficiently strong lead time choose secrecy to avoid information disclosure, while those with weaker lead time patent to facilitate licensing revenue. Intellectual property policy affects growth through the expected value of innovation and firms' endogenous patent propensity, which determines the extent of patent thickets that impose a licensing burden on future innovators. We show that when firms have access to effective informal protection, strengthening patent protection may encourage patenting without fostering innovation, consistent with the empirical pattern known as the patent puzzle.

title: From Forecasting Tool to Financial Asset: The Institutionalization of Prediction Markets and the Emergence of Event Risk Trading
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: From Forecasting Tool to Financial Asset: The Institutionalization of Prediction Markets and the Emergence of Event Risk Trading
detail.abstract: Prediction markets have historically been viewed as specialized forecasting mechanisms that aggregate dispersed information into market prices. Recent developments, however, suggest a structural transition toward a more financialized model. In 2026, major professional market makers and proprietary trading firms began providing two-sided liquidity on platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket, linking regulated and decentralized venues in ways that resemble traditional financial market infrastructure. This paper examines whether prediction markets are evolving from information aggregation tools into a distinct institutional asset class focused on trading event risk. This paper synthesizes foundational prediction market research, recent work on decentralized market microstructure, empirical studies of manipulation risk, and contemporary industry developments. The analysis finds that institutional liquidity provision can improve market depth, tighten bid-ask spreads, and enhance real-time price discovery. At the same time, institutionalization introduces new concerns involving market manipulation, insider trading, oracle integrity, cross-venue arbitrage, and regulatory fragmentation. The paper argues that the key transformation is not simply greater participation by large firms, but the emergence of prediction markets as venues where event risk itself becomes a tradeable financial exposure. This shift has implications for market design, regulation, and future research on the boundaries between forecasting, derivatives, and speculative finance.

title: Rungs Removed or Scaffolds Built? A Dynamic Theory of Autonomy, Review, and Learning in Early-Career Labor Markets
affiliations: Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California

detail.title: Rungs Removed or Scaffolds Built? A Dynamic Theory of Autonomy, Review, and Learning in Early-Career Labor Markets
detail.abstract: How a firm configures generative AI determines whether the technology develops or hollows out its junior talent. We build a dynamic equilibrium theory of early-career skill formation in which tasks generate both current output and future expertise and AI either performs work autonomously or assists a worker who reviews its output. Because reviewing AI output can itself teach, the effect of delegation on skill depends on how it is configured. Two results are central. First, whether AI raises or erodes a workforce's long-run expertise turns not on how capable the AI is but on how intensively humans review its output: above a critical review intensity the same technology permanently builds expertise, and below it permanently erodes it. Second, a competitive market will not choose the configuration that develops the workforce. Because the expertise a worker gains is general and portable, and review is hard to contract on, a reviewing firm bears the cost but captures only part of the return. It therefore favors high autonomy and thin review, and competition sharpens rather than disciplines the resulting underprovision of review. This holdup in the formation of general human capital falls hardest at career entry, where the foregone tasks are precisely those a novice learns from. The remedy is configuration, not slower adoption: the optimal policy withholds autonomy from juniors until they can verify and grants it to seniors, so that autonomy builds expertise rather than removing rungs. AI deployment is thus a talent-development decision, to be set by task and seniority rather than as a uniform automation target.

title: Critical Tax Meets Law and Political Economy: A Conversation
affiliations: , Pace University - School of Law, University of South Carolina - Joseph F. Rice School of Law, University of Pittsburgh - School of Law, University of Southern California Gould School of Law, University of Connecticut - School of Law, Ohio State University (OSU) - Michael E. Moritz College of Law and University of South Carolina School of Law

detail.title: Critical Tax Meets Law and Political Economy: A Conversation
detail.abstract:
This Essay grew out of a roundtable conversation at the Inaugural Conference of the Association of Law and Political Economy held in Richmond, Virginia, in February 2026. The participants in that roundtable were law professors engaged in scholarship examining how tax law shapes inequality and the distribution of power. They identify as critical tax scholars, LPE scholars, or neither. Written in dialogue form, the Essay explores the intellectual relationship between critical tax theory and the law and political economy (LPE) movement. The focus is on the two traditions' shared commitments to examining hierarchy, democratic accountability, and institutional design, as well as their differing methodological and normative orientations. 

Written in dialogue form, this Essay makes three principal contributions: historiographical, analytical, and suggestive. First, it explores how critical tax theory anticipated many of the LPE movement's central concerns by demonstrating how ostensibly neutral tax rules reinforce hierarchies of race, gender, sexuality, class, and citizenship. Second, the authors consider areas of convergence and tension between the two frameworks, including debates over efficiency, redistribution, class analysis, and the relationship between technocratic tax design and democratic legitimacy. Third, this Essay considers how engagement between and among critical tax and LPE scholars may expand the scope of inquiry, encouraging greater attention to labor markets, family structure, administrative design, and the political uses of complexity. By bringing critical tax theory and LPE into direct conversation, this Essay underscores the importance of tax scholarship in illuminating how legal and fiscal systems shape economic life and democratic governance.

title: When ESG Rating Divergence Reduces Volatility: The Moderating Role of Information Asymmetry in China's A-share Market
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Fuzhou University

detail.title: When ESG Rating Divergence Reduces Volatility: The Moderating Role of Information Asymmetry in China's A-share Market

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by Fujian Province Education Science Planning Project under Grant FJJKB25155.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of ESG rating divergence on stock volatility using a panel of 4,223 Chinese A-share listed firms from 2019 to 2022. We find no significant association between ESG ratings and stock volatility. However, greater ESG rating divergence is significantly associated with lower stock volatility. This volatilityreducing effect is moderated by information asymmetry: the negative relationship weakens as information asymmetry increases. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect is more pronounced among private firms and firms with high-quality information disclosure, but insignificant for state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and firms with low disclosure quality. The results are robust to two-step system GMM, alternative ESG rating providers, and propensity score matching. By highlighting how ESG rating divergence provides incremental information that improves market efficiency in an emerging market, this study offers practical insights for risk-averse investors and regulators in China and other developing economies.

detail.abstract: Comparative research in the gig economy indicates that platforms despite pressures for standardization, localise their labour strategies in response to national institutional contexts. This paper advances this debate by introducing the concept of contextual realities, actor-created, mediating conditions producing specific national-sectoral institutional configuration in key IR arenas leading to diversified platform labour strategy. We compare the evolution of Uber's labour strategy in India and the United Kingdom (UK) since its market entry across the regulatory, collective-representation and labour-market arena. We find that, in the UK, the configuration of contextual realities created credible operational risk and retention costs, producing a high-constraint environment in which Uber adapted core elements of its labour strategy. In India, however, politically mediated enforcement, constrained union capacity and worker's limited exit options produced weaker constraints, enabling Uber to adapt selectively while maintaining core elements of its standard labour strategy. We contribute to comparative employment relations and gig economy research by showing that localisation of platform labour strategy depends on whether contextual realities translate national-sectoral institutions into operational constraints, helping explain deviations from first-glance institutional expectations.

title: Extreme Heat and the Distribution of Crop Yield Losses Across US Counties
affiliations: University of Innsbruck

detail.title: Extreme Heat and the Distribution of Crop Yield Losses Across US Counties
detail.abstract: I estimate the distribution of corn-yield sensitivities to extreme heat across US counties using a long-difference design and causal forests. The average effect masks large heterogeneity: a one-degree-day increase in extreme heat exposure above 29°C during the growing season has negligible effects in some counties, while reducing yields by nearly 1% in others. The machine learning analysis isolates irrigation coverage, prior extreme heat exposure, and educational attainment as the main predictors of this heterogeneity. Together, they explain 26% of the cross-county variation in estimated heat sensitivities. The interaction analysis sheds light on where adaptation support may be most valuable.

title: Schedules and Prioritization: A Behavioral Foundation for Multi-armed Bandits and Stopping Problems
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill

detail.title: Schedules and Prioritization: A Behavioral Foundation for Multi-armed Bandits and Stopping Problems
detail.abstract: Bandit models typically begin with arms, states, rewards, and transition rules. This paper instead begins with preferences over stopped local contingent schedules: possible unfoldings of a responsibility, project, experiment, or opportunity in its own local time. Behavioral axioms on single schedules characterize a generalized stopping representation with current utility, local discounting, and a broad continuation aggregator. A common-tail compensation axiom then allows calendar time to be priced across schedules. Imposing a tight elapsed-calendar constraint generates a rested generalized bandit and yields index optimality: the index is the shadow price of advancing a local clock. Expected-utility, learning, robust, rank-dependent, Choquet, and Pandora models arise as special cases.

title: Between Faith and Aspiration: Religion, Patriarchy, and the Educational Aspirations of Young Women in Pakistan

detail.title: Between Faith and Aspiration: Religion, Patriarchy, and the Educational Aspirations of Young Women in Pakistan
