detail.abstract: Scholarly and policy debates on women's education in Muslim-majority societies remain structured by a foundational binary: religion as barrier, or religion as enabling resource. This conceptual paper argues that both framings are analytically insufficient and proposes an alternative. Drawing on Islamic feminist theology (Wadud, 1999; Barlas, 2002), postcolonial feminism (Mohanty, 2003; Spivak, 1988), the capability approach (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2000; Unterhalter, 2003), and intersectionality (Crenshaw, 1989; Collins, 2000), the paper develops the Religious Negotiation of Educational Aspiration (RNEA) Framework — a seven-component architecture that theorises religion as a structurally embedded, discursively contested, and agentically deployed force in the formation of young women's educational aspirations. The framework makes four interrelated theoretical contributions: it advances a multi-directional account of religion's role in aspiration formation; it demonstrates the analytical productivity of combining Islamic feminist theology with the capability approach; it applies intersectional analysis to disaggregate the category of 'young Pakistani women'; and it theorises aspirations — critically distinguished from adaptive preferences — as the primary analytical unit. The paper situates this argument in the specific conditions of Pakistan, attending to the role of sectarian geography, postcolonial state formation, digital technology, and the extended patrilineal family in structuring aspiration formation. Implications for education policy, gender equity programming, and Southern theory are drawn throughout.

title: 'Chucking Their Stuff into ChatGPT and Hitting Send': AI Slop in the Administrative State
affiliations: University of York

detail.title: 'Chucking Their Stuff into ChatGPT and Hitting Send': AI Slop in the Administrative State
detail.abstract: Most research on AI in the administrative state focuses on its use by officials. This paper addresses a comparatively neglected issue: the impact of the use of AI tools by the public themselves. Drawing on a qualitative survey with over 500 UK civil servants, it argues that AI use by the public is increasingly disrupting the front-line of the administrative state. The argument is put in three parts. First, as the administrative state increasingly relies on text-based inputs, officials use correspondence as a proxy for individuals-a longstanding assumption of 'autographic' authorship that the diffusion of generative AI tools unsettles. Second, the problem can be characterised as 'AI slop': AI-generated correspondence with high volume and velocity that adopts a particular voice in interactions with officials. Third, this 'AI slop' causes three forms of disruption: to the signals officials draw from correspondence, to trust between officials and the public, and to systems ill-equipped to deal with it. The paper concludes by arguing that the status quo itself fails to adequately meet the needs of many people accessing services, and that systems need redesigning not only for a society with AI slop, but in ways that address the drivers of it too.

title: The Attack Surface of Public Certification

detail.title: The Attack Surface of Public Certification
detail.abstract: Public certification can fail not because the certifier is uninformative, but because certification leaves a record that opponents can attack. This paper studies a committed public certifier facing an external challenger who can selectively disclose truthful admissible fragments of the certified record. The central object is the attack surface of a certificate, the residual evidence that can still be made publicly salient after certification. In a finite-record model, damaging challenges are characterized by cell-conditional likelihood ratios within an institutional claim language. This gives an equilibrium foundation for an upper-tail likelihood-ratio object as the constraint generated by post-certification hard-evidence contestation. Robust certification value is characterized through feasible attack plans and no-challenge inference. Informativeness has nonmonotone value. More detailed reports can reduce credibility by isolating dangerous residual fragments, but can also increase credibility by preempting selective contestation through official context and denominators. The main design result is a pool-or-lose principle. A fine claim-language atom whose posterior is below the trust threshold contributes to robust credibility only when pooled with enough contextual records to restore trust. In ordered-threshold environments, nested residual tails yield survivability criteria, minimal safe contexts, and a dynamic program for optimal ordered reports.

title: Loss Function Sensitivity, Volatility Forecasting, and Dynamic Model Choice: Evidence from Foreign Exchange and Equity Markets

detail.title: Loss Function Sensitivity, Volatility Forecasting, and Dynamic Model Choice: Evidence from Foreign Exchange and Equity Markets

keywords: dynamic model choice JEL Codes: C22

detail.abstract: This paper examines how volatility model rankings depend on the choice of loss function when the true conditional variance is unobservable and forecast evaluation must rely on noisy volatility proxies. Using daily data for EUR/USD and the S&P 500, it compares GARCH, GJR-GARCH, and EGARCH through rolling one-step-ahead forecasts under four evaluation criteria: MSE, MAE, QLIKE, and joint VaR–ES loss. The results show that model rankings are loss-dependent: EGARCH performs best overall under MSE, QLIKE, and joint VaR–ES loss, whereas GJR-GARCH performs relatively better under MAE. At the same time, model confidence set results indicate that the three models are not sharply distinguishable in finite samples at the 10% level, implying that a superior model set is often more defensible than a unique winner. Dynamic model averaging and dynamic model selection also fail to deliver stable improvements over the best static model in the current sample. The paper contributes by integrating loss-function sensitivity, joint tail-risk evaluation, and dynamic model choice into a unified framework, showing that volatility model comparison is fundamentally conditional on the evaluation criterion, volatility proxy, and market environment.

title: Farmers' Health Capital as Economic Infrastructure: Human Mining, Biological Depreciation, and Macroeconomic Stability in India
affiliations: Maharashtra Agriculture Price Commission

detail.title: Farmers' Health Capital as Economic Infrastructure: Human Mining, Biological Depreciation, and Macroeconomic Stability in India
detail.abstract: Modern agricultural economics treats farm labor as a faceless, static number. This paper challenges that view, mapping out a destructive extraction process we call "Human Mining." By analyzing a field survey of 150 sugarcane cultivators in Maharashtra, India, we connect raw physical health directly to economic output. The field data reveals a severe rural crisis: 92% of households systematically delay medical treatment because they cannot afford upfront costs. Our logit models prove a striking behavioral law: a farmer's physical vitality is the single statistically significant predictor of their confidence to invest in the next crop season (odds ratio = 1.035; p < 0.001). This paper proves mathematically that a minor upfront preventative investment (calibrated at ₹5,000) slows down human biological depreciation. This front-end protection stops harvest delays, unlocks 10% labor efficiency, and generates ₹26,597 in new wealth while saving the state treasury ₹7,000 per family in hospital deficits.

title: Infrastructure Connectivity and Supply Chain Resilience: Dual Empirical Evidence from Indonesia's IMIP and the Baltimore Bridge Collapse
affiliations: Josai International University

detail.title: Infrastructure Connectivity and Supply Chain Resilience: Dual Empirical Evidence from Indonesia's IMIP and the Baltimore Bridge Collapse
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the dual role of physical infrastructure in shaping supply chain efficiency and vulnerability. Using two contrasting natural experiments-the construction-driven vertical integration of the Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park (IMIP) coking coal complex (2018-2025) and the disruption caused by the collapse of Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge (March 2024)-we develop a comparative framework grounded in the Cobb-Douglas production function augmented with transport infrastructure capital. For the IMIP case, a system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimation reveals a strong autoregressive coefficient of approximately 1.33 in coke output dynamics, confirming that infrastructure-enabled capacity accumulation follows a compounding process. For the Baltimore case, a multi-period Difference-inDifferences (DID) model using EIA quarterly coal export data identifies a 29.1% reduction in Baltimore's exports during the shock period, relative to the Norfolk (Virginia) control group, with the parallel trend assumption supported by pre-event placebo tests. Together, these findings demonstrate that infrastructure is not merely a passive carrier of productive capacity, but an active multiplier-and that single-point failures can generate severe, though partially transitory, supply chain disruptions. Policy implications for the Belt and Road Initiative and industrial park planning are discussed.

title: Farmer decision-making as an assembling process: implications for agri-environmental policy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Farmer decision-making as an assembling process: implications for agri-environmental policy
detail.abstract: Agri-environmental policy rests on particular assumptions of how farmers make decisions. They assume that preferences are stable, that incentives produce predictable responses, and that the farmer can be separated from the farm. Yet on-farm conservation decisions vary in ways this account cannot explain, with the same pressure producing different choices across farmers and within the same farmer over time. Drawing on assemblage thinking and walking interviews with 28 Australian farming households, this paper argues that farmer decision-making for biodiversity conservation is best understood as an assembling process, in which heterogeneous relations, among them economic, intergenerational, epistemic, affective, more-than-human and temporal relations, are configured, held, and at times re-formed. The paper makes three contributions. It sets this process-relational account against the objectivist assumptions embedded in agri-environmental policy. It uses paired comparisons to show that conservation outcomes follow from how relations are configured rather than from any single relation, a result that single-factor accounts struggle to reconstruct. And it identifies design implications for the policy mix, including the mechanism by which an instrument can reconfigure the relations that hold a conservation practice in place rather than only act within them. For the field of ecological economics, the account offers a way to specify when and why incentives reinforce or displace existing motivations. Australia is the worked case and the assumptions questioned apply more widely.

title:
The Formation of the Subject in Intimate Relationships 
The Other, Joint Attention, and the Economy of Attention

detail.title:
The Formation of the Subject in Intimate Relationships 
The Other, Joint Attention, and the Economy of Attention
detail.abstract: This paper, the fifth in a series on the philosophy of intimacy and the theory of justice, defends a single thesis with three consequences. The thesis: the subject of an intimate relationship is not a pre-given entity that subsequently enters relation, but is formed and continuously sustained through a specific mechanism, the presence of the other and the practice of joint attention. Part One assembles the theoretical ground, organizing accounts of the relational subject not by school but by the type of constitutive mechanism each proposes: mirror mechanisms (Cooley, Mead, Winnicott, Lacan), triadic mechanisms (joint attention in developmental psychology; Davidson's triangulation), and symbolic mechanisms (Vygotsky, Saussure, Althusser, Butler), with the enactivist correction of theory-of-mind orthodoxy. Part Two argues that the triadic mechanism is the missing middle term between mirror and symbol, offers a layered reconciliation of Lacan and Tomasello, and answers a Levinasian difficulty: in the dyad, the first third party is the shared object itself. Part Three transfers the mechanism to adult intimacy under an explicit no-overclaim discipline, proposing the reflexive triangle: the mature form of intimate joint attention takes the relation itself as its shared object. Part Four develops the consequences: a critique of the attention economy as a parasite on the triadic structure (the algorithmic feed as a pseudo-shared object); a Hohfeldian analysis showing why there can be no claim-right to attention, and what structural criterion of attentional justice should stand in its place; and a new category for the theory of justice, constitutive injustice, the systematic degradation not of a subject's holdings or rights but of the conditions of its formation.

title: Shadow Space for Bounded Node-Degree Distributions Moment Completion, Residual Fingerprints, and Sampling-Frequency Invariance with an Application to Financial Networks

detail.title: Shadow Space for Bounded Node-Degree Distributions Moment Completion, Residual Fingerprints, and Sampling-Frequency Invariance with an Application to Financial Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: DS4H Interdisciplinary Fellowship

detail.abstract: Empirical networks are finite objects, hence their node-degree distributions have bounded support. Yet degree laws are often summarized through power-law tail fits or moment-based statistics that implicitly refer to unbounded comparison worlds. This paper proposes a shadowspace representation for bounded node-degree distributions. Each empirical degree law is projected onto an admissible finite-moment shadow family and decomposed into a fitted shadow quantile plus a residual quantile signature. The resulting shadow fingerprint contains coordinates, residual mismatch, and a normalized moment-gap profile. We show that any finite degree sample admits such a representation and that, after projection, the entire shadow moment ladder is well defined. When a raw moment exists, its shadow counterpart can be studied as a regularized statistic with projection bias; when the raw moment is infinite in an unbounded comparison law, the shadow moment is a finite surrogate rather than an estimator of a nonexistent quantity. For indexed families of networks, fingerprints trace paths in shadow space, and a closed-form consensus fixed point yields sampling-invariance diagnostics. The main application is to financial networks estimated across sampling frequencies, where the method separates unstable power-law fits from stable degree-law geometry and produces finite risk-functionals from the structural shadow law.

title: Down-Projection Fragility is Universal Under Low-Bit Quantization: A Four-Architecture Study of Quantization-Error Interaction
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Down-Projection Fragility is Universal Under Low-Bit Quantization: A Four-Architecture Study of Quantization-Error Interaction
detail.abstract: Mixed-precision post-training quantization allocates bit-widths by measuring each layer's sensitivity in isolation and summing the predicted loss increases. We set out to test the assumption underlying this practice-that quantization errors across layers are additive-and in doing so measured the per-layer and per-matrix interaction structure of low-bit quantization across four open-weight 7Bparameter transformers (Mistral-7B-v0.3, Llama-2-7B, Falcon-7B, Qwen2.5-7B), at four bit-widths (2, 3, 4, and 5 bits) and two granularities (whole-layer and per-projection-matrix). Our clearest result is architectural. At per-matrix granularity, the MLP down-projection is the single most-fragile matrix class on every architecture tested and at both 2-bit and 3-bit precision-gated (down_proj) in Llama/Mistral/Qwen, non-gated (dense_4h_to_h) in Falcon-surviving the transition between the two. The same down-projection sensitivity has been reported independently under an entirely different quantization method (Walsh-Hadamard-rotated weight quantization) with the same residual-stream compounding mechanism, which places the finding beyond any single quantizer. On the additivity question: at 2-bit precision the additive predictor undershoots true ΔL by a factor of 2.1× to 2.7× on three of the four architectures, with 82-91% of pairwise interaction terms positive-errors amplify, not cancel-collapsing to the noise floor at 3-bit and above. Qwen2.5-7B is the exception, with a milder 2-bit ratio of 1.20 (50% positive ε) but a residual 3-bit interaction signal (69% positive ε) the other architectures lack. The non-additivity is therefore universal at the 2-bit cliff and architecture-dependent in magnitude; sensitivity-based mixed-precision allocators undercount the damage of their own multi-unit allocations exactly in the aggressive low-bit regime the field is pushing toward.

title:
Social Identification and Uprising Support: 
Evidence from Cali, Colombia
affiliations: , International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) and Universidad ICESI

detail.title:
Social Identification and Uprising Support: 
Evidence from Cali, Colombia
detail.abstract: A dominant prediction of the social identity literature is that strong identification with a group fuels political participation, including support for high-cost collective action. We test this prediction using a large, representative population survey of 2,750 residents of Cali, Colombia, fielded a few months after the 2021 uprising that left dozens of demonstrators dead and the city blockaded for six weeks. Our outcome variable is self-reported support for the uprising (with perceived legitimacy of the strike as a parallel measure). Our identification measure is the trust each respondent reports in a member of one of four ingroups (district, class, religion, politics) and four outgroups (migrants, ex-combatants, riot police, rioters), relative to an average Colombian. Across specifications with district fixed effects and a rich set of socio-demographic controls, strong ingroup identification is negatively correlated with support for the uprising. Universalists, whose trust budget extends to an average Colombian no less than to a member of their own group, are systematically more supportive. Proximity to violent hot-spots in the city does little to displace this pattern. We argue that polarized post-conflict cities in the developing world are a class of contexts in which the dominant hi-identifiers prediction reverses, and we discuss what this means for the positive and welfare economics of revolt and for policy in fractured social contracts.

title: Collateral Validity and the Limits of Seniority in Private-Credit Back-Leverage : A Loss-Given-Default Framework for Warehouse Financing

detail.title: Collateral Validity and the Limits of Seniority in Private-Credit Back-Leverage : A Loss-Given-Default Framework for Warehouse Financing
detail.abstract: A senior, secured lender can lose nearly the whole of its advance with no prior movement in observed credit spreads, reported collateral values, or the loan-to-value ratio it underwrote. This paper formalises why. The recoverable value of a collateral pool is decomposed into three multiplicative factors-validity, perfection, and liquidation-and a closed-form loss-given-default is derived for a senior tranche financed at advance rate α. The central analytic result is a break-even condition: the senior lender is impaired precisely when the product of the three factors falls below α. Because a first-loss cushion is conventionally sized against ordinary credit deterioration, which moves perfection and liquidation only modestly, it is structurally blind to a discrete downward jump in validity-the signature of collateral fraud. At a severe-state reference point, the local sensitivity of loss-given-default to validity is about 1.8 times its sensitivity to the advance rate; the advance rate is first-order under moderate collateral impairment but becomes second-order when validity collapses. A transparent Monte Carlo simulation, used as a robustness stress on the exact loss function rather than as evidence about fraud incidence, confirms a bimodal loss distribution whose expectation is governed-in the calibrations examined-by the probability of entering the control-failure state rather than by any contractual term. The paper is motivated by public reporting around a 2026 provision taken by a global bank against back-leverage financing linked to a private-credit warehouse; the model is not a reconstruction of that exposure. Implications are drawn for pricing, capital, covenant design, and the operational architecture of private-credit market infrastructure, distinguishing throughout between reporting rights and verification rights.

title: Toward a Just Proposal: Epistemic Injustice Theory and the Practice of Intimate-Relationship Proposals

detail.title: Toward a Just Proposal: Epistemic Injustice Theory and the Practice of Intimate-Relationship Proposals
detail.abstract:
A marriage proposal is, beneath its romance, a request that one person make a high-stakes, contract-like, life-structuring decision, and one that is, in L. A. Paul's sense, transformative (Paul 2014): its acceptance reshapes the values and self by whose lights it would be assessed. This paper argues that the conventional staging of the proposal, the engineered emotional peak, the social script that demands an immediate answer, and the asymmetry of information and preparation between the two parties, can, even in the complete absence of ill will and of any identity-based prejudice, compromise the epistemic agency of the person asked.

I do not claim to have discovered a new kind of epistemic injustice. The wrong is better understood with a framework already in hand. I read the proposal through Catala (2025), The Dynamics of Epistemic Injustice: Situating Epistemic Power and Agency, whose pluralist account of epistemic agency and analysis of hermeneutical domination and epistemic empowerment supply exactly the apparatus the case requires. On Catala's account, epistemic agency is not exhausted by the propositional exchange of testimony; it includes a non-propositional, non-verbal, self-interpretive dimension, the agent's capacity to make sense of her own experience to herself (self-to-self intelligibility) before and apart from conveying it to others (self-to-others intelligibility). The proposal, I argue, is a site where this self-interpretive agency, at the very threshold of a transformative choice, is placed under conditions, temporal, affective, informational, that impede its exercise.

This installment does not yet write the body. Following the principle that the conceptual core should be secured before the argument is built upon it, it does two things. First, it verifies, against the literature current to 2025, the post-Fricker development of the field, Fricker's two originals, Dotson on testimonial smothering, Pohlhaus Jr. on willful hermeneutical ignorance, Medina on resistance, and the philosophical work on gaslighting, and then expounds Catala's framework in detail, since it is the framework the paper will use. Second, it shows precisely how the proposal situation maps onto Catala's categories: which dimension of epistemic agency is at stake, why the wrong is a form of hermeneutical rather than testimonial difficulty, and why locating it within an existing account is more defensible than minting a new term. The constructive half of the full paper will then derive the normativity of an epistemically just proposal: separation of the affective moment from the decision, full disclosure before the asking, removal of immediate-answer pressure, the ring re-grounded from "seal of a concluded bargain" to "token and waiting," and a deferred-commitment mechanism, each reconstrued as a condition of epistemic empowerment in Catala's sense.

title: Navigating the Compliance Labyrinth: Challenges and Best Practices for Indian SaaS Startups under the DPDP Act 2023 and GDPR

detail.title: Navigating the Compliance Labyrinth: Challenges and Best Practices for Indian SaaS Startups under the DPDP Act 2023 and GDPR

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; this is a doctrinal legal analysis involving no human participants or personal data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Indian software has quietly turned into a global industry, and most of its companies sell abroad before they sell at home. That one commercial fact lands the average Indian SaaS startup in the middle of two data-protection regimes at the same time. At home, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 finally has teeth: the DPDP Rules, 2025, notified on 14 November 2025, fixed the timelines, switched on the Data Protection Board, and set a hard compliance horizon. Abroad, the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation has applied since 2018 and reaches any Indian firm that touches a European user. The question this paper takes up is a working founder’s question, not an abstract one: how do you satisfy both regimes at once without building two of everything? My argument is that you should not try to. The two laws agree on what matters most —notice, purpose, security, the rights of the individual—and part ways mainly in their machinery. Where they differ, the differences are specific and manageable: a fixed eighteen-month clock running to May 2027; an Indian breach-reporting duty that layers awkwardly over the GDPR’s own seventy-two-hour rule; a Consent Manager with no European cousin; a permissive “negative-list” on cross-border transfers where Europe is restrictive; verifiable parental consent that bites hardest in EdTech; and a heavier audit-and-assessment burden for anyone large enough to be named a Significant Data Fiduciary. Build one programme to the stricter European standard, bolt the India-specific pieces on top, and most of the labyrinth straightens out. The paper sets out the law, the SaaS-specific pressure points, a clause-level comparison, and a phased roadmap—and closes with recommendations for founders and regulators alike. Compliance, handled well, is not a tax. For a company that sells trust, it is part of the product.

title: Growing Downward: Persistent Inequality in Publishing in Economics *
affiliations: Monash University

detail.title: Growing Downward: Persistent Inequality in Publishing in Economics *
detail.abstract: This paper documents new facts about concentration in publishing in economics. First, the profession grows downward. The number of economists grew almost sixfold since 1990, but new entrants publish in lower-tier journals while incumbents hold the top. Second, there is high and persistent concentration at the top. Along with the downward growth, the top-1% authors accounted for 38.4% of top-5 publication credit in 1990 and for 78.3% in 2025. Third, the persistence is widespread within cohorts, within subfields, and within gender. Fourth, new journals only slightly dilute concentration. Fifth, elite authors diversify on topics faster than the rest of the profession. We interpret the findings with a screening model of attention under information overload. The evidence is consistent with the model: as the field grows, citations concentrate on established work and the conditional citation premium of top-author papers narrows.

title: Impossibility Results for Stability and Nonbossiness in Matching Markets with Commitments
affiliations: and University of York - Department of Economics and Related Studies

detail.title: Impossibility Results for Stability and Nonbossiness in Matching Markets with Commitments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: Rui He gratefully acknowledges financial support from JSPS (KAKENHI Grant-in-Aid 25KJ1635)

detail.abstract: Stability and nonbossiness are important properties in matching theory. We show that they are incompatible in senior-level matching markets with commitments, even though commitments weaken the standard stability requirement. The incompatibility holds both for standard nonbossiness and for a commitment-related version that accounts for commitment states.

title: Dysfunctions and Transformational Processes in Social Systems under Contemporary Global Changes
affiliations: Trakia University and Kaneff University Hospital

detail.title: Dysfunctions and Transformational Processes in Social Systems under Contemporary Global Changes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: not applicable

detail.abstract: The present study examines social systems as complex and dynamic structures that function through the interaction of institutions, social groups, norms, and values. In the context of globalization, technological transformations, and increasing interdependence among societies, social systems are subjected to growing transformational pressure and various forms of dysfunctionality. The article analyzes the main theoretical approaches to the study of social systems, focusing on the concepts of Talcott Parsons and Niklas Luhmann. Particular attention is given to the mechanisms of systemic stability, adaptation, and integration, as well as to the factors that may lead to disruptions in the functional balance of social structures. The study identifies the main directions of dysfunctionality in social systems, including accelerated social change, global external shocks, institutional instability, structural rigidity, and technological transformations. Specific manifestations of these processes in Bulgaria and the European Union are also examined, such as social inequality, regional disparities, the crisis of institutional trust, and demographic challenges. In conclusion, the study emphasizes that the resilience of social systems depends on their ability to develop adaptive mechanisms, modernize institutional structures, and maintain a balance between stability and change. Effective management of social risks, the reduction of social inequality, and the strengthening of institutional legitimacy are considered key factors for the sustainable development of contemporary societies.

title:
The Six Institutional Laws 

An Applied Integration of Five Traditions in Community Bank Governance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The Six Institutional Laws 

An Applied Integration of Five Traditions in Community Bank Governance

No external funding supported the preparation of this paper.

It does not involve the collection of primary data from human participants, experiments, surveys, or any procedures requiring institutional review board (IRB) or ethics committee approval.
