detail.abstract: This paper develops the Six Institutional Laws (Integrity, Responsibility, Discipline, Competence, Cohesion, Courage) as an applied integration of five established traditions in institutional theory, governance scholarship, banking history, virtue ethics, and the literature on institutional leadership under pressure. The framework was derived inductively from practitioner observation across general leadership and community bank engagements in the United States and is presented here as a synthesis suitable for application to community bank governance, examiner review, and director education. The paper situates the Laws within existing scholarship rather than claiming novel theoretical contribution. Each Law is mapped to the traditions it operationalizes, with attention to the specific conditions of community banking institutions. Implications are developed for board oversight, executive evaluation, and supervisory practice. Limitations are addressed including the inductive method, the absence of controlled comparative data, and the bounded geographic scope of the originating observations. The paper concludes with an agenda for empirical validation and further development.

title: The Predictable Tail: Lottery Characteristics Price Drawdown, Not Return -A Look-Ahead-Clean Audit in Which a Dissolving Return Anomaly Reappears as a Robust Risk Factor
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Predictable Tail: Lottery Characteristics Price Drawdown, Not Return -A Look-Ahead-Clean Audit in Which a Dissolving Return Anomaly Reappears as a Robust Risk Factor

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: On a single point-in-time U.S. equity panel (715 names, 2009–2025) we document a sharp asymmetry: the cross-section of forward returns is barely predictable, while the cross-section of forward drawdowns is strongly predictable — by the same characteristics, on the same data. Total volatility has a rank information coefficient of ( , insignificant) against the forward 60-day return and ( ) against the realized 252-day maximum drawdown — a sixtyfold difference in predictive content for one variable. Lottery characteristics (payoff asymmetry, idiosyncratic skewness, MAX) show the same inversion at roughly fivefold. We organize the paper as four acts. Act 1 (the dissolving return anomaly): we take payoff asymmetry (PA) as a representative distributional signal and trace its apparent return premium through five separable artifacts — look-ahead contamination, mean-versus-rank divergence under fat tails, overlapping- window dependence, circular ex-post conditioning, and a spurious overlapping control — to a volatility-conditional residue that then fails a sector control, reversing within technology and carried by a single sub-period; the return signal is, at root, a healthcarecomposition effect. Act 2 (the inversion): repointed at realized drawdown, those same characteristics predict ruin robustly. Quality (high = safe) and the lottery axis (high skew/PA = fragile) survive an autocorrelation-corrected horserace against the volatility zoo and a Bonferroni correction across all trials ( down to ); the effect is out-of-sample stable and, for quality, strengthens in crises. Act 3 (why standard tooling misses it): on fat-tailed drawdown labels the Sharpe-based Deflated Sharpe Ratio reads while distribution-free gates (median NeweyWest, horserace, a Probability of Backtest Overfitting of ) are overwhelmingly significant — mean-Sharpe multiple-testing is the wrong instrument for a fat-tailed target — and we exhibit a momentum "ruin signal" that is pure overlap leakage, vanishing under a proper embargo. Act 4 (economic magnitude): the risk finding is not merely statistical — fragility-quintile membership separates the out-of-sample one-year probability of a drawdown from 4% to 44%, an actionable spread of a kind the return sort never produces. Throughout we use, and contribute, an adversarial validation gauntlet (look-ahead-clean construction, distribution-free inference, factor horserace, purged out-of-sample folds, multiple-testing penalties, and a continuousevaluation decay loop) whose job is to falsify its author's findings. The unifying message reframes the lottery literature: these characteristics are weak and fragile as return anomalies but strong, robust, and economically large as risk factors — and under fat tails, methodology fixes not just the magnitude but the sign of what one measures.

title: On Hilbert's 8th Problem: II
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: On Hilbert's 8th Problem: II
detail.abstract: The Riemann Hypothesis is reformulated probabilistically and reduced to a single positivity requirement. Using the Hadamard factorisation of the Riemann ξ-function, RH is shown equivalent to Thorin's condition: that ξ(1 2)/ξ(1 2 + √ s) be the Laplace transform of a generalised gamma convolution (GGC). A GGC random variable realising this transform is constructed explicitly and unconditionally in the zero-free region Re > 1, from Lévy representations of the Gamma function and the Euler product for the zeta function; its Thorin density is the boundary value of ξ ′ /ξ on a vertical line, carried to the critical line by a half-power subordination acting as a Poisson extension. The Mellin transform onto the critical strip is then computed directly from the moment sequence, no positivity enters, leaving a single residual requirement, nonnegativity of the resulting Thorin measure, whose atoms are the zeros: nonnegativity holds if and only if every non-trivial zero lies on the critical line.

title: 3D-MolFusion: A Geometry-Enhanced Adaptive Fusion Framework for Multimodal Molecular Property Prediction
affiliations: Nantong University

detail.title: 3D-MolFusion: A Geometry-Enhanced Adaptive Fusion Framework for Multimodal Molecular Property Prediction
detail.abstract: Molecular property prediction is a fundamental task in computer-aided drug discovery. Accurate predictions require the coordinated integration of heterogeneous molecular evidence, including substructural priors, topological connectivity, and three-dimensional conformational geometry. However, existing methods typically rely on a single molecular representation or employ fixed fusion rules to combine multiple views, which constrains fine-grained cross-modal alignment and fails to account for molecule-dependent modality reliability variations. To address these limitations, we propose 3D-MolFusion, a geometry-enhanced adaptive fusion framework that synergistically integrates 3D conformational geometry, 2D molecular topology, and fingerprint-based substructural priors. Specifically, a direction-aware visual encoder captures orientation-sensitive geometric features from six orthographic projections of molecular conformers, while a geometry-enhanced graph Transformer incorporates distance, angle, and relative-direction biases into node-level attention mechanisms to jointly model topological and conformational information. To overcome fixed fusion limitations, 3D-MolFusion employs bidirectional token-level cross-modal attention across view, node, and fingerprint representations to enable fine-grained information exchange and leverages descriptor-guided adaptive gating to dynamically assign molecule-specific modality weights. Comprehensive evaluations on eight MoleculeNet benchmarks demonstrate that 3D-MolFusion achieves state-of-the-art performance on five benchmarks and attains the highest average scores across both classification and regression tasks.

title: Operational Value of Earth Observation and Reanalysis Predictors for Subnational Maize Yield Forecasting in Nigeria
affiliations: , Africa Business School, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University (UM6P) and Africa Business School, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University

detail.title: Operational Value of Earth Observation and Reanalysis Predictors for Subnational Maize Yield Forecasting in Nigeria
detail.abstract: Accurate, spatially explicit crop yield forecasts are critical for food security monitoring in climate-vulnerable regions, yet the operational value of different Earth observation (EO) data streams remains poorly quantified. Using a Random Forest model with a predictor-block ablation design evaluated under strict Leave-One-Year-Out cross-validation, this study isolates the marginal contribution of four EO inputs: MODIS NDVI phenology, CHIRPS rainfall, ERA5-Land air temperature, and MODIS land surface temperature (LST), for subnational maize yield forecasting across Nigeria. Two findings are especially salient for operational forecasting. First, MODIS LST added negligible forecast skill beyond ERA5-Land air temperature (ΔRMSE = 0.001 t ha⁻¹), an outcome explained by strong collinearity between the two variables at this scale (Pearson r = 0.89). Second, a simple persistence baseline based on prior-year state yield outperformed the full EO-only model, establishing a stringent benchmark for seasonal satellite and reanalysis predictors. The best EO-only configuration achieved RMSE = 0.475 t ha⁻¹ and MAPE = 29.4%, while adding soil properties and lagged yield reduced these to 0.407 t ha⁻¹ and 22.6%, respectively. Detrended analysis confirmed that EO variables capture genuine interannual anomaly signal beyond the secular trend. Forecast skill varied sharply across agroecological zones, with zone-level RMSE nearly perfectly predicted by yield variability. The EO-only model failed to beat a constant-mean forecast in three of nineteen evaluation years, each associated with distinct non-climatic disruptions. These findings clarify which EO data streams justify inclusion in operational forecasting systems and show that effective crop monitoring depends on selective predictor design rather than data-maximal accumulation.

title: The Hidden Asset: How Social Capital Shapes Professional Success beyond Individual Competence
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Hidden Asset: How Social Capital Shapes Professional Success beyond Individual Competence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could be perceived to have influenced the development, analysis, or conclusions of this study. This research is conducted independently and is based solely on academic literature review and theoretical synthesis.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, clinical data, or experimental procedures. Therefore, ethical approval and informed consent were not required. The research is based on secondary literature and theoretical analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted as an independent academic work.

detail.abstract:
The belief that hard work, education, and individual competence alone determine success remains deeply embedded
in modern society. While skills, knowledge, and expertise are undoubtedly important, growing evidence suggests that
social relationships, networks, and reputation play a significant role in shaping access to opportunities. This paper
explores the relationship between human capital and social capital, arguing that competence alone is often insufficient
to explain variations in career advancement, professional success, and life opportunities.
Drawing upon the theoretical contributions of Pierre Bourdieu's Social Capital Theory, Mark Granovetter's Strength
of Weak Ties Theory, Robert Putnam's work on social networks and civic engagement, and contemporary perspectives
from Malcolm Gladwell, Meg Jay, Dale Carnegie, and Keith Ferrazzi, this conceptual paper examines how trust-based
relationships facilitate access to information, resources, mentorship, and opportunities. Through a qualitative
literature-based analysis, the study synthesizes findings from sociology, psychology, and professional development
literature to understand the mechanisms through which social capital influences individual outcomes.
The analysis suggests that while human capital creates capability, social capital creates visibility, trust, and opportunity
access. Individuals who intentionally cultivate meaningful relationships and professional networks are often better
positioned to benefit from emerging opportunities than those who rely solely on competence. The paper concludes
that success in modern society is best understood as the interaction between individual capability and social
connectedness, with important implications for education, career development, and personal growth.

title: When the Memory Knows the Old You

detail.title: When the Memory Knows the Old You
detail.abstract: This report emerges from a single documented session, May 6, 2026, in Midland, Ontario. It is not peer-reviewed laboratory science. It is field-sourced conceptual work with external literature support that arrived on the same day as the observation it supports. The findings are named honestly. The limits are stated directly. The everyday person is not the limitation of this research-they are the only valid instrument for it.

title: The "Last-Patent Problem" in Patent Portfolio Licensing

detail.title: The "Last-Patent Problem" in Patent Portfolio Licensing
detail.abstract: Companies often license patents in portfolios because doing so can reduce transaction costs and infringement uncertainty. However, some companies include static royalty rates in their patent portfolio licenses, requiring licensees to pay the same royalty rate until the last patent in the portfolio expires or is invalidated. Such a practice turns the last remaining patent in the portfolio into a lever and imposes a “public-domain tax” that inflates prices, depresses output, and stifles innovation. This Article introduces and analyzes the problem created by such a practice as the “last-patent problem.” Part I explains why companies transact in patent portfolios and how patent portfolio licenses with static, non-diminishing royalty rates, though often efficient ex ante, become distortionary as the patents in the portfolio expire or are invalidated. Part II formalizes the last-patent problem with several simple economic models showing that a static portfolio royalty rate magnifies price–cost wedges over time relative to a proportional step-down rate tied to the share of remaining value-bearing patents. Part III situates the analysis in the history of the U.S. patent system. Part IV shows that the patent-misuse doctrine, narrowed by statute and case law, does not reach the last-patent problem, and that because relief under antitrust’s rule of reason is costly, under-deterrence follows. Part V proposes structural and behavioral remedies that administrative agencies, legislatures, and courts can adopt or mandate to alleviate the last-patent problem.

title: Is Money Overrated? Misperceived Satisfaction from Income
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Is Money Overrated? Misperceived Satisfaction from Income
detail.abstract: People often make important choices in pursuit of higher income, but do they place too much weight on income when deciding what path to take? We propose a simple model of misspecified learning in which individuals overestimate the marginal satisfaction from income—the expected effect of an income increase on overall life satisfaction—and therefore give income too much importance in their decisions. Guided by this model, we designed a pre-registered experiment that elicits beliefs about the marginal satisfaction from income and randomly assigns scientific evidence about it. Respondents substantially overestimate the marginal satisfaction from income both for themselves and for others, but especially for themselves. These biases shrink when respondents are exposed to scientific evidence, and the effects persist one month later. To study whether these beliefs matter for behavior, we measure income-versus-non-income tradeoffs using job-choice scenarios tailored to each respondent and a real-world decision the respondent is facing. To elicit the latter, we make a methodological contribution: an AI-led interview method that moves beyond static, predefined survey instruments by combining the flexibility of qualitative interviewing with the discipline of closed-ended survey measurement. We find that biased beliefs are consequential: after learning that income matters less for life satisfaction than they initially thought, respondents place less weight on income in their decisions.

title: Endogenous Breaks in India’s Agricultural GDP and the Role of Good Governance
affiliations: Vidyasagar University - Tamralipta Mahavidyalaya and Independent

detail.title: Endogenous Breaks in India’s Agricultural GDP and the Role of Good Governance
detail.abstract: India’s agricultural GDP from 1960–61 to 2019–20 underwent multiple endogenous structural breaks, identified through a modified Bai-Perron methodology that effectively captures key transitions in the sector’s growth trajectory. Five statistically significant breaks were detected, corresponding to major historical events such as the Green Revolution, wars, severe droughts, and shifts in governance and agricultural policy. Analysis of compound annual growth rates (CAGR) across these segments reveals pronounced fluctuations, with phases of contraction (e.g., -0.12865 and -0.11918) followed by strong recoveries (e.g., 0.143987 and 0.133829), reflecting the disruptive impacts of shocks and the restorative influence of good governance, targeted interventions, institutional reforms, and policy-driven initiatives. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test confirms the stationarity of the series, indicating that the observed shifts stem from structural rather than stochastic factors. While numerous exogenous events influenced agricultural growth, only a few, often in combination with governance challenges, caused significant deviations, resulting in identifiable breaks along the growth path.

title: Income or Vintage? A North Carolina Case Study of Flood Insurance Retention under Risk Rating 2.0

detail.title: Income or Vintage? A North Carolina Case Study of Flood Insurance Retention under Risk Rating 2.0
detail.abstract: Using a reconstructed public OpenFEMA policy-term panel for North Carolina, this paper asks whether post-Risk Rating 2.0 (RR2.0) flood-insurance retention risk is better marked by area income or by legacy/pre-FIRM subsidy exposure (building vintage). The design is a single-state case study: prior national work documents RR2.0 demand effects and income/subsidy heterogeneity; here those public markers are placed in the same policy-level renewal model. We estimate discrete-time lapse models with quarter and county fixed effects and within-policy intensive-margin models. RR2.0 coincided with a 39% rise in median single-family out-of-pocket policy cost ($602 to $836), but aggregate lapse did not surge: household lapse stayed broadly stable across the reform window. Differential exit is concentrated among legacy/pre-FIRM policies, whose post-reform lapse rate rises 1.1 percentage points (≈12% of the ~9% base; p < 0.001; max-t adjusted p = 0.001), robust to alternative linkage keys, dropping the post-treatment premium control, primary-residence and coastal restrictions, logit specification, ZIP-cluster bootstrap, and excluding Hurricane-Helene-affected counties. The effect is small in absolute terms but grows in the event study as statutory rate caps phase in. By contrast, the area-income signal is weak: the only marginally significant income interaction in an income-only model (p = 0.047) is not robust once legacy enters (p = 0.18), and the income block remains jointly weak. Legacy/pre-FIRM status remains the stable marker and also predicts higher deductibles among stayers. Because observed premiums are capped and risk-endogenous, these estimates are not structural price elasticities. In this case study, legacy/pre-FIRM exposure is the stronger public-data marker of differential retention; whether that pattern generalizes is a national question.

title: How Withdrawal Behavior Destroys Leverage Capacity: Evidence from Leveraged FIRE Portfolios
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Withdrawal Behavior Destroys Leverage Capacity: Evidence from Leveraged FIRE Portfolios

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants, personal data, or animal subjects were involved in this study. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In leveraged retirement portfolios, the method of withdrawal determines not merely the sequence of asset liquidation, but whether the portfolio retains its capacity to sustain leverage over time. We formalize Leverage Capacity (LC_t = C_t × h / CR_min) as an observable state variable in the context of leveraged retirement portfolios, representing the maximum margin position supportable by the collateral base at time t. Under Physical-First withdrawal (Strategy A), each withdrawal permanently shifts the future path of leverage capacity downward, progressively reducing the excess returns that leverage generates. Using a half-Kelly leveraged S&P 500 portfolio ($1,000,000 physical, $140,000 margin) with inflation-adjusted annual withdrawals of $40,000 (Bengen, 1994) and two independent simulation methodologies—stationary block bootstrap and GARCH(1,1)—we compare three strategies: Physical-First (A), Margin-First without Rebuild (C), and Margin First with Rebuild (B). The liquidation-order effect (C vs. A) accounts for only 7% of the median terminal wealth difference, while the leverage-maintenance effect (B vs. C) accounts for 104%. Strategy B reduces portfolio depletion risk from 10.84% to 0.07% over 30 years. Results are robust to interest rate variation (2% 6%) and transaction costs up to 20 basis points.

title: The Limits of Prediction: A Comparative Analysis of Market Efficiency Across Three Kalshi Prediction Market Events (A Case Study in Forecasting Precision, Liquidity, and Information Incorporation)
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Limits of Prediction: A Comparative Analysis of Market Efficiency Across Three Kalshi Prediction Market Events (A Case Study in Forecasting Precision, Liquidity, and Information Incorporation)
detail.abstract: This paper examines three distinct Kalshi prediction market events-the US PPI MoM release, the FOMC rate decision with dissent count, and the 10-year Treasury yield-to explore the relationship between event characteristics, market liquidity, and forecasting precision. We find that prediction markets exhibit varying degrees of efficiency depending on the nature of the underlying event, the availability of information, and the liquidity of the contract. The PPI market, with its scheduled release and clear consensus forecast, demonstrated the most gradual information incorporation. The FOMC contract, with its combination of policy decision and human judgment (dissents), exhibited noisy information flow and overestimation of dissent probability. The Treasury yield contract, with its thin liquidity and lack of a specific announcement time, showed the most dramatic late-stage repricing. These findings have implications for the design of prediction markets, the interpretation of their prices as probability estimates, and the limits of forecasting in financial markets.

title: The Epistemic Puzzle of Digital Market Regulation

detail.title: The Epistemic Puzzle of Digital Market Regulation
detail.abstract: Contract law has always depended on knowledge of market practices, party preferences, and surrounding social realities. This article argues that the digital economy has produced a structural rupture in that dependence-the "epistemic puzzle": knowledge required to regulate contracting has been systematically captured by private actors, rendering classical mechanisms for producing and legitimizing regulatory knowledge increasingly obsolete. The article reconstructs contract law's conventional "epistemic triangle" connecting courts, legislatures, and contracting parties, exposing its reliance on heuristics and its incomplete account of structural inequalities in epistemic power. Building on this foundation, it traces how the digital economy strains this infrastructure through three developments: the privatization and commodification of contractrelevant knowledge within platform ecosystems; the fragmentation of markets into platformgoverned regulatory silos; and the automation of contract formation through smart contracts and blockchain, replacing interpretive legal fact-finding with ostensibly self-executing code. These observations inform a critical examination of co-regulation and standardization as the predominant regulatory responses to knowledge privatization-arguing that each risks entrenching the very asymmetries it purports to mitigate, without offering meaningful alternatives to the status quo. The article proposes reorienting contract law's epistemics around three pillars: accessibility, accountability, and participation in knowledge production. The future legitimacy of contract law hinges on preventing epistemic asymmetry from hardening into persistent epistemic monopoly.

reference: Forthcoming in fall 2026 (Volume 2, Issue 6) African Journal of International Economic Law
title: Harmonization and Lawyers’ Labour Mobility in Africa: Legal Education, AfCFTA and The Role of an Integrative Legal Pedagogy
affiliations: McGill Law Faculty

detail.title: Harmonization and Lawyers’ Labour Mobility in Africa: Legal Education, AfCFTA and The Role of an Integrative Legal Pedagogy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in fall 2026 (Volume 2, Issue 6) African Journal of International Economic Law

detail.abstract: The success of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) turns in part on whether the legal profession is equipped to service the commercial relationships it will generate. Yet this precondition has attracted surprisingly little deliberate attention. This paper suggests that the challenge of ensuring that African lawyers are educationally and professionally equipped for cross-border legal practice is one that policymakers and the African legal academy have not adequately reckoned with. Two structural deficits are identified. First, the procedural liberalisation of legal services markets, standing alone, cannot produce professionally competent cross-border lawyers in the absence of corresponding curricular and pedagogical reforms. Second, continental and regional frameworks for legal education harmonisation as they exist today remain too generic and too underdeveloped to meaningfully support the cross-border mobility of lawyers. Undergirding both deficits, among others, is the phenomenon of sovereign sensitivity, whereby states retain a peculiar interest in confining legal education and professional admission to nationally defined parameters. The paper suggests that, rather than waiting for the resolution of these macro-level institutional obstacles, African law schools and individual legal educators can begin to address the competence gap through micro-level pedagogical reform. Two integrative approaches are conceptually mapped out: comparativist legal pedagogy, which exposes students to the plurality of legal traditions operating across the continent, and transsystemic legal pedagogy, which invites students to reason across and beyond jurisdictional boundaries simultaneously.

title: Confidence Without Competence: How Naming an Asset Inflates Language-Model Conviction in Financial Forecasts
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: Confidence Without Competence: How Naming an Asset Inflates Language-Model Conviction in Financial Forecasts
detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as financial copilots: they summarize research, draft investment rationales, and answer questions like whether we should long or short a given stock. These models tend to answer in a very confident tone, and that confidence can mislead a reader about how reliable the underlying decision actually is. This paper asks whether that confidence is earned. We hold the market data fixed and change only one thing, whether the model is told which stock it is looking at, then measure how confident it sounds and how often it is actually right. The task is hourly price-direction prediction, finegrained enough that memorized training data is not a real concern. Across six models and six stocks, naming the stock makes the model more confident but no more accurate: its accuracy stays at the coin-flip level an efficient market implies, so the added confidence is unearned. The one exception is the largest model, whose extra confidence comes with a small but real accuracy gain. The practical message is that when a language model sounds confident about a named stock, that confidence reflects how familiar the name is, not how good the forecast is, and a product should not pass it on to users as a measure of reliability.

title: Determinants of Women’s Participation in Leadership and Management of Agricultural Cooperatives in Endamohoni, Tigray, Ethiopia
affiliations: Humera Agricultural Research Center - Tigray Agricultural Research Institute, Mekelle University and The Australian National University

detail.title: Determinants of Women’s Participation in Leadership and Management of Agricultural Cooperatives in Endamohoni, Tigray, Ethiopia
detail.abstract: Women's participation in all economic, social, and political spheres is crucial for a country’s development. In most developing countries, such as Ethiopia, women’s participation in various managerial activities is low, particularly in leadership and decision-making. The objectives of the study were to assess the governance structure of agricultural cooperatives, examine the extent of participation of women members in leadership positions, and identify the factors that affect women’s participation in agricultural cooperative leadership. A multi-stage sampling procedure was followed for the selection of sample women members.  Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and an ordered logit regression model. The participation of women in each leadership position should ideally be 50% or a minimum of 30%. However, for the study cooperatives, it was 11.11%. 40% women never participated in the main cooperative activities. Findings from the ordered logistics show that age, experience and education level of the household head and the household’s family size, non-farm income earning, livestock endowment, farm land endowment, and home distance to cooperative were found to be the determinant factors that affect the level of women’s participation in management and leadership of cooperatives. Helping women improve their involvement in non-farm income activities is recommended to enhance their participation level in decision-making positions. The Cooperative Promotion Office and other stakeholders should work to address the identified constraints to women’s participation in cooperative leadership.

title: Are we Better Off Interacting with Humans or AI in Conflict and Coordination Settings? *
affiliations: McMaster University, McMaster University and Toronto Metropolitan University

detail.title: Are we Better Off Interacting with Humans or AI in Conflict and Coordination Settings? *

declarations.ethicsApproval: The project has ethics approval from McMaster MREB #6107 and from TMU REB #2025-503.

detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly acts autonomously in economic and social environments, understanding how humans and AI interact strategically has become a central scientific and societal question. We report controlled experimental evidence on how humans and autonomous AI agents behave toward one another in repeated conflict and coordination settings. Unlike prior work using pre-programmed strategies or hypothetical judgments, we embed autonomous LLM agents directly into an incentivized laboratory experiment as strategic decision-makers interacting with both humans and other AI agents. Thus, AI agents in our study independently interpreted instructions, formed expectations, made gameplay decisions, generated round-by-round reasoning for their decisions and adapted dynamically to feedback. Specifically, humans and AI agents play either a 40-round repeated Prisoner's Dilemma or Battle of the Sexes, 20 rounds against each counterpart type. We elicit both humans' and AI's earnings beliefs before and after an initial 20-round block of play against each counterpart type, and observe dynamic behavior across human-human, human-AI, and AI-AI dyads under identical laboratory conditions. Humans show no strong ex ante preference between human and AI counterparts, but exhibit more reciprocity, cooperation and accommodation toward fellow humans. In contrast, AI agents display a systematic in-group bias toward AI. AI's thought processes highlight its aim to maximize joint payoffs, establish mutual cooperation and achieve coordination. Consequently, AI-AI pairs achieve the highest payoffs in both games. Our findings show that social preferences are endogenous to counterpart identity in mixed agent systems. These counterpart-contingent social preferences generate markedly different equilibrium dynamics across dyad types.

title: Finance and Tax Evasion: Evidence from Housing
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Wharton School of Business - Business Economics and Public Policy Department, Queen Mary University of London, Imperial College London and Queen Mary University of London

detail.title: Finance and Tax Evasion: Evidence from Housing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: Exempt
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: We study how mortgage finance relates to tax evasion in housing transactions. Using administrative data from São Paulo and Mumbai, covering 1.6 million and 180,000 transactions, respectively, we show that cash transactions bunch sharply at government guidance values, while mortgaged transactions bunch far less. These patterns persist within fine geography-year comparisons and property-value controls. An event study of Brazil's major 2015 mortgage-credit contraction shows that bunching rises when mortgage access falls. Back-of-the-envelope calculations imply transaction-tax revenue gains of 0.38-1.83% in São Paulo and 0.85-3.33% in Mumbai if cash transactions reported like mortgaged transactions.

title: Technology-Enabled Monitoring, Information Asymmetry, and Humanitarian Accountability: Evidence from the Afar Region of Ethiopia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Technology-Enabled Monitoring, Information Asymmetry, and Humanitarian Accountability: Evidence from the Afar Region of Ethiopia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research was conducted in accordance with IASC Operational Guidance on Data Responsibility in Humanitarian Action (2021) and ALNAP principles for ethical research in humanitarian settings. Voluntary participation, confidentiality, and informed consent were ensured throughout. No institutional review board was required as the research was conducted independently.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how technology-enabled monitoring systems transform information flows and accountability relationships in humanitarian operations in Ethiopia's Afar region. Drawing on 42 semistructured interviews and direct field observations conducted between March and August 2025, the research traces the socio-technical chain from the lived reality of communities to the dashboards used for strategic decision-making. The study introduces the concept of the Information Transformation Chain a framework that maps how data is systematically filtered, simplified, and reinterpreted at each node of the monitoring ecosystem. Contrary to the assumption that digital monitoring reduces information asymmetry, findings show it often redistributes and reshapes asymmetry in new and consequential ways. The analysis reveals a central paradox: systems designed to enhance accountability frequently strengthen upward accountability to donors while weakening downward accountability to affected communities. The Afar context-with its pastoral mobility, remoteness, infrastructure deficits, and linguistic diversity magnifies these dynamics in ways that have broader theoretical relevance. The study concludes by arguing for a shift from monitoring for verification toward monitoring for understanding. The "connectivity exclusion paradox" identified here whereby the communities most in need are systematically excluded from digital monitoring because they lack the infrastructure those systems require-deserves particular attention from practitioners and system designers.

title: The Role of Characters and Productivity for Economic Inclusiveness in Decentralized Economies: An Agent-Based Model
affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: The Role of Characters and Productivity for Economic Inclusiveness in Decentralized Economies: An Agent-Based Model
detail.abstract: Characters-understood as persistent preferences, habits, and behavioral dispositions-shape economic outcomes by influencing agents' pricing, purchasing, and consumption decisions. Through decentralized interactions, character heterogeneity affects access to essential goods and income, thereby determining who can sustain adequate living standards over time. This paper studies the role of character in shaping economic inclusiveness-defined as collective survival at adequate living standards-in decentralized market economies. We develop an agent-based survival model with heterogeneous characters. The simulations reveal a systematic trade-off between extractive characters and economic inclusiveness mediated by merit-based entitlement. Extractive agents leverage their productivity and market power to translate higher productivity into a larger share of the surplus when "productivity-based merit" entitles them to do so, at the expense of less productive agents, thereby gradually excluding them. This mechanism reduces economic inclusiveness in the absence of redistribution. Extractive characters increase short-term economic performance through selectionby eliminating low-productivity agents-while undermining long-term economic inclusion, which is fundamental to sustained prosperity. The results indicate that the inclusiveness and performance of decentralized market economies depend on the distribution of characters, and that cultivating generative characters is central for long-term economic inclusiveness in decentralised economies.

title: The Offer and the Threat: Foundations for a Positive Economics of Coercion
affiliations: Advisory House AG

detail.title: The Offer and the Threat: Foundations for a Positive Economics of Coercion
detail.abstract: Economics has an exact science of the offer and no equally exact science of the threat. We supply the missing half with a single criterion. Relative to the position the addressee holds by right, an interaction is an offer if declining it leaves them no worse than that baseline, and a threat if declining it leaves them worse. The baseline does three jobs that the older "rejection at no cost" formula could not. It dissolves the objection that every declined offer carries a cost, because the cost of a declined offer leaves the addressee at the baseline while a threat pushes them below it. It covers non-physical bads such as damage to reputation, which a criterion built on control of means cannot reach. And it keeps the criterion value-neutral, because the baseline enters as a declared parameter rather than as a verdict, and the apparatus is invariant across the admissible baselines. Classification can therefore be settled without settling justice. The catallactic mirror breaks at one point. Coerced compliance is a choice but not a demonstrated preference for mutual gain, so the welfare theorems of exchange do not carry over. This licenses a parallel science of coercion, distinct from conflict economics, which models objective payoffs and abstracts the structure of the act away, and it places that science beside Munger's euvoluntary exchange as its nearest cousin.

title: Decision-Based Portfolio Attribution: Exact Decomposition of Analyst Signals and Portfolio-Manager Decisions
affiliations: and

detail.title: Decision-Based Portfolio Attribution: Exact Decomposition of Analyst Signals and Portfolio-Manager Decisions
detail.abstract: We develop a telescoping attribution framework for evaluating analyst and portfolio-manager (PM) decision quality in equity portfolios. The framework builds a sequence of intermediate portfolios in which each adjacent step changes exactly one decision dimension, giving an exact decomposition of active return with no interaction term. The default specification is a hybrid market-cap-weighted (MCW) / equal-weighted (EW) chain: PM sector allocation is measured in Brinson-Fachler form against the MCW sector returns of the reference, while within-sector analyst and PM decision effects are measured on an EW basis. The framework's central contribution is the PM membership decomposition. Rather than routing the analyst-signal-to-PM-holdings gap through intermediate counterfactual portfolios, we classify each position on each day by whether it was held and whether it was currently BUY-rated, yielding an exact per-name-day identity that partitions the membership bridge into PM Selection (D6), PM Timing (D7), a structural equal-weight set-size residual (D8 PM Breadth), and PM Sizing (D9). Contribution magnitudes depend only on point-in-time realized state; the analyst ever-BUY and PM ever-held sets enter only to label each contribution as selection versus timing, never to size it. This labels-not-sizing property is what lets the decision-level partition preserve exact telescoping. For portfolios benchmarked against a broad external MCW index, the front-of-chain is organised as a 2 × 2 coverage/allocation taxonomy whose four chains telescope to the same total active return, with the six decision-side components D4-D9 numerically identical across all four. We verify exact telescoping on two fully worked examples. We use "skill" only as shorthand for "decision-attributed contribution" and treat the framework as diagnostic rather than predictive: components measured over a single window describe what happened, while forward-looking use requires the separate persistence and factor-risk analysis we identify as priority extensions.

title: A Cognitive Footprint in Archival Data: A Behavioral Sufficient Statistic for Cognitive Biases and M&A Success
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, University of Brasilia and

detail.title: A Cognitive Footprint in Archival Data: A Behavioral Sufficient Statistic for Cognitive Biases and M&A Success
detail.abstract: Drawing on behavioral sufficient statistic theory, we propose a reduced-form approach to examine the influence of cognitive biases in the decision-making process involving mergers and acquisitions (M&As). We re-conceptualize managerial ability not merely as an efficiency metric, but as a proxy for instrumental rationality and cognitive resource availability. Thus, our reduced-form model considers managerial ability as a sufficient statistic to investigate cognitive biases. We assume that more (less) able managers are less (more) susceptible to the influence of cognitive biases. Using large-scale archival financial data, we conduct two sets of tests. First, we validate our proxy by adapting the empirical frameworks of prior studies and substituting their cognitive-bias measures with the managerial ability score. We find robust evidence that managerial ability functions as a strong proxy for cognitive biases. Second, we test our proxy in the context of M&As. The main results reveal that a positive and statistically significant association between the premium paid on M&As-accounting goodwill-and firm returns emerges only in the top decile of managerial ability (where decision-making is less afflicted by behavioral distortions). Our findings indicate an M&A failure rate of 87%, suggesting that the majority of premiums paid in M&A deals represents the materialization of judgment errors rather than economic substance.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35382
title: When GDP Misleads: Inferring Living Standards from the Value of a Statistical Life
affiliations: University of Oxford and Stanford University

detail.title: When GDP Misleads: Inferring Living Standards from the Value of a Statistical Life

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Real GDP per person is a widely used proxy for living standards, but it can be a poor welfare measure when new goods or quality improvements matter, when nonmarket goods are significant, and when preferences are nonhomothetic --- all of which are true in practice. We propose an alternative that is robust to these concerns: under weak conditions, the growth rate of the value of a statistical life (VSL), together with standard Euler-equation objects, identifies the growth rate of lifetime utility. The intuition is that people routinely trade off consumption against mortality risk, and their willingness to pay for small risk reductions reveals the value of remaining lifetime utility. Implementing this approach for the United States suggests that lifetime utility may have risen by more than a factor of five since 1940, whereas conventional consumption-based calculations using a stable log/CRRA flow utility imply much smaller gains, on the order of a doubling. This calculation is sensitive to measures of the growth rate of the VSL, the rate of time preference, and the interest rate. For example, if the correct interest rate is 4 percentage points higher than the T-bill rate, then lifetime utility would be measured to have declined by more than half since 1940.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Explaining Station-Level Weather Sensitivity in Bike-Sharing Systems: A Spatial Analysis of Chicago's Divvy Network
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago and University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: Explaining Station-Level Weather Sensitivity in Bike-Sharing Systems: A Spatial Analysis of Chicago's Divvy Network
detail.abstract: Weather conditions are widely recognized as important determinants of bike-sharing demand. However, existing research has primarily focused on estimating average weather effects at the system, city, or user-group level, providing limited insight into why some stations are substantially more weather-sensitive than others. This study develops and applies a station-level Weather Sensitivity Index (WSI) to examine the spatial, built-environment, and socioeconomic determinants of weather sensitivity within Chicago’s Divvy bike-sharing system. The analysis proceeds in three stages. First, station-specific weather-response functions are estimated using three years of daily bike-sharing data and Negative Binomial regression models. Second, station-level responses to temperature, precipitation, snowfall, and wind are transformed into four dimensions of weather sensitivity and combined through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to construct a composite WSI. Third, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and spatial econometric models are employed to identify the factors associated with variation in weather sensitivity across stations. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity in station-level weather responses. Highly weather-sensitive stations are concentrated along Chicago’s lakefront and within recreational, tourism-oriented, and destination-focused environments, whereas stations located in more residential and activity-rich areas exhibit greater demand stability. Built-environment and socioeconomic characteristics explain a substantial share of observed variation in weather sensitivity. Stations located closer to Lake Michigan and within highly connected street networks tend to exhibit greater weather sensitivity, whereas higher activity density, larger shares of low-wage workers, and higher proportions of households owning multiple vehicles are associated with lower weather sensitivity. Spatial diagnostics reveal strong spatial clustering and significant spillover effects, indicating that weather sensitivity is influenced not only by local station characteristics but also by neighboring stations. The study contributes to the literature by shifting attention from average weather effects to variation in weather sensitivity, introducing a composite WSI, and demonstrating the importance of spatial processes in shaping weather-related vulnerability within urban bike-sharing systems. The findings provide practical guidance for targeted resilience planning and weather-responsive management of shared micromobility networks.

title: Missed Trips as an Indicator of Hidden Mobility Deprivation: Roles of Individual Constraints, Transportation Resources, Perceived Barriers, and Neighborhood Accessibility
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago, University of Illinois Chicago and University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: Missed Trips as an Indicator of Hidden Mobility Deprivation: Roles of Individual Constraints, Transportation Resources, Perceived Barriers, and Neighborhood Accessibility
detail.abstract: Transportation disadvantage is commonly evaluated using indirect indicators such as income, vehicle ownership, or transit availability, despite the fact that these measures do not directly capture whether individuals are ultimately able to complete intended travel. This study investigates missed or uncompleted trips as a behavioral manifestation of hidden mobility deprivation and realized accessibility failure. Using a weighted transportation survey in the Chicago metropolitan region integrated with neighborhood-level built-environment indicators from the EPA Smart Location Database (SLD), the study examines how sociodemographic characteristics, household transportation resources, perceived transportation barriers, and neighborhood accessibility conditions shape the likelihood of experiencing missed trips. A sequential binary logistic regression framework was employed to progressively incorporate transportation-resource variables, perception-based latent constructs, neighborhood accessibility indicators, and interaction effects. The results indicate that mobility impairments, constrained household transportation resources, lower perceived pedestrian safety, and weaker neighborhood accessibility conditions are significantly associated with higher probabilities of missed trips. Descriptive findings indicate that work-and health-related travel represented the most commonly missed trip purposes, while unavailable transportation options, affordability barriers, and excessive travel time burdens were among the most frequently reported constraints. Interaction analyses further reveal that the adverse effects of poor transit accessibility are substantially amplified among individuals living in zero-vehicle households, while higher neighborhood transit service frequency significantly reduces the probability of missed trips among individuals without driver's licenses. The findings demonstrate that unmet mobility needs emerge through the interaction between personal mobility constraints, transportation resources, subjective transportation experiences, and surrounding accessibility conditions. The study contributes to the transportation equity and accessibility literature by conceptualizing missed trips as a realized accessibility outcome and by integrating objective and perceived accessibility dimensions within a unified analytical framework. Overall, the findings support accessibility-oriented and equity-focused transportation policies aimed at reducing hidden mobility deprivation among vulnerable populations.

title: Stablecoins, Currency Digitalization and Optimal Policy

detail.title: Stablecoins, Currency Digitalization and Optimal Policy
detail.abstract: We study how stablecoins and digital payments reshape taxation, seigniorage, and public debt in a two-sector monetary model with endogenous sector choice, government bonds, and either fully reserved stablecoins or a central bank digital currency (CBDC). Four results follow. First, in the baseline cash economy a strict Laffer-curve trade-off binds inflation seigniorage against the formal tax base, while endogenous sector choice generates multiple equilibria. Second, once we add banks and government bonds, a larger public-debt stock lowers bond yields, opposite to a standard open-market operation, due to the removal of fixed inflation and passive fiscal accommodation. Third, private stablecoins-narrow banks backing tokens with Treasuries-create a macro-fiscal tension: their reserve demand subsidizes government borrowing but starves banks of collateral, and their circulation may also reduce seigniorage. Hence they improve welfare only within a narrow window, from issuer satiation near three times the current U.S. float (2% of the bill stock) to bank collateral scarcity near eight; considering issuer misrepresentation, a monopolist holds about half a competitive market's reserves: a safer reserve ratio but a smaller yield subsidy. Fourth, a parallel CBDC path lacks this captive demand, sparing bank collateral but burdening the Treasury with a debt volume that forces money growth from about 4% to 21%; the two trade off oppositely-at a common fiscal target the stablecoin path attains higher welfare and smaller trading-wedge losses, while at a common inflation rate the CBDC path attains higher welfare on lower government expenditure.

title: From Transit Service Gaps to Mobility Deprivation: The Role of Perceived Accessibility in Shaping Missed Trips and Automobile Dependency
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago, University of Illinois Chicago and University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: From Transit Service Gaps to Mobility Deprivation: The Role of Perceived Accessibility in Shaping Missed Trips and Automobile Dependency
detail.abstract: Transportation disadvantage and hidden mobility deprivation are increasingly recognized as important equity concerns in urban transportation systems. Although previous studies have extensively examined transit service quality and accessibility, relatively limited research has investigated how perceived transit-service deficiencies influence accessibility perceptions and mobility deprivation outcomes within an integrated analytical framework. This study examines the relationships among transit service gaps, perceived accessibility, missed trips, and automobile dependency in the Chicago metropolitan area. Transit service gap indicators were constructed by comparing respondents’ perceived importance and satisfaction levels across multiple transit-service attributes, including reliability, accessibility, transfer convenience, information availability, cleanliness, affordability, and safety. Exploratory factor analysis identified two latent dimensions of transit-service gaps, labeled Operational Gap and Experience Gap. The analytical framework was estimated using weighted Generalized Structural Equation Modeling (GSEM), allowing the simultaneous examination of perceived accessibility, binary missed-trip outcomes, and ordered automobile-dependency outcomes. The results indicate that larger Operational Gaps significantly reduce perceived accessibility, while stronger neighborhood-level transit accessibility improves accessibility perceptions. Lower perceived accessibility was associated with both a higher likelihood of experiencing missed trips and greater automobile dependency. Indirect-effects analysis further suggests that transit-service deficiencies and neighborhood accessibility conditions influence mobility deprivation outcomes partly through perceived accessibility pathways. In addition, mobility impairments, zero-vehicle households, and household transportation-resource constraints substantially increase the likelihood of experiencing missed trips, while low-income status and limited transit proximity contribute to greater automobile dependency. The findings suggest that transportation disadvantage cannot be fully understood using infrastructure availability or objective accessibility measures alone. Instead, subjective accessibility perceptions represent an important pathway through which transportation conditions influence mobility outcomes. The study contributes to transportation equity research by conceptualizing transit service gaps as indicators of unmet mobility needs and by integrating transit-service deficiencies, perceived accessibility, and behavioral mobility deprivation outcomes within a unified analytical framework.

reference: NBER Working Paper No. w35384
title: When Medicaid Pays the Bill: Routine Vision Benefits, Eye Care Use, and Eyeglasses Spending Among Dual-eligible Medicare Enrollees
affiliations: , University of California, Irvine and Tufts University

detail.title: When Medicaid Pays the Bill: Routine Vision Benefits, Eye Care Use, and Eyeglasses Spending Among Dual-eligible Medicare Enrollees

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Vision problems are prevalent among Medicare beneficiaries, with the majority having treatable conditions including uncorrected refractive error and cataracts. However, traditional Medicare does not cover routine eye exams or eyeglasses, and Medicare Advantage supplemental vision benefits often include low annual limits. We examine the effects of Medicaid routine vision benefits among adults dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, a population with high rates of vision impairment, morbidity, and disability. Using 2002-2019 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey data and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate that Medicaid routine vision benefits increase past-year eye exams, eyeglasses purchases, and Medicaid spending on eyeglasses while reducing out-of-pocket spending. We also find suggestive evidence of spillovers to Medicare Advantage spending on eyeglasses, consistent with Medicaid routine vision coverage inducing additional eyeglasses purchases among Medicare Advantage enrollees with supplemental vision benefits, although estimates are modest.

title: China's Economic Statecraft, Export Sophistication, and Business Cycle Dynamics along the Belt and Road: Evidence from the South Caucasus Region
affiliations: , Southeast University and Communication University of China

detail.title: China's Economic Statecraft, Export Sophistication, and Business Cycle Dynamics along the Belt and Road: Evidence from the South Caucasus Region
detail.abstract: This study examines how China's OFDI and infrastructure projects affect export sophistication in 60 BRI countries (2013-2024). Using two-way fixed effects and system GMM, we find no significant average effect, but substantial heterogeneity by income level. Chinese OFDI boosts export sophistication in middle-income countries, while infrastructure projects do so in low-income countries. Neither works in high-income countries, yet global FDI consistently drives upgrading. In the South Caucasus, evidence suggests Chinese OFDI has stronger effects during economic contractions than expansions (β = 0.0057, p < 0.05), though small-sample caution is warranted. Significant intra-regional heterogeneity exists-Azerbaijan achieves high sophistication despite low Chinese investment, while Georgia shows the opposite. Findings highlight the need to tailor economic statecraft to host countries' development stages and specific characteristics.

reference: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/iKIET/215; i-KIET Issues & Analysis, No. 215
title: From Trade to Supply Chains: Policy Implications of the Korea-India Summit

detail.title: From Trade to Supply Chains: Policy Implications of the Korea-India Summit

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/iKIET/215
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Recently, South Korea and India agreed to expand bilateral trade to USD 50 billion by 2030 and to advance cooperation centered on supply chains and emerging industries, laying an institutional foundation through expanded strategic-industry cooperation, the establishment of an Industrial Cooperation Committee, and the resumption of negotiations to improve the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA). The new Industrial Cooperation Committee is expected to serve as the core institutional foundation of Korea-India cooperation, addressing the fragmentation of existing cooperation channels and building a whole-of-government platform specialized in industrial cooperation. 

The summit marks a turning point in Korea-India cooperation, shifting the focus from trade-centered cooperation to supply chain and industrial cooperation. It strengthens supply chain resilience and transforms the bilateral cooperation framework toward a production-and technology-based model through expanded cooperation in strategic resources and high-value-added industries. Expanding cooperation with India will require proactive efforts to address India's trade balance concerns, as improving the trade balance remains an important policy priority and an important consideration in trade negotiations; building a sustainable partnership calls for establishing global production and export hubs and increasing the local sourcing of intermediate goods. Raising CEPA utilization requires reforming rules of origin and related systems, as complex origin criteria and certification procedures constrain use of the agreement. Stronger linkage between development cooperation and Korea-India industrial cooperation is also needed, as the limited integration of official development assistance (ODA) with industrial cooperation reduces the effectiveness of implementation.

title: Mobility Styles, Transportation Barriers, and Missed Travel: A Latent Class Analysis of Urban Travelers in the Chicago Metropolitan Area
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago, University of Illinois Chicago and University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: Mobility Styles, Transportation Barriers, and Missed Travel: A Latent Class Analysis of Urban Travelers in the Chicago Metropolitan Area
detail.abstract: Understanding how individuals organize and experience daily travel is essential for promoting equitable and effective transportation systems. While previous studies have identified distinct travel behavior segments, relatively little attention has been devoted to understanding how transportation barriers, accessibility conditions, and unmet mobility needs differ across mobility styles. This study applies Latent Class Analysis (LCA) to identify mobility styles among urban travelers based on their use of six transportation modes: driving, walking, public transit, ride-hailing, taxi services, and micromobility. To further examine the characteristics and implications of the identified classes, R3STEP models are used to investigate factors associated with class membership, and BCH analyses are employed to compare mobility-related outcomes across classes while accounting for classification uncertainty. Three mobility styles were identified: Transit-Oriented Multimodal Travelers, Shared-Mobility-Oriented Travelers, and Automobile-Dependent Travelers. The results indicate that vehicle ownership, driver's license possession, transit accessibility, transit service availability, built-environment characteristics, transportation barriers, and transportation-related perceptions of safety and equity are significant correlates of mobility style membership. The findings also reveal important differences in mobility outcomes across classes. Transit-Oriented Multimodal Travelers reported the highest level of daily activity participation but also the highest prevalence of missed travel, suggesting that active engagement in daily travel does not necessarily imply that mobility needs are fully satisfied. In contrast, Shared-Mobility-Oriented Travelers exhibited the most favorable outcomes, including higher well-being and neighborhood resources, more positive evaluations of Ride-hailing service quality, greater trust in Ride-hailing services, and the lowest prevalence of missed travel. The findings demonstrate that mobility styles reflect broader differences in transportation opportunities, constraints, and experiences rather than simple variation in mode use. By linking mobility styles to transportation barriers, accessibility conditions, and unmet mobility needs, this study contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of transportation disadvantage and hidden mobility deprivation. The results further highlight the value of incorporating missed travel measures into transportation planning and evaluation frameworks, as observed travel activity alone may not fully reflect whether individuals are able to satisfy their daily mobility needs.

title: The Rise of Türkiye's Drone Diplomacy In Africa: A Critical Assessment

detail.title: The Rise of Türkiye's Drone Diplomacy In Africa: A Critical Assessment
detail.abstract: I wrote this paper because I kept reading news about Turkey selling drones to African countries, but nobody was talking about what actually happens on the ground. So I collected reports from Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, the International Crisis Group, and Foreign Policy magazine covering 2023 to 2025. What I found surprised me. Yes, Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones help governments fight insurgents. But in Burkina Faso, one set of strikes in January 2024 killed at least 60 civiliansmostly women and children. In Somalia, a Turkish drone killed seven young people, including an eight-year-old, after the military misidentified a target. Turkey does not publish any data on its strikes, and it refuses independent monitoring. This paper argues that Turkey's "no-strings-attached" drone diplomacy has a hidden cost that scholars have mostly ignored. My study is limited because I only used Englishlanguage sources and no interviews.

title: "Fire Sale" after Fire Disasters: Safety Risk and Housing Prices
affiliations: Deakin University - Department of Finance, Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance and

detail.title: "Fire Sale" after Fire Disasters: Safety Risk and Housing Prices
detail.abstract: This paper examines how a salient residential fire disaster affects the pricing of safety risk in housing markets. Using the Wang Fuk Court fire in Hong Kong in November 2025 as a shock, we study whether old residential estates that are not physically damaged but share similar safety-related characteristics experience a valuation decline after the disaster. We find that, three months after the fire, prices of old-estate units decline by about 2% relative to newer-estate units, compared with their pre-fire difference. The decline is 2-3 times larger for high-floor units and old government-related projects, but is not limited to nearby districts, suggesting a city-wide repricing of safety risk. We also document a surge in transaction volume by 16-19% among old estates, suggesting that motivated selling by owners serves as a potential underlying mechanism.

title: Evaluating Interventions with Many Outcomes: Evidence from the Big Brothers Big Sisters Experiment
affiliations: Georgia State University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Evaluating Interventions with Many Outcomes: Evidence from the Big Brothers Big Sisters Experiment
detail.abstract: Many social interventions are intended to affect broad sets of related behaviors rather than a single outcome. In such settings, treatment effects may be spread across multiple measures, making individual outcomes difficult to detect even when an intervention meaningfully changes the underlying construct it was designed to influence. This paper revisits the experimental microdata from the 1991 Big Brothers Big Sisters randomized evaluation, which collected hundreds of survey measures without a formal pre-analysis plan, and reported mostly insignificant results. I introduce a directional permutation test designed for settings where treatment is expected to move many related outcomes in a common direction. The test uses the number of correctly-signed estimates as its test statistic and, by permuting treatment assignment, automatically accounts for dependence across outcomes. Applying this approach to a battery of 21 behavioral outcomes asked in the original RCT, I find that 18 favor the treatment group, a pattern that arises in fewer than 1 in 1,000 permutations of the treatment assignment (p = .0003). Summary indices and joint significance tests yield similar conclusions. The findings provide strong evidence of broad short-run behavioral improvements and help interpret recent evidence on the long-run effects of mentoring (Bell, 2026a,b). More broadly, the results illustrate how analyses focused on individual outcomes may understate evidence of meaningful change-and how directional information can be used to recover that evidence when treatment effects are dispersed across many related measures. JEL codes: C12, J13, J62

title: Reviewing the EU Merger Guidelines - Response to the public consultation on the draft text of the new EU Merger Guidelines
affiliations: University of Leeds School of Law

detail.title: Reviewing the EU Merger Guidelines - Response to the public consultation on the draft text of the new EU Merger Guidelines

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: In this response to the European Commission’s public consultation on the Draft EU Merger Guidelines, I provide expert comments on a series of issues, new and old, addressed in the guidelines that are important for substantive merger review and enforcement practice such as: i) common ownership and minority shareholdings – including their occasionally needed differential treatment and their proper integration into EU merger control enforcement, ii) structural indicators, safe harbours and theories of harm – their restructuring, links between them and their potential interaction with the newly introduced “innovation shield”; iii) the “theory of benefit”, efficiencies and procedure – the practical implications and significance of the former concept in effectively incorporating efficiencies in the merger review process; iv) objectives, discretion and the role of EU merger control – the recognition that a more strategic and pragmatic EU merger policy that is open to broader objectives and merger benefits and expands the Commission’s discretion needs to be counterbalanced by a narrower and more objective standard for its application. In discussing these issues, I analyse both positive developments and weaknesses in the draft text and focus on how the analytical framework can be fine-tuned to enhance substantive rigour and coherence but also to provide clearer guidance to business thus suggesting specific ways in which the final text can be improved.

title: Constitutions as Credible Constraints on Despots

detail.title: Constitutions as Credible Constraints on Despots
detail.abstract: Powerful and unconstrained leaders often hinder the development of their nations. This phenomenon has often been linked to the commitment issues that result from the lack of constraints facing such leaders. Therefore, restricting the powers of such leaders through constitutions has been widely considered as a potential solution to these issues. Nonetheless, it remains unclear when the de jure stipulations of a constitution would translate into de facto constraints on a powerful leader, particularly when these constraints rely on enforcement by other self-interested actors who can be swayed through bribery or threats of violence. Through a theoretical model I investigate what characteristics ensure that constitutions provide credible constraints on a powerful leader. Specifically, I emphasize the role of constitutions in incentivizing opposition against a leader, and the challenge of designing them to fulfill two conflicting objectives. My investigation reveals why similar constitutions may not always be respected when implemented in different contexts. Moreover, it also reveals a link between majority decision rules and transparency in voting, which helps explain the prevalence of these characteristics in modern constitutions.

title: The Village Framework: A Maternal-Centered Model for Social Support, Clinical Care, and Structural Equity Across the Reproductive Continuum

detail.title: The Village Framework: A Maternal-Centered Model for Social Support, Clinical Care, and Structural Equity Across the Reproductive Continuum

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No external funding was received for this work. This manuscript was developed from a public health capstone project conducted at St. Francis College, Brooklyn, New York.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: The cultural proverb "it takes a village to raise a child" has shaped collective understandings of social support for decades. Yet a fundamental omission persists within this construct: the mother herself is rarely positioned as a primary beneficiary of the village she is expected to build. This paper presents The Village Framework, a maternal-centered conceptual framework proposing that the health and wellbeing of mothers across the reproductive continuum depend on the stability and interaction of three interdependent pillars: Social Support, Clinical Care, and Structural Support. These pillars rest on a Cultural and Equity Foundation that functions as the operative lens through which each pillar must be evaluated and delivered. Drawing on Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, the Social Ecological Model, the Convoy Model of Social Support, the Fourth Trimester Framework, and the Reproductive Justice Framework, this paper synthesizes previously separate strands of theory into a single maternal-centered architecture. The framework advances three core propositions: first, that the mother must be recentered as a primary unit of care within the village construct; second, that the village is structurally unstable when any single pillar fails, regardless of the strength of the others; and third, that the period from preconception through the first year of the child's life is a foundational developmental window for both maternal and child health. A complete village is hypothesized to reduce maternal mortality risk, improve continuity of care, reduce postpartum mental health burden, strengthen mother-infant bonding, decrease perinatal substance use disorders, and create healthier developmental conditions for children. Four testable hypotheses are proposed to guide future empirical work. The framework is universal in scope and equity-conscious in application, with particular relevance to populations for whom systemic pillar failures have been most persistent.
