title: The Legal Fiction of Non-Entry under the New Pact on Migration and Asylum: Reflections on the Danané and Others Judgment
affiliations: University of Minho - Research Centre for Justice and Governance (JusGov)

detail.title: The Legal Fiction of Non-Entry under the New Pact on Migration and Asylum: Reflections on the Danané and Others Judgment

keywords: New Pact on Migration and Asylum
Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU)

publicationDetails.journalName: JusGov Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal fiction of non-entry within the framework of the New Pact on Migration and Asylum, with particular attention to the judgment of the Court of Justice of the European Union in Danané and Others (Joined Cases C-50/24 to C-56/24). The analysis explores how the progressive functionalisation of borders within the Common European Asylum System has transformed the traditional territorial conception of the border into a differentiated legal regime based on screening procedures, border procedures and mechanisms of early classification. Against this background, the paper assesses the implications of Danané and Others for the development of a functional conception of the border and for the operation of the legal fiction of non-entry under EU asylum law. It argues that, although the judgment confirms the possibility of maintaining applicants under a border regime despite their physical presence within the territory of a Member State, it simultaneously reaffirms that effective control over the individual continues to trigger obligations derived from fundamental rights. Particular attention is paid to the role of effective control, non-refoulement and access to international protection as material limits to the operation of territorial fictions in contemporary European migration governance.

title: Cost of Capital, Concessional Finance and Adaptation Investment
affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business, Ca Foscari University of Venice and Utrecht University

detail.title: Cost of Capital, Concessional Finance and Adaptation Investment

declarations.funderStatement: Irene Monasterolo and Karl Naumann-Woleske acknowledge financial support from the ESG Risk Management Framework for the Financial Sector (ESGRM, Grant Agreement ID: 101145727). Irene Monasterolo also acknowledges support from NATURE 3B, funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No. 101182455. Andrea Mazzocchetti acknowledges financial support from the European Union – NextGenerationEU, under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), Mission 4, Component 2, Investment 1.3, in the framework of the GRINS – Growing Resilient, Inclusive and Sustainable project (GRINS PE00000018 – CUP H73C22000930001).

detail.abstract: Adaptation investments are crucial to build economic resilience to climate risks and maintain economic competitiveness. However, the high cost of capital is a barrier to increased investment, especially in emerging markets and developing economies. The role of National development banks' (NDBs) concessional lending to ease access to adaptation finance has been advocated but we know little about the conditions under which it can effectively catalyze adaptation investments, and its macro-financial implications. Here we quantitatively study the impact of NDBs' concessional finance on the cost of capital for adaptation investments, on future economic damage reduction, and on economic recovery. We model climate resilient capital and a national development bank in a Stock-flow Consistent macro-financial model, which integrates forward-looking disasters risks from the Network for Greening the Financial System short-term climate scenarios. We calibrate the model to Brazil and the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES). We find that concessional lending can crowd-in private investments in resilience, and increase the share of resilient capital in the economy to up to 20% over 10 years, easing firms' access to banks' co-financing in the aftermath of the natural disasters. Furthermore, BDNES' derisking of adaptation investments contributes to increase Brazilian banks' financial stability: higher firm resilience to climate risks dampens the increase in default probabilities and credit risk following natural disasters. At the same time, our results show a balance-sheet trade-off in the design of concessional lending depending on the level of concessionality. Thus, scaling up adaptation through NDBs may require complementary fiscal and financial measures.

title: Do Foreign Portfolio Investors Drive Indian Equity Returns, or Do They Simply Follow Market Momentum?

detail.title: Do Foreign Portfolio Investors Drive Indian Equity Returns, or Do They Simply Follow Market Momentum?
detail.abstract: Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) activity is frequently mentioned as a major driver of Indian equity market performance. This paper investigates the relationship between monthly FPI net flows and NIFTY 50 returns between March 2021 and March 2026. Four regression models are estimated to evaluate both contemporaneous and predictive relationships, while controlling for global risk sentiment using the CBOE Volatility Index (VIX). Results indicate a statistically significant contemporaneous association between FPI flows and NIFTY returns. However, this relationship disappears when FPI flows are lagged by one month. In contrast, the VIX emerges as a statistically significant predictor in the lagged specification. These findings suggest that foreign portfolio flows move alongside market performance but do not provide reliable predictive information regarding future returns.

title: The Effects of Reducing Minimum Staffing Requirements on Nursing Home Staffing and Quality: Evidence from Florida

detail.title: The Effects of Reducing Minimum Staffing Requirements on Nursing Home Staffing and Quality: Evidence from Florida
detail.abstract: Given a strong association and causal relationship between staffing levels and quality of care, many states have imposed minimum staffing requirements for nursing homes. However, relatively few studies have attempted to evaluate the causal effect of these requirements. In this study, I exploit an April 2022 reduction in Florida's minimum staffing requirement (HB 1239), which lowered the state's mandated 2.5 Nurse Aide (NA) Hours Per Resident Day (HPRD) to 2.0 and permitted nursing homes to meet the 3.6 HPRD direct-care requirement using other non-nursing staff (such as therapists), and evaluate the effects of the policy on staffing and risk-adjusted quality outcomes. Using event study and difference-indifferences models with entropy-balanced weights that weight non-treated states based on their similarity to Florida's pre-treatment characteristics, I find that Florida's nursing homes responded almost entirely through reductions in NA HPRD, a 6.8 to 8.8 percent reduction, with negligible changes among other occupational categories despite the option to substitute toward them. Consistent with the theoretical model, these reductions are statistically larger at lower-acuity facilities, which are more likely to be bound by the mandate, and statistically smaller at high-acuity facilities. Entropy-weighted quality estimates, which adjust for Florida's distinct attributes, show statistically significant increases in riskadjusted hospitalizations, with partially offsetting reductions in emergency department visits, among both short-and long-stay residents. Since these outcomes are mutually exclusive by construction, this pattern is consistent with residents reaching to the emergency department in worse health and being admitted rather than discharged, implying lower-quality care.

title: The Private Gate: Gated Biological Artificial Intelligence, the WHO Pandemic Agreement, and the Governance Vacuum in Pandemic Preparedness

detail.title: The Private Gate: Gated Biological Artificial Intelligence, the WHO Pandemic Agreement, and the Governance Vacuum in Pandemic Preparedness

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I was previously working with the world health organisation and the United Nations office project services, however those previous engagements do not influence my study. So there is no conflict of interest in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not relevant

detail.abstract: On 29 May 2026, OpenAI launched the Rosalind Biodefense programme, built on a specialised life-sciences reasoning model, GPT-Rosalind. The programme combines an open, sponsored “developer track” with a restricted “government track” limited to select United States federal agencies and allied partners. This paper argues that, whatever the programme’s clinical merits, its architecture concentrates the most capability-rich tier of a dual-use biological technology in a single private firm, governed by undisclosed vetting and data-handling terms, and outside any multilateral legal framework. The timing is decisive. The WHO Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, cannot open for signature until its Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) annex is adopted; the Seventy-ninth World Health Assembly (May 2026) extended those negotiations to 2027, and entry into force will require sixty ratifications thereafter. The public, treaty-based architecture is thus years from binding effect while the private architecture is being entrenched in months. Drawing on the Pandemic Agreement (notably Articles 12 and 31), the 2024 International Health Regulations amendments, the Convention on Biological Diversity and Nagoya Protocol, and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, the paper identifies a governance vacuum and proposes that AI-derived analytical capability be treated as a benefit subject to sharing; that frontier biological models embedded in public-health systems meet published, independent vetting and audit standards; and that States, India among them, develop sovereign and regional computational capacity. The argument is offered as a contribution to the PABS annex negotiations and to plurilateral fora including the Quad and BRICS.

title: Mutual Fund Regulation in India: Legal Reforms After the Franklin Templeton Case

detail.title: Mutual Fund Regulation in India: Legal Reforms After the Franklin Templeton Case
detail.abstract: The Franklin Templeton debt fund crisis of 2020, which triggered the abrupt winding-up of six schemes amid severe liquidity constraints during the COVID-19 pandemic, exposed critical vulnerabilities in India’s mutual fund regulatory architecture. Affecting over three lakh investors and assets worth more than ₹25,000 crore, the episode raised profound concerns regarding investor consent, trustee oversight, fund governance, and regulatory efficacy under the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996. This research critically examines the legal and institutional shortcomings revealed by the case and evaluates SEBI’s subsequent regulatory reforms. Key measures include enhanced liquidity risk management frameworks, mandatory stress testing, swing pricing mechanisms, strengthened disclosure norms, and reinforced trustee responsibilities. While these reforms have significantly bolstered investor protection, transparency, and systemic resilience, persistent gaps remain in enforcement efficiency, trustee independence, and proactive crisis management.

title: Regulatory Compliance For Artificial Intelligence-Based Insurance Systems In The United States

detail.title: Regulatory Compliance For Artificial Intelligence-Based Insurance Systems In The United States
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence ("AI") has rapidly become embedded in nearly every facet of the American insurance industry. Insurers now deploy machine learning models to price risk, underwrite policies, detect fraud, adjudicate claims, and tailor consumer communications. Yet the legal infrastructure governing these systems has lagged behind their operational sophistication. Because the McCarran-Ferguson Act preserves the primacy of state regulation of insurance, 1 the federal government has played a comparatively limited role in policing algorithmic decision-making in this sector. Into that vacuum, state insurance regulators have stepped with widely varying speeds, methods, and ambitions. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners' ("NAIC") 2023 Model Bulletin on the Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems by Insurers 2 , Colorado's pioneering algorithmic governance regulation, 3 and the New York Department of Financial Services' July 2024 Circular Letter No. 7 4 collectively represent the emerging contours of an AI compliance regime built on three pillars: corporate governance, quantitative bias testing, and consumer transparency. This Article offers the first comprehensive descriptive and normative analysis of that emerging regime. It argues that, although the current state-led approach has produced impressive substantive innovations particularly Colorado's quantitative testing requirements 5 and New York's principles-based fairness framework 6 the regime as a whole suffers from three structural pathologies: (1) compliance arbitrage produced by uneven state adoption; (2) over-reliance on internal selfpolicing without external audit or independent verification; and (3) ambiguity regarding the proper analytical framework for algorithmic fairness in insurance, an industry whose entire business model depends on risk classification. Drawing on a comparative review of the NAIC Model Bulletin, the Colorado regulations, the New York Circular Letter, and emerging guidance from a dozen additional states, the Article proposes a framework for harmonizing existing requirements, strengthening external accountability, and reconciling fairness-testing methodologies with the actuarial fairness norms that have long animated insurance law.

title: Can Mortality Drive Monarchs Toward Democratic Reforms?

detail.title: Can Mortality Drive Monarchs Toward Democratic Reforms?
detail.abstract: Do monarchs expecting brief reigns have the incentives to establish democratic institutions? In contrast with prevailing theories in political economy, I argue that the prospect of a short reign may in itself incentivize self-interested monarchs to establish democratic institutions that constrain their powers. To support this argument, I analyze a model of elite-driven democratization, using the reign of Jigme Dorji Wangchuck in Bhutan to illustrate its mechanisms and implications. In this model, absolute monarchy may prove costly and inefficient due to the short time horizons of monarchs who fear death. Consequently, such monarchs may seek to implement democratic institutions which limit their powers, establishing a more efficient constitutional monarchy. In light of this, I highlight how salient signals of a monarch's mortality, such as observable health problems, may act as catalysts for democratic reforms.

reference: Control de Convencionalidad. Impacto, Transformaciones y Desafíos, Rodrigo Mudrovitsch, Mariela Morales Antoniazzi y Eduardo Ferrer Mac-Gregor (Eds.), Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos, Tirant lo Blanch y Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law, 2026 (forthcoming)
title: Conventionality Control and Its Next Frontier: From ESCERs to Sustainable Economic Governance
affiliations: University of Washington School of Law

detail.title: Conventionality Control and Its Next Frontier: From ESCERs to Sustainable Economic Governance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Control de Convencionalidad. Impacto, Transformaciones y Desafíos, Rodrigo Mudrovitsch, Mariela Morales Antoniazzi y Eduardo Ferrer Mac-Gregor (Eds.), Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos, Tirant lo Blanch y Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law, 2026 (forthcoming)

detail.abstract:
On the twentieth anniversary of the Case of Almonacid Arellano et al. v. Chile, the judgment that initiated conventionality control in the Inter-American System, this essay analyzes the evolution of this tool and proposes its next frontier of impact. First, we briefly review the expansion of the jurisprudential line of conventionality control. Second, we document the strengthening of the direct justiciability of economic, social, cultural, and environmental rights (ESCERs) through the invocation of Article 26 of the American Convention and the technique of integrating “missing rights,” borrowed from the African Human Rights System. On that basis, this research argues that the natural frontier of conventionality control is the architecture of economic governance—the debt, fiscal, monetary, and tax policies that determine the very guarantee of ESCERs. Through the proposal of a Right to a Sustainable Economy, the author argues that economic decisions with a direct, foreseeable, and significant impact on human rights must be subject to a reasonableness test, governed by the principles of intergenerational equity, non-regressivity, due diligence, proportionality, and transparency, without replacing the technical function of economic authorities. The article is part of the project for a Latin American Ius Constitutionale Commune and engages in a dialogue with recent work from other regional and international systems, as well as with the United Nations’ mandates on development and extreme poverty.

This paper is forthcoming as a chapter in: Rodrigo Mudrovitsch, Mariela Morales Antoniazzi, and Eduardo Ferrer Mac-Gregor (eds.), Control de Convencionalidad. Impacto, Transformaciones y Desafíos, Inter-American Court of Human Rights/Max Planck Institute for Comparative Public Law and International Law, Tirant lo Blanch, 2026. This version is posted as a working paper preprint. The author retains the right to share pre-publication versions of her own contributions.

title: Momentum Effect in Indian Mid-Cap Equities: Evidence from the NSE Midcap 150

detail.title: Momentum Effect in Indian Mid-Cap Equities: Evidence from the NSE Midcap 150

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the presence and persistence of the momentum effect in Indian mid-cap equities using monthly return data for 130 constituent stocks of the NSE Nifty Midcap 150 index over the period April 2019 to March 2024. Employing a two-factor regression framework incorporating market excess return and the Winners Minus Losers (WML) momentum factor as the primary specification, and testing robustness through the full Carhart (1997) four-factor model over a data-constrained sub-period, we construct momentum-sorted quintile portfolios and test whether past return momentum generates statistically significant risk-adjusted returns. The WML factor earns a mean return of 1.470% per month, equivalent to 19.14% on an annualised basis, confirming the presence of a robust momentum premium in the Indian midcap segment. The winner portfolio (P5) exhibits a strongly positive and statistically significant WML factor loading of +0.472 (t = 5.908), while the loser portfolio (P1) loads negatively at-0.790 (t =-9.755), both significant at the 1% level. These findings persist in the post-COVID sub-sample (April 2020 to March 2024), with the winner portfolio's momentum loading strengthening to +0.517 (t = 5.146), suggesting that momentum profits are not confined to any specific market regime. Comprehensive diagnostic testing confirms the validity of OLS assumptions across all specifications. Our results contribute to the growing body of empirical asset pricing literature on Indian equity markets and carry implications for investment practitioners, market regulators, and the broader debate on market efficiency in emerging economies.

title: Intersecting Gender and Age Inequalities in Earnings and COVID-19 Income Loss: Evidence from Thailand
affiliations: National Institute of Development Administration, National Institute of Development Administration and National Institute of Development Administration (NIDA) - School of Development Economics

detail.title: Intersecting Gender and Age Inequalities in Earnings and COVID-19 Income Loss: Evidence from Thailand
detail.abstract: Using survey data from the Bangkok Metropolitan Region, this study examines gender- and age-based disparities in the labor market and analyzes the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on income loss across demographic groups. The results indicate that older women experience intersecting age and gender inequalities and have the lowest average employment income. Household chore responsibilities are negatively associated with earnings. Although 84.3% of women report at least one housework responsibility, those with heavier burdens are more likely to work as self-employed workers in the informal sector. Consequently, they earn less and face greater income losses during the pandemic due to limited social protection. Overall, the pandemic resulted in income losses, with stronger effects among working-age individuals than older respondents. Self-employed workers are the most affected group relative to workers in other employment sectors.

title: 'The Right to Education', 'The Right to Health' and 'The Right to be Heard': The Intermingled Lullaby of 'The Good, Bad and The Ugly' in the Dream of a Sustainable World
affiliations: Burdwan Medical College and Hospital

detail.title: 'The Right to Education', 'The Right to Health' and 'The Right to be Heard': The Intermingled Lullaby of 'The Good, Bad and The Ugly' in the Dream of a Sustainable World
detail.abstract: "Education is the special manifestation of man; Education is the treasure which can be preserved without the fear of loss; Education secures material pleasure, happiness and fame; Education is the teacher of the teacher; Education is God incarnate; Education secures honour at the hands of the State, not money; A man without education is equal to animal". [Bhartruhari, Neethi Shatakam (First Century B.C.), (As cited in Unni Krishnan, J.P. and Others v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Others, AIR1993SC2178, para. 178)] Education is the most important element for development and progress of human society and civilisation. In the annals of human civilisation, it has been proved time and again that societies which gave priority to education, progressed, flourished, and inscribed their names in golden words. Unfortunately, in The Constitution of India, 'Right to Education' wasn't there in its present form since the beginning; rather it was incorporated in Article 45 of DPSP as 'Free and Compulsory Education'. It was only after the Supreme Court Judgements in the cases of 'Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992)' and 'Unnikrishnan JP v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993)', that education was seen as 'essence of right to life' which 'flows from Article 21' and finally in the 86 th amendment of Constitution of India [2002], 'Right to Education' was inserted in Article 21A. Later on, 'Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act' was enacted in 2009 in line with the Article 21A. More than a decade has passed since then yet there are a lot of loopholes in the system to realise the dream of an educated India that was seen by the writers of the Constitution. When we talk of an enlightened mind, how can health be forgotten, as it is said 'Mens sana in corpore sano'. 'Right to health' of a child is ensured by Article 21 of Constitution linked with 'Right to life'. While 'Right to Education' and 'Right to Health' has been debated for long, it was only recently that 'Right to be Heard' came into limelight after the 'UN Committee on Rights of the Child' stated that 'Children should be included in the decision-making processes.' In the arena of 21 st Century, it would be naive to see all these three rights as separate entities, but somewhere down the line they would be found intertwined as notes to a symphony, where if one note gets missed, the entire harmony collapses. This doctrinal study is an attempt to tread through each of the threads of the fabric that covers the body of the child securing the soul of the nation in the hope of a healthy, educated and decisive future.

title: Aging, Housing, and Long-Term Care The Role of Care-Location Choice in Retirement
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa, The University of Texas and University of International Business and Economics (UIBE)

detail.title: Aging, Housing, and Long-Term Care The Role of Care-Location Choice in Retirement
detail.abstract: We develop a life-cycle model in which health, housing, and care-location choice jointly determine optimal demand for private LTC insurance and reverse mortgages. Retirees face uncertainty over health transitions, medical and LTC expenditures, and housing values, while housing provides both financial resources and consumption utility through aging-in-place benefits. Preferences are health-and location-dependent, allowing the marginal utility of consumption to differ between non-LTC states, home care, and nursing-home care. Moderately disabled individuals may optimally choose where to receive care. Calibrating the model to Health and Retirement Study data, we find that LTC insurance demand is robust and typically close to full coverage whenever available, whereas reverse-mortgage demand is highly sensitive to preferences and financial conditions once insurance is offered. Allowing endogenous care-location choice fundamentally alters the interaction between the two products: with meaningful home-attachment benefits, LTC insurance crowds out reverse-mortgage borrowing; without such benefits, the two remain complementary. We find that a substantial share of welfare gains arises from care-location flexibility itself. The option to move allows retirees to better align care arrangements with health states and consumption needs, reducing the reliance on purely financial mechanisms for smoothing consumption.

title: Impossible Consent: Generative Search, Browsewrap, and the Rights-Information Harm to Cognitively Disabled Users

detail.title: Impossible Consent: Generative Search, Browsewrap, and the Rights-Information Harm to Cognitively Disabled Users
detail.abstract: A person searches for the law that protects them and receives, at the top of the page, an authoritative answer that is wrong, accompanied by a cited source that confirms the error rather than correcting it. This paper examines that event as a distinct kind of harm, separate from the commercial deception that dominates discussion of generative search. When an automated system delivers false information about a person's own legal rights to a member of the protected class those rights exist to serve, the injury is not a lost sale but a right unasserted, a wrongful denial accepted, a deadline misjudged. I argue that this harm falls hardest on people with neurodevelopmental conditions, intellectual and developmental disabilities, and cognitive decline, who are least able to independently evaluate the answer and most exposed to acting on it, and I name the mechanism that defeats their last line of defense: counterfeit verifiability, in which the citation that is supposed to let a careful reader check the claim instead confirms the false claim. I then turn to the platform's anticipated defenses, which rest on terms a logged-out search user is said to accept by mere use. Drawing on the current acceptance language of a major provider, I show that this is browsewrap, the weakest form of online assent, and that for cognitively disabled users it is not merely weak but structurally unattainable. I call this condition impossible consent: agreement imputed to a person through a channel that the nature of their disability makes it impossible to satisfy. Because the provider's liability disclaimers and any dispute-resolution terms rest entirely on that imputed assent, they fail precisely against the population the harm reaches. The inaccessibility of the consent channel is itself an access problem, which moves the analysis from contract into disability law. I close by distinguishing what this clears, the defenses, from what remains open, the affirmative cause of action.

title: Does Sukuk Offer Portfolio Diversification Benefits During Crisis? Evidence from GARCH Analysis
affiliations: and Jamia Millia Islamia

detail.title: Does Sukuk Offer Portfolio Diversification Benefits During Crisis? Evidence from GARCH Analysis
detail.abstract: Islamic finance has gained prominence as a credible alternative to conventional finance, particularly following its resilience during the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. This study examines the volatility dynamics of Sukuk and conventional bond across the World, MENA and GCC regions, with a special focus on the Covid-19 pandemic period and its implication for investors. Using daily data from January 2019 to February 2021, a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH) model is employed to analyse the return volatility. The results reveal that Sukuk indices outperformed conventional bond indices in certain regions during specific period, while the opposite was observed in others. GARCH results indicate that although both asset classes exhibit high volatility persistence, Sukuk indices generally display lower volatility persistence than their conventional counterparts. Overall, the results suggest that Sukuk may serve as a viable diversification instrument, offering relatively lower volatility during the period of financial distress.

title: Symbolic Pure Time: Reading Time Within Linear Algebra

detail.title: Symbolic Pure Time: Reading Time Within Linear Algebra
detail.abstract:
Ordinary least squares on time series carries three structural limitations: it requires pre-testing for non-stationarity, it treats the residual distribution as a nuisance to be controlled rather than a source of information, and it recovers the predictable component and the innovations as two separate objects. This paper removes all three at once. 

The move is to run the same closed-form OLS solve on the kinematic state of the series level, rst dierence, and second dierence, stacked as a vector rather than on the lagged scalars. The t returns an operator M instead of a coecient vector, and from that single solve three simultaneous readings emerge. The memory innovation (M-I) decomposition reads temporal dependence (∆) and the distributional character of the one-step residuals (κ) as two orthogonal channels. The polar decomposition separates the direction of the dynamics from their intensity. The grade decomposition reads the isotropic gain, plane-wise kinematic coupling, and per-step volume change from the algebraic structure of M. 

Non-stationary and cointegrated trajectories require no pre-testing to set up the t; in population, the integration order is encoded in the eigenvalue spectrum of M and read algebraically without a DickeyFuller step (Proposition 3.3). 1 Any innovation distribution is characterised by the innovation channel rather than assumed or controlled away. The third limitation treating the residual distribution as a nuisance to be validated rather than as a dynamic quantity to be read is removed by treating κ as a rst-class output of the t alongside ∆: the OLS residuals are the Wold innovation sequence, orthogonal to the tted operator by the projection theorem, and their distributional character is read directly rather than assumed away. A kernel variant, SPT-K, recovers the same operator reading for nonlinear dynamics via the Jacobian of the feature map. 

Applied to S&P 500 daily returns (19902026), the M-I decomposition separates two crises that volatility lters conate: the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, where both ∆ and κ rose (systemic, memory-building), from the 2020 COVID shock, where κ spiked ninefold while ∆ stayed near baseline.

title: The Witnessing Self
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Witnessing Self
detail.abstract: Three traditions converge on a single insight about phobia and trauma. Grinder's NLP Double Detachment protocol places the patient outside their own observing, a meta-position from which the fear response can be witnessed without being relived. Advaita Vedanta arrives at the same stance through the doctrine of the sāks. hin: the true self is the unchanging witness, not the body, mind, or stream of emotion. Bayesian decision theory provides the formal account: a phobia is not a miscalibrated probability but a distorted utility that has contaminated belief. The double-detachment move restores the P and U independence that maximum expected utility requires. Therapy is applied Bayes, and ancient Vedanta knew it first.

title: Multiplex Identity: A Formal Model of the Human Agent in Socio-Technical Systems Mathematical Companion

detail.title: Multiplex Identity: A Formal Model of the Human Agent in Socio-Technical Systems Mathematical Companion
detail.abstract: This companion sets out, in self-contained form, the formal apparatus of the multiplex-identity model of the human agent in sociotechnical systems. The agent is represented not as an atomic network node, but as a matrix of layer-specific states stabilised by a structure of personal invariants. A measure of inter-layer incoherence is defined and used to characterise the agent's transmorphance-the capacity to vary layer-specific states while preserving invariant structure. It further shows how the institutional invariants of a system may emerge from the compatibility of the personal invariants of its agents, and develops a tensor representation in which transitions between institutional contexts are governed by a connection whose curvature and holonomy characterise structural vulnerability. Within this geometry, destructive cognitive influence is formalised as a perturbation of the connection. The resulting apparatus provides a formal language for describing and measuring the structural integrity of the human agent on which cognitive security depends.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper explores the paradigm shift of Artificial Intelligence (AI) from a niche technological tool to a foundational organizational utility, drawing a parallel to the historic industrial adoption of electricity. While traditional automation sought to replace routine manual labor, contemporary AI operates as an omnipresent infrastructure that fundamentally alters cognitive workflows, decision-making hierarchies, and organizational design. Positioning AI as a structural utility rather than an IT intervention, this paper introduces a multi-level conceptual framework examining its impact across Macro (structural), Meso (team/process), and Micro (individual behavior) dimensions of management. The paper concludes with a strategic agenda for empirical research, specifically targeting the operational realities of emerging corporate landscapes in India.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates caste gaps in cognitive achievement among Indian children aged 8 to 11 using two rounds of the India Human Development Survey (2004-05 and 2011-12). Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe children score substantially below Brahmin children on reading, arithmetic, and writing in 2012 after conditioning on household socioeconomic status and state fixed effects. Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition shows that SES deficits account for 61 to 90 per cent of raw gaps. Urban caste penalties are statistically insignificant by 2012, whereas large rural penalties persist. Formal pooled regressions with wave-caste interactions show that OBC and SC arithmetic gaps narrowed significantly between 2004 and 2012 (Δ = +0.180 and +0.128 respectively), but reading convergence is not significant for any group. The ST reading gap widened by 0.137 standard deviations (p = 0.020). Convergence was confined to numeracy; the ST divergence and the arithmetic-reading asymmetry are the paper's central empirical contributions.

detail.abstract:
India's fiscal federal architecture rests upon a structural contradiction that has deepened with each passing decade with states bear approximately 60 per cent of total public expenditure yet generate barely 51 per cent of their revenue receipts from own sources. The 16th Finance Commission, reporting for 2026-31, has retained states' share of the divisible pool at 41 per cent, a figure unchanged from its predecessor while simultaneously removing the 2.5 per cent tax-effort weight from horizontal devolution formulas and recommending against revenue deficit grants. With consolidated state outstanding liabilities budgeted at 27.05 per cent of GSDP and gross fiscal deficits at 3.14 per cent for FY2026 (Budget Estimate), the transfer-centric compact of Indian federalism has arrived at an institutional ceiling. 

This paper proposes the State Trading Market (STM) framework as the missing pillar of that compact, an institutional design that repositions subnational governments as market operators and sovereign participants, rather than passive regulators of markets designed elsewhere. Drawing on the RBI's State Finances Report 2025-26, Forum for State Studies data (FY2026 BE: SOTR ₹23.60 lakh crore; total revenue receipts ₹45.72 lakh crore), e-NAM platform statistics (1,656 mandis; ₹4.84 lakh crore cumulative trade as of March 2026), and India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme expansion to 490 obligated entities (January 2026), this paper argues that a properly designed STM framework spanning agricultural spot exchanges, commodity clearing markets, and sub-sovereign carbon credit participation can generate ₹65,000-₹91,000 crore in additional state own-revenues annually by FY2030. A three-phase policy roadmap, grounded in cooperative federalism and the Seventh Schedule, is presented.

title: Introduction to the Theory of Wealth Transfer: An Empirical Analysis of Wealth Transmission to China Through Foreign Direct Investment (1990–2024)
affiliations: California State University

detail.title: Introduction to the Theory of Wealth Transfer: An Empirical Analysis of Wealth Transmission to China Through Foreign Direct Investment (1990–2024)
detail.abstract: Persistent inequality and poverty despite sustained economic growth raise important questions about the limitations of traditional endogenous growth models. This research examines the effects of incorporating the factor Degree of Opportunity (D) into the growth frameworks of Paul Romer and Robert Lucas through the Theory of Wealth Transfer. Using macroeconomic data from China covering the period 1990–2024, the study analyzes the relationships between GDP, capital, labor, foreign direct investment (FDI), and the Degree of Opportunity, represented by labor force participation. The results indicate that capital remains the primary driver of economic growth, while variations in FDI (p = 0.041) and the Degree of Opportunity (p = 0.023) also exert significant effects on economic output. However, the absence of a significant interaction between these variables suggests that they operate through independent mechanisms. The findings support the argument that sustainable development depends not only on capital accumulation and investment inflows but also on the expansion of economic opportunities that enable broader participation in wealth creation.

title: Hidden Tariffs: Production Networks and the Durability of Antidumping Protection
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Hidden Tariffs: Production Networks and the Durability of Antidumping Protection
detail.abstract: Betz & Hummel (2025) shows that domestic production networks help firms obtain antidumping protection. I look at the other side: once granted, does a product's position in the production network affect how long that protection survives? Linking 1,765 US antidumping cases (1978-2024) to industry-level input-output data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis, I find that upstreamness—the share of output consisting of intermediate inputs (II/TO)—reduces the hazard of AD revocation. A one-standard-deviation increase corresponds to an 11.3% reduction in termination risk (HR = 0.887, p = 0.017; clustered p = 0.079), using stratified Cox models with two-digit sector strata. The effect is robust to excluding iron and steel (HR = 0.869, p = 0.035) and to restricting the sample to manufacturing (HR = 0.889, p = 0.022). To illustrate the mechanism: antidumping duties on steel (II/TO = 0.801) have remained in place for a median of 23.3 years—only 10% of steel's production value goes to personal consumption, and even that fraction passes through multiple production layers, dispersing the tariff cost to the point of invisibility. Duties on large residential washing machines (II/TO = 0.669), by contrast, direct 86% of their value to consumers; the South Korean case (initiated 2012) was revoked after 7.3 years. The protective effect of upstreamness is conditional on consumer orientation: among industries with a high share of output sold directly to consumers (PCE share above median), II/TO reduces hazard substantially (HR = 0.658, p < 0.001; clustered p = 0.001); among industries with low PCE share, II/TO has no detectable effect (HR = 1.009, p = 0.927; clustered p = 0.923). The II/TO × PCE Share interaction (HR = 0.857) is significant at p = 0.001 under both unclustered and clustered standard errors. Including industry concentration (HHI) does not weaken the result (HR = 0.904, p = 0.096 in the joint model with Antràs). Capital intensity and average wages do not add explanatory power beyond upstreamness (LR chi-squared = 0.0, p = 0.976). The commonly used Antràs et al. (2012) upstreamness measure—weighted distance to final demand—is not associated with AD survival on its own (HR = 1.010, p = 0.855). When both measures are included together, the intermediate input share is associated with lower hazard (HR = 0.870, p = 0.009), while the independent distance-to-consumers component of Antràs is not significant (HR = 1.064, p = 0.287).

detail.abstract: This submission supports modernising the Serious Fraud Office Act 1990 for digital evidence, but argues that expanded search, remote-access, copying and admissibility powers should not proceed without matching safeguards. The Serious Fraud Office needs workable powers for serious fraud, bribery and corruption in a cloud-based evidence environment. However, digital searches can reach privileged, private, third-party, institutional and offshore information at scale. The submission frames the Bill as a public integrity measure as well as a criminal procedure measure, and proposes a safeguard package covering warrant particularity, privilege, minimisation, third-party data, records, reporting, audit, staged commencement, statutory review and broader Serious Fraud Office Act reform.

title: Do Amenities Enhance the Value of Office Buildings? Dynamic Causal Impact of Modern Retrofitting
affiliations: , University of Tsukuba, Sanko Estate Co., Ltd. and University of Tsukuba

detail.title: Do Amenities Enhance the Value of Office Buildings? Dynamic Causal Impact of Modern Retrofitting

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Sanko Office Foundation and JSPS KAKENHI [grant number JP24K21407].

detail.abstract: The post-pandemic transition toward hybrid work has fundamentally redefined tenant demand, shifting the purpose of the office from a mere workspace to a collaborative, experiential hub. Consequently, aging properties face a severe obsolescence trilemma: undergo retrofitting, transform through conversion, or suffer economic decline. Amid this global "flight to quality" trend, this study quantifies the causal impact of modern retrofitting-specifically the installation of shared tenant lounges-on commercial property performance. Focusing on the Tokyo office market, we employ a staggered difference-indifferences framework utilizing a novel, manually constructed panel dataset tracking shared tenant lounge installations. Our empirical results demonstrate that installing shared lounges shortens the time-on-market by 24.2%-57.0% starting one year after installation, followed by a 1.2-1.8 percentage point reduction in vacancy rates from the second year onward. Ultimately, rent premiums increase dynamically, reaching 7.56% by the fifth year. While acknowledging their inherent limitations, placebo-based robustness checks substantiate our primary results. We also reveal a strategic stabilization mechanism: owners initially prioritize filling immediate vacancies to restore building vibrancy, subsequently commanding rent premiums as tenants' willingness to pay rises. Our findings highlight that amenities create vital functional value to combat obsolescence, thereby fostering the proactive and prolonged use of office buildings.

title: Sequential Search and Exposure-Dependence Design
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and

detail.title: Sequential Search and Exposure-Dependence Design
detail.abstract: This paper studies how intermediaries design dependence across early exposures and how such dependence interacts with consumers' sequential search behavior. Exposure dependence acts as a two-sided screening device. For consumers, it helps infer the value of uninspected exposures and thereby determines whether they continue, switch, or convert, generating a multi-cutoff search policy. For intermediaries, it screens consumers when their match types are not locally observed: exploratory designs broaden coverage after poor initial matches, while confirmatory designs retain consumers after promising ones. The structure of search frictions shifts consumers' cutoffs and thereby determines the intermediary's equilibrium design incentives. However, intermediary objectives generally create a welfare wedge, because conversion metrics do not fully internalize consumers' search costs and outside options.

detail.abstract:
The rapid institutionalization of Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance has increased the importance of independent scholarly evaluation of emerging global policy frameworks. "The International AI Safety Report 2026", produced by the Independent Expert Advisory Panel chaired by Yoshua Bengio and released under the United Kingdom Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), has become a significant reference point for international discussions on AI safety, regulation, and risk governance. Despite its growing influence across governmental, multilateral, and regulatory environments, limited scholarly attention has been devoted to systematically assessing its methodological foundations, governance assumptions, and practical policy implications.

This paper presents a structured policy-audit and governance-analysis framework for evaluating the "International AI Safety Report 2026." Employing a qualitative interpretive methodology grounded in policy auditing, regulatory discourse analysis, publication-integrity assessment, and comparative governance evaluation, the study examines the report's conceptual coherence, evidentiary foundations, transparency, and institutional implications.

The analysis identifies three interrelated governance challenges. First, an evaluation gap persists between laboratory benchmark performance and real-world deployment reliability, raising questions regarding the predictive validity of current safety assessment approaches. Second, an agency paradox emerges whereby AI systems are simultaneously framed as potentially transformative societal risks while continuing to exhibit significant operational limitations and context-dependent fragility. Third, the report reflects elements of a democratic deficit associated with technocratic policy language, centralized expert dependency, and limited mechanisms for broad public engagement and AI literacy.

The study further argues that contemporary AI governance frameworks increasingly depend upon evaluative assumptions and institutional risk models whose pragmatic validation remains uneven across real-world deployment contexts. To explain these tensions, the paper introduces the concepts of technocratic enclosure, operational fragility, and epistemic dependency as analytical lenses for examining the relationship between expert-led governance and democratic legitimacy.

The paper concludes that while the "International AI Safety Report 2026" represents a landmark contribution to international scientific coordination on AI safety, its long-term regulatory effectiveness will depend upon the integration of transparent auditing mechanisms, dynamic environmental stress testing, inference-process accountability, and public-facing literacy infrastructures. By situating AI safety governance within broader debates concerning publication integrity, institutional legitimacy, and democratic accountability, this study contributes an interdisciplinary framework for evaluating emerging global AI governance architectures.

title: The Method on the Shelf: How Ceramic Tile Installation Exposed the Construction Industry's Economic Problem Too Big to See

detail.title: The Method on the Shelf: How Ceramic Tile Installation Exposed the Construction Industry's Economic Problem Too Big to See

detail.abstract:
This paper documents a structural information asymmetry in the construction method supply chain and introduces an instrument to measure it. When a contractor selects an installation method, the cost distribution across specification-compliant assemblies — each producing the same warranted outcome — is invisible at the point of purchase. Drawing on Akerlof's theory of adverse selection and Graham's Mr. Market allegory, the paper reframes this as adverse selection of cost position rather than quality: every method is compliant, but the buyer cannot locate where in the distribution a given purchase falls. The result is a recurring, unrecorded overspend — quantified at $166.74 on a representative backer-board transaction, compounding to $120,051 over three years for a single contractor.

The central contribution is an adaptation of the Sharpe Ratio to method procurement: by treating cost savings as return and the dispersion of compliant method costs as risk, the instrument scores overspending risk before purchase rather than after. Across twelve compliant assemblies, scores range from 7.27 (compressed, low-risk) to −1.47 (collapsed); a single method's score is shown migrating from 1.69 to −0.21 as inflation moves through component costs. The analysis connects to recent evidence on declining U.S. construction-sector materials productivity, offering information asymmetry as a candidate market friction. The paper introduces Method Intelligence — a combinatorial specification ontology indexed by a method identification (MIS) code — as the information layer that renders the distribution legible.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into workplace operations through generalpurpose systems, including large language models, enterprise copilots, foundation-model platforms, and AI assistants. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) explains adoption through performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions, but it gives less attention to whether reliance on an AI system is appropriate, defensible, open to review, and subject to governance in a specific work context. This exploratory vignette study examines perceived architectural fit, defined as the perceived alignment between an AI system's technical and governance supports and the accountability demands of its intended use context. This 2 × 2 vignette experiment surveyed U.S. workers with workplace AI exposure, collecting 350 unique responses and retaining 282 after screening. The manipulation checks supported the intended experimental distinctions; they shifted the planned check measures, and the high-fit condition significantly increased perceived architectural fit. However, assigned conditions did not significantly affect perceived legitimacy or AI reliance intention. In secondary same-source perception models, perceived architectural fit was associated with perceived legitimacy and added predictive value beyond the UTAUT baseline. Perceived architectural fit also showed a significant indirect association with AI reliance intention through perceived legitimacy. This pattern remained similar when the overlapping legitimacy item was excluded and when the reliance-intention items were modeled separately. The study provides construct-development evidence that perceived architectural fit is measurable, shows promise as a UTAUT extension for adoption perceptions, and offers organizations a practical lens for evaluating whether workplace AI systems appear reviewable, traceable, and governable for intended use.

detail.abstract: Cultural tourism worldwide places indigenous communities at an important paradox between creating economic advantages and challenging the commodification of intangible cultural heritage. This interplay was explored through the effect of Aeta traditional healing on tourism development in San Felipe, Zambales. There is limited scholarly knowledge about the subtle, human qualities of the actors involved. This phenomenological study was conducted to investigate the meaning of such lived experiences. Data were gathered through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with ten purposively selected key informants (Aeta healers, LGU leaders, tourists). Thematic analysis revealed that Aeta healing is not merely a practice but a profound spiritual calling and a cornerstone of cultural identity. However, its intersection with tourism is shaped by multifaceted dynamics, a broad spectrum of readiness among healers, a critical knowledge and policy gap within the LGU, and a community-wide ethical negotiation to prevent exploitation, embodied by the principle of kusang loob (voluntary giving). The study concludes that sustainable integration requires a co-created, empathetic framework that prioritizes cultural sovereignty and ensures the Aeta are the definitive agents of tourism development centered on their heritage.

title: Preservation of Multimodularity with Exchangeable Increments in Stochastic Operations
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology - H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, , University of Macau - Faculty of Business Administration and

detail.title: Preservation of Multimodularity with Exchangeable Increments in Stochastic Operations
detail.abstract: Many decision-making problems involve multidimensional discrete choices, where performance measures are driven by partial-sum processes. In such settings, the decision maker's objective can often be expressed as the expected cost or profit associated with these multidimensional partial sums. This paper establishes preservation results for multimodularity in this class of processes. We identify sufficient conditions under which multimodularity is preserved, and provide counterexamples showing that these conditions cannot be relaxed without additional structure. In particular, if the post-realization function (prior to taking expectations) is multimodular, and the increments in each partial sum are nonnegative and infinitely exchangeable random variables, then the resulting performance metric (after taking expectations) remains multimodular. The result is both general and flexible: it accommodates dependence among uncertain increments and captures random shocks such as no-shows, cancellations, deterioration, clearance, and random yield. Building on this preservation result, we further establish multimodularity of the performance metric in several applications, including appointment scheduling in tandem queues, overbooking with product upgrading, perishable inventory systems with random lifetimes, and multisourcing systems with random yields.

detail.abstract: Critical minerals constitute a strategic terrain for South Korea. They are essential upstream inputs for batteries, semiconductors, defense electronics, and other advanced manufacturing core to Korea's economic security. Amidst intensifying U.S.-China competition and China's global dominance over these inputs, the Korean government has constructed an elaborate legislative and policy apparatus to reduce Korea's vulnerability. Using Dani Rodrik's 'ten design principles' for new industrial policy, this paper evaluates this apparatus, arguing that while South Korea has built a substantial middle-power critical minerals policy architecture, the system contains weaknesses that, if unaddressed, raise important questions about its efficacy. The apparatus scores relatively well in identifying vulnerabilities, creating formal authorities, and putting in place a dense set of tools. It is weak, however, in disciplining industrial policy and fostering learning. The article further argues that Korea's policy apparatus is designed for administrative 1 flexibility and discretion. Domestic politics matter in this context as the same policy machinery could support deeper U.S.-aligned trusted-supply-chain integration or a slow-moving diversification effort of 'maximum flexibility' between the U.S. and China. The article concludes with a preliminary assessment of the U.S.-ROK critical minerals cooperation and policy recommendations for a stronger allied partnership.

detail.abstract: Measurement is not a neutral act. The choice of what to measure, how to measure it, and what counts as a valid unit is a prior theoretical commitmentone that shapes what becomes visible, what becomes invisible, and ultimately what becomes actionable. This paper argues that measurement conventions are not descriptions of reality but agreements about which aspects of reality are worth attending to. When those conventions are misaligned with the phenomena they are meant to illuminate, they do not merely produce inaccurate data-they render entire categories of value structurally invisible. This has consequences not only for what we know, but for what we are capable of knowing.

title: Volatility Forecasting and Return Prediction under Market Regimes: Evidence from High-Frequency Chinese Equity Data
affiliations: and University of Warsaw - Faculty of Economic Sciences

detail.title: Volatility Forecasting and Return Prediction under Market Regimes: Evidence from High-Frequency Chinese Equity Data
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether regime-dependent volatility forecasting and machine-learning-based return prediction can be jointly integrated to improve both statistical forecasting performance and economic strategy outcomes in equity markets. Using high-frequency CSI 300 Index data from 2005 to 2023, a sequential twostage framework is developed. In the first stage, realized volatility is modeled using regime-augmented HARQ specifications combined with Markov-switching GJR-GARCH filtering to capture long-memory dynamics, asymmetry, and structural market regimes. In the second stage, volatility forecasts, regime indicators, and return-related predictors are incorporated into an XGBoost return-prediction model estimated through a strictly walk-forward out-of-sample procedure. The empirical results demonstrate that regime-aware volatility forecasting consistently outperforms baseline HARQ models across forecast evaluation metrics and is generally supported by formal forecast comparison tests. In contrast, return predictability remains weak, state-dependent, and concentrated primarily in low-volatility regimes. Although naive predictive trading strategies generally fail after accounting for realistic transaction costs, carefully designed implementations incorporating volatility scaling, low-volatility gating, threshold calibration, and turnover controls can improve defensive economic performance. The findings suggest that the practical value of predictive systems in financial markets may depend less on generating strong unconditional return forecasts and more on transforming weak state-dependent signals into economically robust portfolio allocation rules. Overall, the study contributes by integrating econometric volatility modeling, regime classification, machine-learning return prediction, and implementation realism within a unified framework.

title: Reframing TPO as an Estimator of Moments and Entropy of Equity Markets

detail.title: Reframing TPO as an Estimator of Moments and Entropy of Equity Markets
detail.abstract:
This paper provides the first formal empirical treatment of Market Profile concepts in the SPX cash equity market by treating the weekly Time Price Opportunity (TPO) profile as a moment and entropy estimator of the realized price acceptance distribution. Working with 65-minute SPX bars spanning January 2015 to June 2026 (489 weekly profiles), each distribution is characterised using six shape metrics: skewness, excess kurtosis, Shannon entropy, the Hartigan dip statistic, Value Area Width, and tail occupancy. Four distributional regimes are defined using trailing 52-week rolling percentile thresholds specified prior to any empirical analysis: BALANCED, DIRECTIONAL, TRANSITIONAL, and EXTREME.

Four hypotheses are tested. H1 establishes that weekly SPX TPO distributions are persistently non-Gaussian: 48 of 50 randomly sampled profiles reject normality at p < 0.05. H2 confirms that each regime produces a statistically distinct distributional fingerprint: EXTREME weeks exhibit narrow Value Area Width (mean 0.36, p = 5e-50); TRANSITIONAL weeks show the highest dip statistic (p = 2e-26), confirming genuine bimodality. H3 shows that TRANSITIONAL weeks predict next-week range contraction (0.76x expansion ratio, p = 0.0001), a finding that survives volatility conditioning. H4 yields two null results (POC drift streak; Naked POC magnetism) and one structural finding: when price approaches the prior week's POC from higher ground, the level acts as a reliable floor (67.6% hold rate, p < 0.001); when approached from lower ground, it does not act as a reliable ceiling (42.7%, p = 0.43). Weeks in which the POC fails as support predict higher 13-week forward returns (+5.8% vs +2.1%, p = 0.002), consistent with a capitulation and recovery mechanism. Value area analysis further shows that reaching the POC after penetrating the Value Area High collapses the probability of reclaiming that boundary from 95% to 43%.

All principal findings are validated in six additional instruments (SPY, DIA, IWM, QQQ, XLF, XLK). Five of seven instruments confirm H3, and six of seven confirm the FROM_ABOVE directional asymmetry, establishing both as broadly universal structural properties. The divergence in H1 non-Gaussianity rates between SPX (98%) and ETF replicants (68-76%) is attributed to authorized participant arbitrage smoothing intraday price acceptance. Several widely-held practitioner beliefs, including POC magnet effects and the symmetric support-resistance role of value area boundaries, are empirically rejected or substantially qualified.

title: The African Geopolitical Risk Index: A Daily, Country-Level Measure for Fifty-Four Countries, 1979-2026
affiliations: International University of Casablanca, Business School

detail.title: The African Geopolitical Risk Index: A Daily, Country-Level Measure for Fifty-Four Countries, 1979-2026

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: This research has received no funding

detail.abstract: I introduce the African Geopolitical Risk Index, the first daily, country-level measure of geopolitical risk built specifically for the African continent. The index covers all fifty-four African countries from 1979 to 2026, and is constructed from the global news-event record rather than from a small panel of Western newspapers. For each country and each day I measure the share of that country's news-event coverage that reports conflict or threat, separating the verbal expression of hostility, which I label threats, from its material realization, which I label acts. The measure is article-weighted, so that episodes commanding wide coverage carry more weight than those mentioned in passing, and it is expressed as a share of total coverage, so that it captures the intensity of conflict in the news rather than the overall volume of news. I normalize each series to a common reference window so that levels are comparable over time and across countries, and I produce the index at four levels of aggregation: a continent-wide headline, a separate series for every country, five regional aggregates, and a threats-versus-acts decomposition. I describe two complementary constructions: a long-history, event-based index drawn from the GDELT Event Database and coded through the CAMEO conflict taxonomy, and a modern, fully multilingual, theme-based index drawn from the GDELT Global Knowledge Graph. This paper documents the data, the screening methodology, the aggregation and normalization, and the full keyword and code lists in the appendix, so that the index is transparent and reproducible.

title: The Arabic AI-GPR Index: Measuring Geopolitical Risk from Arabic-Language News
affiliations: International University of Casablanca, Business School

detail.title: The Arabic AI-GPR Index: Measuring Geopolitical Risk from Arabic-Language News
detail.abstract: I construct the first daily index of geopolitical risk built entirely from Arabic-language news. Existing measures read global tension through English-language, predominantly Western, newspapers, an Anglocentric vantage point that is least reliable precisely where geopolitical risk is most concentrated, the Middle East and North Africa. Using a curated corpus of leading pan-Arab outlets accessed through GDELT, I measure risk along two independent tracks: a transparent theme-based screen and a large-language-model reading of each article in the manner of Iacoviello and Tong (2026). The two tracks agree almost perfectly, and I argue that this convergence makes the transparent, reproducible, and costless theme-based measure the preferable one: it delivers an equally responsive signal without the opacity, instability, and expense of article-level inference. The resulting index spans 2015 to 2026, rises at every major regional episode, and co-moves with the original Geopolitical Risk index of Caldara and Iacoviello (2022) and with the AI-GPR (a monthly change correlation of about 0.6 with both), while diverging in levels in economically meaningful ways. Its oil component tracks the Middle East oil risk index of Iacoviello at a correlation of 0.82. I decompose the index by country, country pair, actor, event type, sub-national hotspot, threats versus acts, and oil corridor, and I release the whole series as an open, monthly-updated resource.

title: Ontology Poisoning in Military AI Fusion Systems: Attack Vectors Against Palantir-Class Architectures
affiliations: VTU University

detail.title: Ontology Poisoning in Military AI Fusion Systems: Attack Vectors Against Palantir-Class Architectures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or organizational affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants, patient data, personal data, or animal subjects were involved in this research. Ethics committee approval was therefore not required. The study is based exclusively on publicly available information, threat modeling, and security analysis.

detail.abstract: Palantir Technologies' Maven Smart System (MSS), designated a U.S. Department of Defense Program of Record in 2026 and deployed across NATO's Allied Command Operations, is among the most operationally significant AI fusion platforms in contemporary warfare. Its ontology-based data model integrates over 179 heterogeneous intelligence sources; an embedded large language model (LLM) hub powered by Anthropic's Claude on classified networks compresses sensor-to-shooter decision cycles from hours to minutes. This paper characterises three underanalysed adversarial attack vectors specific to MSS-class architectures. AV-1: Ontology Poisoning-the primary contribution-corrupts the semantic object layer to forge entity relationships, reclassify hostile objects as friendly, and inject phantom units; its coupling to downstream LLM reasoning creates a dual-substrate propagation effect with no direct analogue in existing knowledge-graph poisoning literature. AV-2: LLM Prompt Injection exploits the absence of a cryptographic boundary between trusted ontology context and externally sourced intelligence documents retrieved via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to manipulate AI-generated courses of action. AV-3: Multi-Source Sensor Feed Spoofing exploits MSS's corroboration-based confidence logic to amplify-rather than merely introduce-false classifications across the ingestion pipeline. Each vector is analysed via counterfactual scenarios grounded in the documented deployment contexts of the 2026 Iran conflict, the NATO ACO deployment, and the February 2026 Maduro operation. A three-layer defence framework (D-1 through D-3) incorporating PKI-based object signing, Merkle-tree ontology versioning, and zero-knowledge provenance attestation is proposed, together with a forensic audit extension linking manipulation events to IHL operator accountability. A structured security-property coverage evaluation demonstrates the framework's design coverage properties and identifies residual gaps. Five open research problems are identified.

detail.abstract:
Cold chain failures and inadequate traceability together account for approximately 14% of annual fresh produce losses worldwide. Returnable plastic crates (RPCs), the dominant fieldharvest container in produce distribution, present a distinctive tracking challenge: a single crate undergoes hundreds of operational trips, transfers across several independent organisations, and is routinely unpacked and repacked into individual retail units, yet it has historically lacked a persistent digital identity linking the physical asset to its full handling record.
This study presents and evaluates a blockchain-based traceability architecture engineered for RPC-centric produce supply chains operating under a continuous 11°C cold chain requirement. The system integrates GS1-standard QR identification, a Hyperledger Fabric 2.5 permissioned ledger, Controlant IoT temperature data loggers, Zebra Technologies scanning and label-printing hardware, and purpose-built smart contract logic to generate a tamper-resistant, multi-party provenance record spanning four custody stages.
A session-based parent-child blockchain linkage protocol was developed to address the provenance continuity problem created when bulk crate contents are disaggregated into multiple retail units. Unlike conventional blockchain food traceability implementations that log custody events without reference to verified compliance states, the proposed framework embeds temperature compliance assessment as a mandatory precondition for smart contract execution: a custody transfer cannot proceed unless real-time Controlant logger data confirms that cold chain requirements have been met.

title: Constitutional Intelligence: A Unified, Formally Verified Architecture for Regulated Industrial Autonomy
affiliations: Universal Standard Axiom Corp

detail.title: Constitutional Intelligence: A Unified, Formally Verified Architecture for Regulated Industrial Autonomy
detail.abstract: The constitutional economy comprises thirty industry kernels — pharmaceutical, aerospace, finance, energy, healthcare, defense, and twenty-four others — each operating under its own instantiation of the Russell Unified Axiomatic Stack (RUAX). These kernels must communicate. A pharmaceutical robot must transmit patient data to a hospital database; an autonomous vehicle must report its trajectory to an energy grid controller; a drone must receive weather data from a meteorological kernel. Cross-kernel communication introduces a critical risk: translation loss, semantic drift, and corruption of constitutional constraints. This paper presents the Cross-Kernel Interoperability Handshake: a pure constitutional mathematics protocol, expressed in WAD arithmetic (1018-precision integer arithmetic, standardized in DeFi and now generalized to constitutional systems), that requires both sender and receiver to cryptographically prove they operate under identical constitutional axioms before any data is exchanged. The handshake proceeds in three phases: (1) Axiom Declaration via SHA3-256 (NIST FIPS 202) constitutional hash comparison; (2) Fixed-Point Verification grounded in the Banach Contraction Mapping Theorem; and (3) WAD-Arithmetic Challenge-Response using the R3 refinement operator. Once completed, both kernels share a verified constitutional context. Data exchange proceeds without translation — because the axioms are provably identical. No trust is required. No central authority is needed. The entire handshake completes in under 1 microsecond on ANRI-PHOTON hardware.

title: How to deal with machine learning bias in economic history
affiliations: University of Southern Denmark, University of Southern Denmark and University of Southern Denmark

detail.title: How to deal with machine learning bias in economic history
detail.abstract: Machine learning (ML) has rapidly transformed economic history, lowering costs of digitization, data linkage, and imputation, and making information in historical text usable at scale. This paper offers a practical guide to using these tools well. However, ML tools have also created new problems. Prediction errors are often systematically correlated with covariates of interest, so even highly accurate models can distort and sometimes reverse coefficients, and standard validation cannot detect this. Given that ML tools often perform worse for historical data, this problem is especially severe for the field of economic history. We also identify a solution to this problem. We show that recent debiasing methods can correct such bias for a wide class of applications, using a small, randomly sampled set of expert-coded labels while retaining the efficiency of large-scale prediction. We organize the field with a taxonomy of three ML tasks, survey the literature along it, and indicate where debiasing applies and where validation against proxies remains the only recourse. We close with best-practice guidance on digitization, model choice, and reproducibility.

title: From Access to Capability: How Digital Public Infrastructure Converts into Financial Inclusion across Indian States and Union Territories
affiliations: Indian Council of Social Science Research

detail.title: From Access to Capability: How Digital Public Infrastructure Converts into Financial Inclusion across Indian States and Union Territories
detail.abstract: India's digital public infrastructure (DPI) has made formal financial access nearly universal, yet access and the welfare outcomes inclusion should deliver have diverged across its states. Treating DPI as a government information infrastructure whose public value is realized only downstream of access, we ask when access converts into capability and resilience, and which conditions decide. Drawing on Sen's capability approach and its concept of conversion factors, we develop the Access-Use-Capability-Resilience (AUCR) framework and operationalise it as a transparent, reproducible state-level composite index for India's states and union territories (28 states and 8 union territories; 34 in the analytical sample), built entirely from open official data. The index is robust across three weighting schemes (Spearman ρ = 0.89-0.94) and predicts welfare outcomes it does not contain-state income and household consumption-even after the poverty-linked component is removed. Pairing fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) with necessary condition analysis (NCA) on 34 jurisdictions shows that access is a statistically significant necessary floor (NCA d = 0.48, p = 0.03) but enters no sufficient configuration, whereas the combination of active use and a human-development base is sufficient for high capability (consistency 0.89; conservative and parsimonious solutions coincide; robust across twelve specifications and on the 28 states alone). The absence of use-especially access without useforms a conversion trap that captures even high human-development states such as Kerala. The findings reframe DPI policy from an access agenda to a conversion agenda.
