detail.abstract: I take up a situation that recurs across the humanities and social sciences: one party asserts the state of a contested domain while an independent source documents what that domain was, and we lack a general, reproducible way to measure the gap between the two without sliding into treating the gap itself as proof of motive. I define that gap as a formal object, representational divergence, and I use the term in a specific sense, distinct from its looser appearances elsewhere. Given an assertion surface and an independently constructed realization surface, registered over a shared domain and time index and coerced to a common comparison space, representational divergence is their signed, directional difference, reported not as a raw quantity but as the excess over a pre-specified baseline of non-motivated processes (error, inaccessibility, recording effort). I demonstrate the construct across three domains that share nothing but the logic of the object itself: colonial cartography, public-health service coverage, and corporate financial reporting. I state the method's defining property as a formal limit: excess divergence is necessary but never sufficient evidence of intent, which has to be established from an evidence stream independent of the measure. To show the instrument fixed end to end, I rehearse a pre-registered confirmatory application to Dutch colonial cartography of the Darien, 1609 to 1714, in which the instrument, baseline, inference plan, and falsification conditions are locked before any data are seen.

title: Adapting the Black-Litterman Framework to Fixed-Income Portfolios

detail.title: Adapting the Black-Litterman Framework to Fixed-Income Portfolios

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no relevant financial or non-financial conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Classical mean-variance optimisation underpins portfolio construction but faces challenges in fixed income, where returns deviate from normality and input estimates are unstable. Many managers default to benchmarks or equal weighting to avoid estimation risk. The Black-Litterman framework offers an alternative by combining market-implied returns with investor views in a Bayesian update. 

This dissertation develops a fixed-income Black-Litterman framework that translates macroeconomic views into return expectations, calibrates view confidence, and imposes long only, fully invested portfolios. Using monthly data for five fixed-income asset classes from 2000 to 2025, three risk regimes (aggressive, moderate, conservative) are evaluated. Two BL variants are tested: BL , which retains the prior covariance, and BL (BL), which uses the posterior covariance, and both are compared with historical mean variance optimisation, the strategic benchmark, and an equally weighted 1/N portfolio.

Back-tests on rolling 60-month windows with one-month out-of-sample holds show that BL improves mean returns and delivers the strongest risk-adjusted performance among the BL variants in the moderate and conservative regimes, although it does not consistently beat the benchmark or 1/N. BL (_BL) achieves the highest return in the aggressive regime, but at the cost of higher volatility and trading intensity. The 1/N portfolio remains a strong baseline, with relatively high Sharpe ratios, shallow drawdowns, and very low turnover (~0.5% per month with monthly rebalancing). Overall, BL can be tailored to fixed income, but careful calibration of priors, risk aversion, and view confidence is essential, and simple diversification remains a formidable benchmark.

title: Zero-Sum Seas: Nodal Monopoly, Cartographic Secrecy, and the Recurring Grammar of State-Directed Maritime Control, 1415 to 1920

detail.title: Zero-Sum Seas: Nodal Monopoly, Cartographic Secrecy, and the Recurring Grammar of State-Directed Maritime Control, 1415 to 1920

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationship that has influenced or could be perceived to have influenced this research. The article is independent historical scholarship and is unconnected to the author's other professional activities.

detail.abstract: This article argues that state-directed maritime commercial monopoly constitutes a recurrent but not continuous institutional form: each of the four systems examined here, the Portuguese feitoria network (1415 to 1580), the Spanish Casa de Contratacion and Carrera de Indias (1503 to 1778), the Dutch chartered companies (1602 to c. 1800), and the American Jones Act regime (1920 to the present), represents a rupture from its predecessor and a reinvention of the same underlying logic rather than a linear institutional inheritance. The unifying logic is mercantilist and strictly zero-sum: state power is measured by bullion accumulation, wealth gained by one political entity is wealth denied to all others, and the control of maritime nodes, routes, and spatial knowledge is the primary instrument of accumulation. Drawing on institutional history, the historiographical framework developed by William J. Novak for understanding the infrastructural American state, and the cartographic theory of J.B. Harley, the article demonstrates that each system achieved commercial dominance through three coordinated mechanisms: nodal capture (the physical or legal control of chokepoint ports and straits), route secrecy (the institutional suppression of navigational and hydrographic knowledge), and the public-private hybrid (the formal delegation of state commercial power to licensed monopoly entities that preserved the legal fiction of private enterprise while executing state strategy). The rupture-andreinvention thesis distinguishes this analysis from continuity arguments: what passes between systems is not institutions but a structural logic that political actors in each period discovered independently under conditions of intensified zero-sum competition. This article establishes the institutional and conceptual framework for these claims and identifies the empirical spatial evaluation that this framework makes testable across the cartographic archives of all four systems.

title: Structural Performance and Exposure to Research-integrity Risks in the University Systems of the Arab States: A Multilevel Morphological Characterization with SIR and IRIS 2026
affiliations: ,  and Prisma Global Cía

detail.title: Structural Performance and Exposure to Research-integrity Risks in the University Systems of the Arab States: A Multilevel Morphological Characterization with SIR and IRIS 2026

keywords: university systems of the Arab States

detail.abstract: The comparison of university systems relies on instruments that describe research performance and research integrity separately, yet the reach of the frameworks that articulate both dimensions beyond their region of origin remains little explored. This study applies to the university systems of the Arab States a multilevel morphological characterization framework that organizes the description of a system into four successive levels of resolution: distributed structural performance, distributed exposure to risk, the internal concentration of that exposure, and the composition of its components. Each level adds detail to the previous one without replacing it. Performance is measured through the HES Index derived from the SCImago Institutions Rankings 2026, and risk through a synthetic measure derived from the IRIS 2026 integrity indicators over the relevant exposure block. The universe comprises the ten Arab States systems with at least nine higher education institutions registered in SIR 2026. The results show that system size, structural performance, and exposure to risk are not ordered along a single gradient. Systems of similar performance can occupy opposite positions of exposure, so that the plane is read as a morphological field rather than as a scale. The fourth level reveals a heterogeneous composition of drivers, led by Hyperauthored Output, within which Discontinued Journals Output retains an appreciable differentiating weight and connects, as in the previous Latin American study, with the pattern of the systems of greater relative exposure. The stability of the positions was assessed through bootstrap resampling with 5,000 replicates, which confirms the main archetypes of the plane and shows that uncertainty increases significantly in the systems closest to the legibility threshold. The study identifies Bahrain as the threshold system of the analyzed universe and suggests that the frontier of bibliometric visibility and the transferability of the framework can be examined beyond the region that originated it.

title: Cervical Cancer Mortality in HPV Vaccine-Eligible Birth Cohorts in Argentina, 2005–2024: An Ecological Time-Series Study
affiliations: GESICA Foundation, Argentine Ministry of Health, Argentine Ministry of Health, Argentine Ministry of Health and Argentine Ministry of Health

detail.title: Cervical Cancer Mortality in HPV Vaccine-Eligible Birth Cohorts in Argentina, 2005–2024: An Ecological Time-Series Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Background: HPV vaccination prevents infection with oncogenic HPV types and high-grade cervical lesions, but population-level evidence from Latin America on invasive cervical cancer and mortality remains scarce. Argentina introduced HPV vaccination in 2011 for 11-year-old girls born in 2000 or later. We assessed early mortality and cytology patterns in birth cohorts potentially eligible for vaccination.

Methods: We did an ecological time-series study using national vital statistics for deaths from cervical cancer (ICD-10 C53) among women aged 20–69 years in Argentina from 2005 to 2024, with official annual female population denominators. Women aged 20–24 years in 2024 were defined as the index group. We compared 2024 with 2005–2018 using Poisson models and log woman-years as offset. As a complementary precursor outcome, we analysed HSIL or worse among evaluable cervical cytology samples from the public health-care network of Buenos Aires city in 2019–2025.

Findings: We analysed 19 080 cervical cancer deaths and 259 538 948 woman-years. Among women aged 20–24 years, mortality decreased from 0·44 per 100 000 woman-years in 2005–2018 to 0·23 in 2024 (rate ratio 0·51, 95% CI 0·19–1·40; p=0·19). In women aged 25–69 years, mortality increased from 7·99 to 10·14 per 100 000 woman-years (1·27, 1·20–1·34; p<0·0001). In Buenos Aires city, HSIL or worse decreased in women aged 20–24 years from 0·93% in 2019–2022 to 0·46% in 2023–2025, but increased in women aged 25–64 years from 2·24% to 2·64%.

Interpretation: Mortality and cytology data showed divergent patterns in birth cohorts potentially eligible for HPV vaccination at the target age. Although ecological and still early, these findings are consistent with an emerging cohort signal and support continued population-level monitoring of HPV vaccination impact in Argentina.

title: Diabetes Care Coverage under Chile's Explicit Health Guarantees, 2011–2023: A Municipal Latent-Class Analysis of Glycaemic Control and Retinopathy Screening
affiliations: University College London, Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Valparaíso, University College London, University College London - Institute for Global Health, University College London, Government of the United Kingdom - Moorfields Eye Hospital and University of Oxford - Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences

detail.title: Diabetes Care Coverage under Chile's Explicit Health Guarantees, 2011–2023: A Municipal Latent-Class Analysis of Glycaemic Control and Retinopathy Screening

University College London supported the presentation of preliminary results at the Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology 2025 Annual Meeting (Salt Lake City, UT, USA).

detail.abstract:
Background: Diabetes care depends on distinct clinical processes, yet glycaemic control and diabetic retinopathy screening are usually monitored together or only at the national level, which can hide local divergence within decentralised health systems. We examined whether municipalities in Chile, a decentralised system operating under the Explicit Health Guarantees (GES/AUGE) reform, follow distinct local trajectories of two programme-based indicators, and whether these trajectories track socioeconomic position.

Methods: In this retrospective longitudinal analysis we used annual municipality-level data from Chile's National Cardiovascular Health Programme for 2011–2023 (299 municipalities). We modelled effective glycaemic-control coverage (EGCC; the proportion of monitored patients with HbA1c <7% [<53 mmol/mol]) and diabetic retinopathy screening coverage (DRSC) separately with latent class mixed models selected from 140 candidate specifications, cross-classified municipal class membership, and examined membership by deprivation, urbanicity, and geographical zone. Reporting followed STROBE.

Findings: We identified four trajectories for each outcome. 272 of 299 municipalities (91·0%) followed glycaemic-control trajectories that stayed below 50% coverage throughout, far short of the 80% national target. DRSC trajectories were more heterogeneous. Glycaemic-control and screening memberships overlapped only weakly (Cramér's V 0·106; p=0·34), indicating statistically independent local processes. Trajectory membership showed no clear gradient by deprivation, urbanicity, or geographical zone.

Interpretation: Chile has made diabetes care broadly equitable across municipalities without making it adequate. Because glycaemic control and retinopathy screening behave as independent local processes, composite indicators obscure which process is failing where, and monitoring systems should track chronic-disease management and complication screening separately.

title: Market Segmentation and Return Drivers of Indian Infrastructure Investment Trusts and REITs

detail.title: Market Segmentation and Return Drivers of Indian Infrastructure Investment Trusts and REITs

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether Indian Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) and REITs behave as part of the global infrastructure asset class or as a segmented domestic market, and what drives their returns. Using daily data from 2020 to 2026 across seven category portfolios spanning Indian and global infrastructure assets, we estimate GJR-GARCH and DCC-GARCH models and apply the Diebold-Yilmaz spillover framework. The total spillover index of 21.95% sits well below the 58.9% benchmark for developed REIT markets; foreign shocks explain only 2.47% of Indian InvIT variance at a 10-day horizon. Multi-factor regressions reveal a three-tier explanatory structure: adjusted R 2 reaches 67.9% for infrastructure stocks, 6.2% for REITs, and 2.5% for InvITs. The demeaned 10-year yield and Amihud illiquidity measure are the most relevant domestic state variables for InvIT pricing. These findings characterise Indian listed infrastructure as an early-stage segment shaped by idiosyncratic and liquidity risks.

detail.abstract: Repeated directed human movement along fixed corridors produces measurable diffusion effects in knowledge, biology, language, environment, and material culture that no individual participant observes and no single source records. This paper proposes a framework, a methodology, and a set of computational instruments for recovering those effects, and it advances a specific, falsifiable claim for others to test: that the directed topological structure of a historical movement network predicts its observed spatiotemporal diffusion better than geographic proximity, undirected network distance, or directed shortest-path distance, and that circuit-structured systems are separable from convergence-structured systems by a measurable spectral signature. The proposal models historical human movement networks as time-evolving directed simplicial complexes and characterizes them with two distinct operators: directed path homology for topology and a directed, non-reversible diffusion generator for dynamics; the paper specifies why the two cannot be the same operator. It introduces a dual-layer evidence model that separates what the network structurally transmitted, recoverable from topology, from what the traveler's narrative reports, recoverable from text, and formalizes the gap between the layers as a directed Hausdorff distance.

detail.abstract: We introduce Topological Threshold Dynamics (TTD), a unified measurement framework in which any cognitive, physical, or informational system at time t is represented as a directed weighted graph G(t) = (V, E, w), and its structural state is characterized by the directed persistent homology of that graph via the path-homology complex of Grigor'yan, Lin, Muranov, and Yau. Phase transitions are detected by a threshold dynamic tau defined over the eigenstructure of the directed path-Laplacian operator L_p, which tracks topological change in the allowed p-chain spaces of the directed complex. The developmental delta between two time points is the bottleneck distance d_B between persistence diagrams, stable under perturbation by the Cohen-Steiner theorem. The framework is domain-invariant: the same formal apparatus measures cognitive growth in multi-instance learning, phase transitions in financial markets, sensory decay in neurophysiology, manifold deformation in computer vision, structural anomalies in spacetime geometry, conformational change in molecular biology, bifurcation dynamics in chaos theory, and equilibrium topology in game-theoretic environments. We introduce the NELE algorithm as the topological state oracle that scans, memorializes, and evaluates topological change across the multi-instance ensemble, outputting developmental deltas as finite-difference ratios of bottleneck distance and inter-instance divergence matrices. Perturbation amplification is grounded in the Ollivier-Ricci curvature of the directed graph and in the non-normality of the directed transition operator, locating sensitivity to initial conditions in the curvature geometry rather than in the contractive Laplacian spectrum. Regression specifications for machine learning are grounded in the Morse-Smale complex of the discretized gradient vector field rather than in level-set topology alone. TTD implies improved optimization algorithms, new observational targets for astrophysics, and a general theory of phase-transition detection across physical and informational scales.

title: Rotation-Robust Skin Lesion Classification Using Gated EfficientNet–Vision Transformer Fusion with Spatial Transformer Preprocessing
affiliations: The University of the South Pacific, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Rotation-Robust Skin Lesion Classification Using Gated EfficientNet–Vision Transformer Fusion with Spatial Transformer Preprocessing
detail.abstract: Skin lesion classification in dermoscopy is challenging due to visual similarity between lesion categories, severe class imbalance, and variable image acquisition conditions—including orientation. Most classifiers are developed and evaluated at a single fixed angle, yet clinical images arrive at arbitrary rotations, and rotation-induced performance degradation is rarely characterized in the literature. This paper presents a hybrid classifier that addresses these gaps through local-global feature fusion: EfficientNet-B0 extracts fine-grained local convolutional features, and Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16) contributes global patch-level representations, with the two streams combined via projection-based alignment and a learned scalar gating mechanism. A shared spatial transformer network (STN) preprocesses both encoder inputs before feature extraction to provide explicit geometric correction. Experiments on HAM10000 (10,015 dermoscopic images, seven lesion classes) establish the contribution of each design element through a systematic ablation. Label smoothing at  raised validation accuracy from 78.89% to 86.97%; incorporating the STN pushed accuracy to 91.16% and reduced maximum relative rotation degradation (RRD) from 3.14% to 0.89%. A complete 24-angle evaluation (0° to 345° in 15° steps) confirms that the two-seed ensemble holds accuracy above 89.47% across all tested orientations, with a canonical RRD of 0.99%—below that of specialized equivariant architectures, which require a fully custom backbone design. These results indicate that local-global feature fusion with STN-based geometric preprocessing provides a practical, reproducible route to orientation-robust dermoscopic classification, with direct implications for decision-support systems deployed under uncontrolled acquisition conditions

title: Monetary Tightening and the Divergence in Firm Innovation: Who Cuts Back and Who Pushes Forward?
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance

detail.title: Monetary Tightening and the Divergence in Firm Innovation: Who Cuts Back and Who Pushes Forward?
detail.abstract: I document that monetary policy exerts heterogeneous impacts on firm innovation efforts, and could contribute to market and R&D concentration. Controlling for financial constraints and various firm-level characteristics, a 100 basis point rate hike leads firms with 1% higher existing patent values (innovative firms) to reduce their R&D spending by 4% less than firms without patent values (non-innovative firms). This 4% gap slightly narrows but remains significant at 2.2% level after 12 quarters. Frontier firms-those generating the highest patent values within their sector-even increase their R&D spending by 2.2%, while their peers cut back R&D by 7.1% one quarter after the tightening shock, resulting in a clear divergence in R&D responses. Their sustained R&D activity is financed through additional equity issuance following the tightening. This divergence primarily stems from innovative firms' high marginal value of R&D investment. Additionally, innovative firms are particularly sensitive to R&D cuts, as such reductions may signal them as being non-innovative. When monetary policy raises interest rates, less innovative firms tend to adopt existing technologies due to higher marginal costs, whereas innovative firms persist in developing new ideas. Such monetary tightening further exacerbates the divergence, potentially widening the innovation gap in the future.

title: One Asset, Two Financial Systems: Stablecoins and the Transmission of Runs between Decentralized and Traditional Finance
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Sveriges Riksbank - Research Division and Washington University in Saint Louis, John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: One Asset, Two Financial Systems: Stablecoins and the Transmission of Runs between Decentralized and Traditional Finance
detail.abstract: A stablecoin is two things at once, a claim on U.S. Treasury bonds and the money of decentralized finance. That dual role makes the coin a conduit that carries runs in both directions. We build a model in which the coin is fully backed by Treasuries, pays no interest, and is the gateway to DeFi lending, so that the peg, the liquidation value of the issuer's reserves, and the run on a DeFi protocol are determined jointly rather than fixed in advance. Contagion then runs both ways. A shock that begins in crypto sets off withdrawals, redemptions, and reserve sales, fire-selling Treasuries that would otherwise have stayed calm. A shock to Treasury values runs the other way. It weakens the peg, strips the dollar value from DeFi claims denominated in the coin, and pulls lenders out of a protocol that was never in trouble. The mechanism is a no-interest paradox. Promising only par and paying no interest is what makes a stablecoin look safe on its own; it is also what forces it to depend on DeFi returns, and that dependence carries the shock in both directions. Full backing does not buy safety, because the threshold at which the peg breaks is set by a market the issuer does not control.

title: Does More Funding Mean Better Health? A State-Level Analysis of Public Health Expenditure in India
affiliations: and Christ University (Deemed to be University)

detail.title: Does More Funding Mean Better Health? A State-Level Analysis of Public Health Expenditure in India
detail.abstract: In an effort to enhance government health expenditures and improve state-level health facilities, the Central Government of India adopted the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) in 2000, launched the National Health Mission (NHM) in 2013, and most recently implemented the National Health Policy (NHP) in 2017. This study looks at how public health spending affects important health outcomes, such as the infant mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate, fertility rate, and malaria cases. It takes into account per capita income and spending on water supply and sanitation. The research examines 16 major states from 2000 to 2021. Additionally, it compares the effects of public health spending in both high-performing and underperforming states. The study used secondary data from the Sample Registration System (SRS), Economic Political Weekly Research Foundation (EPWRF), and the annual RBI state finances report. Based on the Hausman test, the study uses panel fixedeffects and random-effects models where suitable. Empirical findings show that overall public health spending decreases malaria cases, infant mortality, and neonatal mortality rates. The study also finds no significant impact between Public health spending and health outcomes, especially in under-performing states. Indian states should boost capital health spending to improve health infrastructure and consider public-private partnerships. This is important for achieving better health outcomes. This study provides key suggestions for shaping public health policy in developing countries.

title: The State Handover Document: A Methodological Note on Recording Intergovernmental Continuity

detail.title: The State Handover Document: A Methodological Note on Recording Intergovernmental Continuity
detail.abstract:
This working paper proposes the State Handover Document as a methodological instrument for recording intergovernmental continuity across successive administrations. Conventional evaluations of political leadership often focus on outcomes observed during a prime minister’s or president’s term, such as GDP growth, employment, wages, prices, fiscal balance, public approval, or stock prices. Such term-bound scorecards may obscure what an administration inherited, what it processed, what remained unresolved, and what was handed over to its successor.

The paper does not claim to prove causation, rank administrations, or construct a political scorecard. Its minimum claim is narrower: a structured handover document can make handover-state facts visible where single-period political evaluation tends to compress or obscure them. The framework separates observed data from interpretive records and records inherited conditions, carried-forward constraints, administrative bottlenecks, external shocks, boundary conditions, source metadata, and uncertainty notes.

The framework is developed with reference to Japan’s recent administrations and includes a coupled pilot on living standards and employment conditions around the Abe–Suga–Kishida transition sequence. The pilot does not treat real wages or employment indicators as standalone verdicts. Instead, it records a mixed handover condition: purchasing-power weakness, employment-access indicators, COVID-19 shock effects, and boundary metadata are placed in the same handover profile. This illustrates how a handover document can preserve ambiguity rather than collapse it into a single positive or negative score.

The paper also addresses risks of misuse, including political ranking, excessive attribution of responsibility, institutional self-protection, indicator gaming, cherry-picking, and downstream simplification by media or political actors. To reduce these risks, it proposes non-ranking output rules, coupled gap profiles, structural metadata requirements, contested classification records, and future development of monthly or quarterly data-access layers.

The State Handover Document is therefore presented as a methodological note and working paper, not as a completed empirical evaluation. Its contribution is to provide a practical recording structure for tracing how past policy decisions, unresolved obligations, administrative constraints, and external shocks may leave observable handover-state traces for successor administrations and later analysts.

title: Label-free SERS fingerprint recognition of salivary biomarkers for Parkinson’s disease using hierarchical silver nanogrooves and transfer learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xi’an Polytechnic University, Xi’an Polytechnic University, Xi’an Polytechnic University, Xi’an Polytechnic University, Xi’an Polytechnic University, Xi’an Polytechnic University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Xi’an Shiyou University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Xi’an Polytechnic University

detail.title: Label-free SERS fingerprint recognition of salivary biomarkers for Parkinson’s disease using hierarchical silver nanogrooves and transfer learning
detail.abstract: Non-invasive identification of neuroprotein biomarkers in complex biofluids using surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) remains challenging. To address this, we developed a hierarchical silver nanogroove SERS substrate combined with a transfer learning strategy for salivary neuroprotein analysis. The hierarchical nanosurface features nanogrooves decorated with nanosynapses, which multilevel architecture enables the confinement of neuroprotein biomarkers within the multidimensional ”hotspots” regions of its nanoscale cavities. Hierarchical silver nanogrooves enabled label-free SERS fingerprint recognition of key neuroprotein biomarkers, such as Aβ, Tau, α-Synuclein and their mixtures. Then, a transfer learning model, trained solely on pure SERS spectra of these three proteins, extracts molecular fingerprints without requiring large mixed-analyte datasets. And the pretrained model was applied to identify α-Synuclein signals in saliva samples from 40 Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients, enabling non-invasive detection without retraining, achieving a high detection probability of 0.9678. In binary and ternary mixtures of α-Synuclein, Aβ, and Tau, the transfer learning program specifically identified the target protein. All probabilities exceeded the classification threshold, demonstrating consistent recognition of α-Synuclein-specific signatures despite complex protein backgrounds and saliva matrices. In sum, a non-invasive, label-free SERS detection of neuroproteins for neurodegenerative diseases using a transfer learning-enhanced hierarchical silver nanogroove platform is presented, this approach offers a promising pathway to facilitate clinical translation of SERS technology and support the diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases, such as PD.

title: Asymmetric and Directional Interactions across the Space, Asset, and Capital Markets in Real Estate: Evidence from 132 Cities in China
affiliations: , University of Washington - College of Built Environments and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Asymmetric and Directional Interactions across the Space, Asset, and Capital Markets in Real Estate: Evidence from 132 Cities in China
detail.abstract: The theoretical foundations of the interactions across the space, asset, and capital markets in real estate are well established. The empirical evidence of these interactions across those three markets remains more limited. This study empirically investigates the dynamic interactions across the three markets, taking China's urban housing markets as an example. Using a panel dataset of 132 cities from 2014 to 2024, we systematically identify the asymmetric and directional interactions through panel vector autoregressions, Granger causality test, impulse response functions, and forecast error variance decompositions. The results show that the capital market functions as the vital regulatory pivot where price shocks drive a price-led yield compression mechanism, which subsequently governs corrective asset devaluation in the asset market and staggered rental escalation in the space market. Further, the growth dynamics of the space and asset markets are mutually insulated within a 10-year forecast horizon. In addition, heterogeneity analysis reveals a structural divergence that high-tier, highland supply , and highland price cities are predominantly governed by this asset-driven transmission framework, whereas other cities are dictated by a space-market channel where rent operates as the leading valuation anchor.

title: Last-Mile Advisory Services and Smallholder Productivity: Evidence from the Philippines

detail.title: Last-Mile Advisory Services and Smallholder Productivity: Evidence from the Philippines

keywords: development operations Last-Mile Advisory Services and Smallholder Productivity

detail.abstract: Smallholder farms in developing countries provide livelihoods to millions of the world's poorest and persistently operate below their potential productivity levels. Governments and supply chain firms have invested heavily in research, training, and advisory programs to improve smallholder productivity, yet these efforts often face severe operational challenges related to geographic dispersion, limited agent capacity, travel costs, and uneven service access. We study agricultural extension systems as a service delivery and operations problem, examining whether physical access to local extension facilities improves farm productivity and practice adoption, and exploring the mechanisms through which proximity affects advisory effectiveness. Methodology/results: We combine proprietary survey data from 1,480 Philippine smallholder coconut farms with environmental and institutional data, and exploit plausibly exogenous variation in extension office locations. Farms located within 10 kilometers of an extension office exhibit 20-26% higher yields, with estimates remaining stable across extensive controls, robustness checks and adjustments for office placement propensity. Surprisingly, proximity is not associated with broad increases in adoption of recommended practices. Instead, exploratory analyses suggest that nearby farms disproportionately adopt a small subset of higher-return practices and implement them more effectively. This suggests that extension agents translate generalized recommendations into locally feasible practices under resource and implementation constraints. Managerial implications: Our findings highlight physical access as an important operational lever in agricultural advisory systems. Despite substantial investment in extension and advisory programs, facility allocation decisions are often driven by administrative or institutional considerations rather than service accessibility. Projections based on our data suggest that simple data-driven facility reallocation rules can substantially expand service coverage and generate productivity gains comparable to costly capacity expansion. More broadly, our results suggest that advisory effectiveness depends not only on transmitting codified recommendations, but also on enabling repeated, context-specific interactions involving tacit implementation support, with implications for the design of advisory systems, digital substitutes, and technology dissemination programs for small, under-resourced firms.

title: DMAF-Net: An Effective Modality Rebalancing Framework for Incomplete Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Leicester

detail.title: DMAF-Net: An Effective Modality Rebalancing Framework for Incomplete Multi-Modal Medical Image Segmentation
detail.abstract: Incomplete multi-modal medical image segmentation faces critical challenges from modality imbalance, including imbalanced modality missing rates and heterogeneous modality contributions. Due to their reliance on idealized assumptions of complete modality availability, existing methods fail to dynamically balance contributions and neglect the structural relationships between modalities, resulting in suboptimal performance in real-world clinical scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a novel model, named Dynamic Modality-Aware Fusion Network (DMAF-Net). The DMAF-Net adopts three key ideas. First, it introduces a Dynamic Modality-Aware Fusion (DMAF) module to suppress missing-modality interference by combining transformer attention with adaptive masking and weight modality contributions dynamically through attention maps. Second, it designs a synergistic Relation Distillation and Prototype Distillation framework to enforce global-local feature alignment via covariance consistency and masked graph attention, while ensuring semantic consistency through cross-modal class-specific prototype alignment. Third, it presents a Dynamic Training Monitoring (DTM) strategy to stabilize optimization under imbalanced missing rates by tracking distillation gaps in real-time, and to balance convergence speeds across modalities by adaptively reweighting losses and scaling gradients. Extensive experiments on BraTS2020 and MyoPS2020 demonstrate that DMAF-Net outperforms existing methods for incomplete multi-modal medical image segmentation. Extensive experiments on BraTS2020 and MyoPS2020 demonstrate that DMAF-Net outperforms existing methods for incomplete multi-modal medical image segmentation.

detail.abstract: This study presents an open-source educational package designed to cultivate foundational evidence-based policymaking (EBPM) literacy among undergraduate public policy students. The package addresses a structural cognitive gap encountered in the introductory module of a 15-week omnibus policy course at Nanzan University (Nagoya, Japan): first-year students must immediately confront a scenario where a retrospective case-control design is the only feasible option, yet the naively computed risk ratio (RR) collapses mathematically owing to the sampling mechanism. The package features a lightweight, single-file R Shiny application that automatically selects the analytical test, renders a distortion-free square mosaic plot via coord_fixed(ratio = 1), and unveils a step-by-step derivation of the odds ratio (OR) and its 95% confidence interval, securing mathematical transparency. A 21-slide English-language lecture deck, a UTF-8 encoded sample dataset (n = 390), and a four-slide RStudio installation guide complete the repository, which is permanently archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20826438; GPL v3.0). A 100-minute lesson plan guides students through five phases. Anonymous LMS clickstream logs from a large-scale in-person deployment (N = 310) confirmed the package’s pedagogical effectiveness: 65.2% of students accessed the Zenodo repository for further information upon temporary unavailability.

detail.abstract: The relationship between corporate ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) performance and financial returns has emerged as one of the most actively contested questions in sustainable finance. While European equity markets have documented a meaningful ESG premium structurally reinforced by the EU Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) and the EU Taxonomy, which collectively channel approximately EUR 3.9 trillion in assets toward sustainability-classified funds [3][4] evidence for emerging markets such as India remains considerably sparser and more mixed [1][12]. This paper investigates whether ESG scores predict stock returns for 100 NIFTY large-cap companies over 2020-2025. Splitting the sample at the median ESG score of 63, High-ESG companies (n=51, mean score 68.3) outperformed Low-ESG companies (n=49, mean score 56.3) across all four holding periods examined, with the widest gap at the three-year horizon (+3.24 percentage points). However, the Pearson correlation between ESG score and five-year CAGR is weak and not statistically significant at the five percent level (r = 0.179, p = 0.075, R² = 0.032), indicating that ESG scores alone explain very little of the variation in individual company returns. Sector effects are substantial: Low-ESG companies lead in four of eleven comparable sectors, including Pharmaceuticals and IT. The findings are broadly consistent with emerging-market literature [1][12][13] and contrast with stronger premia documented in Europe where regulatory capital flows mechanically reprice high-ESG securities [3][4][5]. The ESG premium in India appears nascent, and this paper provides a quantitative baseline for tracking its evolution as the SEBI BRSR framework matures [15].

title: Conflict-Generated Air Pollution and Infant Mortality in 113 Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Wind-Based Natural Experiment
affiliations: University of Hamburg

detail.title: Conflict-Generated Air Pollution and Infant Mortality in 113 Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Wind-Based Natural Experiment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding supported this study

detail.abstract:
Background: Armed conflict is known to cause large numbers of indirect deaths, especially among young children. Existing research has linked this burden to the destruction of infrastructure, displacement, infectious disease, and reduced access to healthcare. Yet these mechanisms are unlikely to capture all pathways through which conflict increases child mortality. One such pathway is air pollution: conflict generates substantial emissions, and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is a leading cause of child mortality in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). However, the contribution of conflict-related air pollution to child mortality has not been quantified.

Methods: To isolate the contribution of conflict-related PM2.5 to infant mortality, wind direction was used as a natural experiment. Whether a location lies downwind of a conflict event depends on the timing of fighting and atmospheric conditions rather than local socioeconomic conditions, generating plausibly exogenous variation in pollution exposure. The analysis covered 305,755 grid cells in 113 LMICs between 2000 and 2017. Individual birth records (N = 527,532) from 143 Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) were used as complementary evidence on birthweight.

Findings: A 5 μg/m³ increase in conflict-related PM2.5—equivalent to the WHO annual guideline—was associated with a 13.0% increase in infant mortality, corresponding to an estimated 64,128 infant deaths over the study period. Associations were 18.2 times larger in areas with poor access to water and 7.0 times larger in areas with poor sanitation. DHS birth-record analyses showed lower gestational birthweight following upwind conflict exposure, with the largest associations in the third trimester.

Interpretation: Conflict-related air pollution is a substantial and under-recognized contributor to infant mortality in LMICs. Because this pathway is not captured by conventional humanitarian monitoring, satellite-based pollution tracking could strengthen early-warning systems. Protecting water and sanitation infrastructure during conflict may also reduce preventable child deaths.

detail.abstract:
Background: Clinically node negative (cN0) T1a papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is frequently complicated by occult central lymph node metastasis (LNM). We aimed to develop and validate prediction models for total and subregional central LNM by comparing machine learning (ML) with a traditional logistic regression model (TLRM) using the probability based ranking model approach (PMRA)., providing a framework for clinical digital decision support.

Methods: This multicenter study involving 4,882 patients from three hospitals was conducted. Prospective data collection was performed for validation. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 1,953 patients from the primary center were used for model development and internal testing (7:3 split). Two independent prospective external testing cohorts included 286 and 176 patients. Eighteen ML algorithms and the TLRM were evaluated. Six feature selection methods were applied, the TLRM was presented as a nomogram, and model interpretability was assessed with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).

Results: Among 2,415 total patients, 32.5% had central LNM. Prelaryngeal, pretracheal, paratracheal, con-paratracheal, and posterior recurrent laryngeal nerve LNM (LNM-prRLN) were observed in 216 (8.9%), 571 (23.6%), 579 (24.0%), 84 (3.5%), and 160 (6.6%) patients, respectively. PMRA analysis identified XGBoost as the best performing algorithm. The AUCs in the internal testing set, validation set 1, and validation set 2 were 0.859, 0.680, and 0.693 for total central LNM; 0.826, 0.858, and 0.907 for prelaryngeal LNM; 0.864, 0.752, and 0.883 for pretracheal LNM; 0.895, 0.848, and 0.931 for paratracheal LNM; 0.961, 0.898, and 0.915 for con-paratracheal LNM; and 0.886, 0.841, and 0.862 for LNM-prRLN. SHAP analysis identified tumor size, age, and sex as the leading contributors to total central LNM; tumor border for prelaryngeal LNM; tumor size for pretracheal LNM; prelaryngeal lymph node metastasis ratio (LNMR) for paratracheal LNM; and pretracheal LNMR for LNM-prRLN. The web calculator provided individualized clinical digital decision support probabilities for total and subregional central LNM.

Conclusion: PMRA identified XGBoost achieved the more favorable PMRA ranking across outcomes. Incorporating intraoperative frozen section data at sequential decision points enhanced subregional prediction. SHAP visualization and the web calculator may support individualized risk assessment and intraoperative decision making in cN0 T1a-PTC.

detail.abstract: Background: Chronological age remains the dominant criterion for retirement policy, despite well-documented heterogeneity in functional capacity among older adults. This study introduces the Retirement Timing Error (RTE) metric-a classification framework that quantifies the policy mismatch arising when age-based retirement thresholds misclassify individuals' capabilities and near-term vulnerability. Methods: Using longitudinal data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) across Waves 4-6 (Börsch-Supan et al., 2013; Malter & Börsch-Supan, 2015), we estimated the incidence of Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) limitation in two transitions (Wave 4→5: n = 32,597; Wave 5→6: n = 39,792) among participants free of IADL limitation at baseline. We compared an age-only logistic regression model (Model A) with a capability-informed model (Model B) incorporating a Capability Composite Index (CCI) derived from grip strength, mobility, cognition, and depressive symptom burden, stratified into three decision bands (Red-risk, Amber, Green). Results: Adding capability zones substantially improved model fit (McFadden's Pseudo-R²: 0.092→0.145 in Wave 4→5; 0.091→0.138 in Wave 5→6). Nested likelihood-ratio tests confirmed that capability zones explained variance beyond age (χ² = 1,174 and 1,257; both p < 0.001). RTE-B individuals (younger but low-capability) faced incident IADL risk of 13.5-Riekert-Age is Not Ability: Retirement Timing Error | Page 2 16.4%, approximately double that of RTE-A individuals (older but capable) at 7.4-8.8%. Women comprised approximately 76% of the Red-risk zone and only 33% of the Green zone in both wave transitions. Findings were robust across tercile, quartile, and continuous CCI specifications. Conclusions: Age is a statistically significant but materially insufficient predictor of functional decline. Capability-informed classification provides a richer, more accurate basis for retirement policy, workforce planning, and targeted early intervention. The RTE metric offers a novel, empirically grounded policy tool for auditing the costs of age-based misclassification and for developing differentiated retain, redeploy, and early-support strategies.

detail.abstract: We study capital raising in the wake of U.S. investment banks transitioning from partnerships to limited-liability forms. Transitioning banks start taking more risk: they underwrite for more uncertain, growth-oriented equity issuers and lower-rated bond issuers. The transition is met with higher IPO underpricing, higher SEO discounts, and more negative SEO announcement returns. Incumbent clients react negatively to news of their bank's reorganization and reduce future capital expenditures, suggesting a devaluation of their underwriting relationships. While risk-taking increases, we find no evidence of weaker screening/due diligence efforts. We conclude that financial intermediary structures shape capital formation with real economic effects.

detail.abstract: Despite the expansion of microfinance and SHG-based livelihoods in India, women-led SHGs continue to face a 'market blind spot' that limits long-term commercial sustainability. This paper argues that the problem is twofold: on the consumer side and on the institutional side. Using survey data, RTI-based evidence, and expert insights, the study examines the gap between awareness and purchase, and between policy intent and market outcomes. It finds that consumer willingness to buy SHG products exists, but is constrained by weak branding, poor visibility, and limited trust. At the same time, public initiatives under DAY-NRLM and related platforms have not yet created a fully coherent market architecture. The paper concludes that SHG sustainability requires moving beyond credit access towards stronger market linkage and a federative cooperative model like AMUL, that can unify quality assurance, logistics, and market-facing identity.

detail.abstract:
Background: Focus assessed transthoracic echocardiography (FATE) is increasingly used for rapid cardiac evaluation, but evidence for artificial intelligence (AI) assisted right ventricular fractional area change (RVFAC) assessment remains limited.

Methods: In this retrospective multicentre study, RVFAC data from 774 participants undergoing clinically indicated transthoracic echocardiography were used to develop, internally test, and externally test an AI assisted FATE model. AI derived RVFAC was compared with manual assessment by expert and novice users.

Findings: The AI model showed high reproducibility, with interobserver and intraobserver intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.936 and 0.977, exceeding manual expert measurements. Expert annotation models achieved internal test correlations of 0.701 and 0.698, and external testing after fine tuning achieved R = 0.642, mean absolute error = 3.42, and root mean squared error = 4.64.

Interpretation: AI assisted FATE can provide reproducible RVFAC estimates across expert and novice users and may reduce operator dependent variability in right heart functional assessment. Further prospective multicentre validation in diverse clinical settings is warranted.

title: Motivating Media Literacy in Wartime Ukraine
affiliations: and

detail.title: Motivating Media Literacy in Wartime Ukraine
detail.abstract: Media literacy interventions can reduce susceptibility to misinformation, but their societal impact relies on voluntary adoption and engagement. Drawing on compensatory control theory, we tested whether framing a free online media literacy course as a means to restore control over one's information environment could increase consumer engagement in wartime Ukraine, a context in which personal control is under chronic ecological threat. In a preregistered field experiment with an international NGO, 5,052 Ukrainian schoolteachers were randomly assigned to share a digital promotional flier with parents, featuring one of three messages: compensatory control-based, fact-based, or status quo. The compensatory control-based message did not influence initial clicks to visit the course website. It did produce slightly higher enrollment than status quo and fact-based messages, but absolute rates were low across conditions. A Meta advertising A/B test (N=321,385) and two online experiments (Ns=1,898 and 3,197), all with Ukrainian participants, found no advantage of the compensatory control-based framing on any measure of engagement. We probe plausible explanations for these differences. Together, this commentary contributes to emerging research on misinformation, adds to an ongoing conversation about the boundary conditions of compensatory control effects, and raises questions about leveraging consumer behavior theory in wartime environments.

detail.abstract: The preservation of seafood is a critical challenge in the fresh food supply chain, particularly when navigating the complexities of dual-channel models and leadership dynamics. This paper investigates the impact of preservation methods (chilled vs. frozen) and leadership structures (centralized vs. decentralized) on seafood supply chains. We examine the strategic decisions of suppliers and retailers regarding preservation mode selection and explore the advantages of supplier-or retailer-dominated supply chains. By incorporating insights from extension models, we highlight how hybrid sales channels, combining chilled and frozen modes, can outperform a single mode under specific conditions related to fixed and variable costs. Additionally, we investigate the conditions under which decentralized supply chains can outperform centralized systems, particularly in markets where product freshness and retailer responsiveness are crucial. Through a comparative analysis, we reveal critical thresholds for trade-offs between supply chain models, emphasizing the importance of cost structures, and propose cost-sharing contracts to enhance coordination and incentivize investment in cold chain logistics. This study contributes to the understanding of fresh food supply chains, preservation technologies, hybrid sales modes, and leadership dynamics, offering practical implications for optimizing seafood supply chain operations.

detail.abstract:
Marketing automation is often treated by companies as a technology-driven modernization project. The primary focus is typically placed on platform selection, systems integration, tracking, lead scoring, and campaign automation. This working paper advances a different argument: marketing automation is primarily an organizational, process, and data challenge, and only secondarily a software challenge.

The paper examines why automation initiatives frequently fail despite the availability of powerful technologies. Common causes include unclear processes, fragmented data structures, conflicting responsibilities, and insufficient coordination between marketing and sales. The analysis combines perspectives from organization theory and business process management with practical corporate challenges such as uncontrolled CRM growth, Excel-based shadow processes, manual handovers, data silos, and inconsistent lifecycle definitions.

Marketing automation is conceptualized as a decision and execution architecture. Workflows, scores, status values, routing rules, and data models translate organizational assumptions into technical processes. Their effectiveness therefore depends on whether processes have been sufficiently clarified, data has been defined in business terms, and responsibilities have been established in a durable governance structure.

The paper develops an integrated perspective on lead management, CRM, data quality, tracking, attribution, process architecture, and governance. A concluding practice-oriented section translates the analysis into eight phases of a marketing automation and CRM implementation: project mandate, current-state diagnosis, target-process design, data modeling, tool validation, pilot implementation, rollout, and ongoing operations.

title: The KANON-Index: Crediting Authorship Structure and Methodological Sophistication in Research Assessment

detail.title: The KANON-Index: Crediting Authorship Structure and Methodological Sophistication in Research Assessment
detail.abstract: Single-number bibliometric indicators such as the h-index ignore two dimensions that scientists treat as central: who did the work (authorship position and the dilution of credit under hyperauthorship) and how methodologically demanding it was. I introduce the KANON-Index, a transparent, editable and multidimensional indicator that combines citation impact (C), an authorship-contribution score (A) that penalises hyperauthorship, methodological sophistication (S) and a venue term (J). Rather than asserting the weights a priori, I calibrated them by cross-validation on 164 Nobel laureates (2005-2024) against a field-matched cohort of equally cited elite researchers, so that the default weights are grounded in profiles of recognised excellence. The central result is one of fairness, not prediction: across 656 clean profiles, the more co-authors a researcher carries per paper, the more the h-index over-credits that researcher relative to KANON (per-field Spearman ρ from-0.57 in Medicine to −0.77 in Chemistry; all permutation p < 10−4), and the authorship component alone separated laureates from matched elites at least as well as the h-index in every field (AUC 0.62–0.82 vs 0.52–0.63). A direct comparison with established author-level indices shows that KANON belongs to the family of authorship-aware indicators — alongside Batista’s hI and Schreiber’s hm — yet is the only one that is multidimensional and reweightable, and it is not redundant with any single fractional count (ρ ≈ 0.62 with hI ). I am explicit about what KANON does not do: under a field-matched benchmark, predicting which elite researcher will be awarded a Nobel remains intractable for any index once controls are matched by field, so the larger superiority reported elsewhere is largely an artefact of unmatched comparison groups. KANON is therefore offered not as a predictive tool but as a complementary, auditable descriptor that is fairer to researchers penalised by a citations-only view; all weights are user-configurable and the pipeline is open source

detail.abstract: According to the 2017 Swiss Re Global Insurance Industry Report (2017), Indonesia represents a fast growing and critical market within South East Asia. This market growth is a result of strong regional economic growth and demand for insurance services, such as life insurance. Despite the importance of this market to the wider economy and Indonesian professional services market, scholars note a high level of salesperson attrition, or churn, in the marketplace due to low sales performance. Additionally, most extant studies investigating this phenomenon have been conducted in Western markets, thus limiting the applicability of findings in a South East Asian context. This study, therefore, investigates the antecedents of insurance agents’ sales performance in an Indonesian context. Adopting thematic analysis, this research analyses interviews with 24 salespeople with results indicating that, among other agent- and-organisation-based factors, salespeople consider spirituality and family support two unique antecedents contributing to their sales performance

detail.abstract:
When people make efficient decisions that ignore some information or cues, they use their natural, intuitive ability to employ heuristics. The effectiveness of heuristics depends on the appropriateness to a given context. Heuristics reduce effort; they do not provide guidelines for reaching a goal. Heuristics do not indicate causality. People exposed to informational cues make a decision that often appears simple, automatic, and results in a seemingly mindless response. These decision heuristics, based on experience, save cognitive processing time (Gigerenzer & Brighton, 2009). Heuristics and biases go hand-in-hand. Incompetent decisions may occur when biases intervene, caused by application within an inappropriate context (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974). We find a similar concept with Weick’s tool-dropping wherein he propositions the need to drop the outmoded aspects of our theories and adapt our heuristics to the new, ever changing and disruptive environment (Weick, 2007).

Armstrong and colleagues (1994, 1996, 2007) researched the Boston Consulting Group (BCG) heuristic and provided evidence that the BCG heuristic influences incompetent decision-making; decision-makers reduced profit in order to beat the competition when biased with market share information. 

The research reported here includes remedial tools to overcome these biases. These tools include using heuristics tools (Gigerenzer, 1999) and tool-dropping methods (Weick, 2007) for training competent decision-making in environments of dynamic complexity (Senge, 1990; Simon, 1956).

detail.abstract: Purpose-This paper aims to investigate whether consumers' identification with a brand community makes them more likely to engage in compulsive buying behavior. Specifically, this research shows that consumers are more likely to experience obsessive passion for brands they identify with if they are also part of brand communities, which, in turn, makes them more likely to engage in compulsive buying behavior. Design/methodology/approach-An online survey (n ¼ 533) among members of the Adorable Representative M.C. for Youth (ARMY) Bangtan Boys (BTS) brand community was conducted. A partial least squares approach was employed to test the validity and reliability of the measurement model as well as to assess the structural equation model. Findings-Results show that brand identification affects harmonious and obsessive passion and that both relationships are moderated by brand community identification. Harmonious passion, in turn, has a positive effect on impulsive buying, whereas obsessive passion has a positive effect on both impulsive and obsessive-compulsive buying. Furthermore, consumer hedonic motivations moderate the relationship between (i) harmonious passion and impulsive buying and (ii) obsessive passion and obsessive-compulsive buying. Originality/value-To the best of the authors' knowledge, this work is the first to examine the potential negative impacts brand community identification has on compulsive buying behavior. Besides contributing to research on the negative aspects of brand community identification, by employing a model that distinguishes between two types of passion and compulsive buying, the study provides clarification on relationships suggested by prior studies.

title: Capability Risk: When AI Systems Become Learnableand Who Bears the Cost
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Capability Risk: When AI Systems Become Learnableand Who Bears the Cost
detail.abstract: This paper introduces capability risk-the risk that a deployed AI decision system's behavior can be learned and exploited through ordinary interaction, by actors who engage with the system more strategically than its designers anticipated. In consumer lending environments, high-volume actors such as loan brokers accumulate inferential knowledge about decision boundaries that individual applicants do not. The result is selection on the capacity to appear creditworthy to the system, not on actual creditworthiness. This distributional asymmetry is not detectable through conventional fairness audits-including demographic parity, equalized odds, and individual fairness as formalized by Dwork et al. (2012)-because those frameworks evaluate differential treatment of similarly situated individuals, not differential capacity to become similarly situated in the system's eyes. Building on adversarial machine learning literature (Tramèr et al., 2016; Biggio & Roli, 2018), this paper documents the production conditions under which capability risk emerges without adversarial intent, explains why confidence laundering amplifies it, and argues that addressing it requires treating deployment monitoring as a research problem distinct from model validation.

detail.title: Strategic Transfer Pricing and Social Welfare under Product Differentiation
detail.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the social impacts of strategic transfer pricing by oligopoly firms, aiming to derive regulatory implications for transfer prices. A notable finding from our model is that the negative effects on social welfare of transfer prices being set above marginal cost are pronounced when either (1) the number of competing firms is large and the product is relatively highly differentiated or (2) the number of firms is small and the product is not very differentiated. This result indicates that even when the number of firms in the industry is significant and the market is thus apparently competitive, the authorities should not overlook the possibility that setting transfer prices above marginal cost might seriously damage social welfare if the product is highly differentiated.

detail.abstract: Purpose-Actor engagement (AE) literature shows inconsistent understandings of engagement intensity. However, a holistic picture of the nature of AE intensity is foundational to advance empirical AE models and measurement frameworks. This paper provides a nuanced understanding of what engagement intensity is and how it unfolds on different network levels. Design/methodology/approach-This conceptual study draws from a literature review and offers a comprehensive classification scheme of AE intensity. The literature review extends beyond marketing and service research and draws from the etymology of AE intensity in management and social science, specifically, the fields of student, employee and civic engagement. Findings-The classification scheme clarifies that AE intensity at the individual level refers to actors' affective and cognitive tone and varying magnitudes (i.e. efforts, duration, activeness) of resource investments. At the dyad level, AE intensity represents relational strength, and at the network level, it refers to the degree of connectedness in the network. Research limitations/implications-The research reconciles conceptual inconsistencies in the AE literature. Our classification scheme goes beyond the individual actor and actor-actor dyad and offers a holistic overview of possible ways to operationalize AE intensity in networks. Practical implications-The classification scheme can be used as a strategic checklist to include AE intensities of individual actors (e.g. customers and employees), relationships between these actors and network connectedness, when further developing engagement measurement tools and benchmarks. Originality/value-This is the first study providing a comprehensive understanding of AE intensity from an individual, dyadic and network perspective

detail.abstract: With trust so central to the function and success of home sharing, this research proposes that trust is best established through interplay of trust entities. However, apart from literature detailing trust in platterm security (Lu, Wang, and Hayes, 2012), in the seller (Ert, Fleischer, and Magen, 2016), or in reviews (Filieri, 2016), litle is understood about how trust is built in home sharing, in order to offer a more refined understanding of trust, we explore the sources of rational, aftective and contextual trust and suggest the value in tracing objects as a key property of trust building in home sharing. We review this emergence through the lens of consumer culture perspectives (Amould and Thorpson, 2005) embedded in organizational trust literature (Korsgaard, Brower, and Lester, 2015) to assist in providing a vocabulary that can serve as an organizing framework. To understand how trust is built in home sharing networks (Airbnb), this study adopts interpretivist research practices. This approach enables an in-depth understanding of participants' Airbnb experiences (shared with hosts or full unit rentals) specifically relating to trust in engaging in the network. This study is based on a three-year multi-sited ethnography of Airbnb consumption experiences that includes netnographic data (Kozinets, 2010) of Airbnb online communities in New Zealand, interviews with guests and hosts and field observation.

detail.abstract: This research is concerned with the mediation of the relationship between co-creation and trust by emotions, particularly in a services context. Respondents were exposed to one of several structured sales scenarios and data generated for analysis. Mediation and moderation is analysed using Hayes Conditional Process Analysis. Emotions are found to partially mediate the relationship between co-creation and trust. When investigating specific scenarios and contexts, the mediating effect of emotions on trust is stronger in business-to-consumer (B2C) situations than in business-to-business situations (B2B), in a services sales context rather than product sales context and for female consumers/clients more so than male consumers/clients. Specifically, in a services context there is full mediation of the relationship between co-creation and trust by emotions for female consumers/clients in a B2C context. The strategic imperative that co-creation is vital in the services industry is underscored, particularly in a consumer situation when interacting with female consumers/clients.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This paper explores the similarities and differences in privacy attitudes, trust and risk beliefs between younger and older adults on social networking sites. The objective of the article is to ascertain whether any notable differences exist between younger (18-25 years old) and older (55þ years old) adults in how trust and risk are influenced by privacy concerns upon personal information disclosure on social media.  

Design/methodology/approach-A Likert scale instrument validated in previous research was employed to gather the responses of 148 younger and 152 older adults. The scale was distributed through Amazon Mechanical Turk. Data were analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling. 

Findings-No significant differences were found between younger and older adults in how social media privacy concerns related to trust and risk beliefs. Two privacy concern dimensions were found to have a significant influence on perceptions of risk for both populations: collection and control. Predictability and a sense of control are proposed as two conceptual approaches that can explain these findings. 

Originality/value-This article is the first one to explore age differences in privacy concerns, trust and risk on social media employing conceptual developments and an instrument specifically tailored to the social media environment. Based on the findings, several strategies are suggested to keep privacy concerns on social media at a minimum, reduce risk perceptions and increase users' trust.

detail.title: Strategic upfront Marketing Channel Integration as an Entry Barrier

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Journal of Operational Research, volume 220, issue 3, 2012[10.1016/j.ejor.2012.02.041]

detail.abstract: This paper investigates an organizational design problem concerning whether duopolistic firms competing in a product market should vertically integrate or separate their marketing channels in a dynamic noncooperative game setting. Previous operational research models have shown that the separation of the marketing channel with the adoption of a two-part tariff contract is the dominant strategy compared with integration for each firm if the two firms face retail price competition, and thereby constitutes the subgame perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE). Contrary to this previous insight, this paper demonstrates that if exogenous parameters that characterize fixed costs, product substitutability, and a demand function fall into a specific region, marketing channel integration dominates the separation strategy when one of the two firms is the incumbent firm while the other is a potential entrant. In other words, the well-known result in the price-setting game can be reversed when we take entry threats into consideration. Specifically, we show that upfront vertical integration of the marketing channel enables the incumbent to deter the entry of the potential competitor and to monopolize the market in the SPNE. This result has operational implications for a firm confronting the threat of potential rivals entering the market, in that the firm can use this apparently inferior strategy as a commitment device, which creates a virtual entry barrier.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) continues to advance rapidly, and leveraging AI travel assistants to foster cultural destination attachment has emerged as a notable trend. However, the effectiveness of AI travel assistants has not yet been explored and verified. To fill this research gap, based on the self-expansion theory, we explore how AI travel assistant contributes to promoting cultural destination attachment, and this impact is mediated by selfexpansion. Through four lab experiments, we indicate that emotionalized (vs. non-emotionalized) AI travel assistant achieves better performance in this process. In addition, we reveal the boundary mechanisms: the scene of cultural tourism where tourists are located (i.e., cultural tourism activity type) and the capability of tourists to understand cultural information (i.e., cultural intelligence). These findings provide new insights into how tourism enterprises can effectively leverage AI technology to promote destination attachment.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how different packaging materials influence consumer perception of taste in carbonated beverages. Although beverage manufacturers often claim that flavor remains consistent across packaging formats, scientific evidence suggests that material composition can subtly affect sensory experience. Previous research suggests that polymer linings in aluminum cans may absorb trace flavor compounds, while acetaldehyde migration from PET bottles may influence sensory perception. To explore this phenomenon, a structured survey was conducted with 60 respondents using a close-ended questionnaire. The study examined preferences and perceived taste differences across three packaging types: aluminum cans, plastic bottles, and glass bottles. Results show a strong preference for aluminum cans, with 30 respondents selecting cans as their preferred format, compared to 15 for plastic and 15 for glass. Participants associated cans with a stronger taste and greater convenience. The findings highlight the role of packaging material in shaping taste perception and consumer choice. This research contributes to the literature on sensory marketing and packaging effects and provides practical insights for beverage manufacturers seeking to optimize product experience and market positioning.

detail.abstract: The large language model did not create a crisis in the humanities. It revealed one already present. This paper argues that when a competent answer can be produced from a hollow prompt, what is exposed is not the tool's capability but the degree to which the academy had already been certifying retrieval as learning. The central formal category is the unknown known, the fourth quadrant of the standard knowledge taxonomy: certainty resting on surface expression with no verified knowledge network beneath it. Drawing on representational divergence as a heuristic formal apparatus, the paper formalizes humanistic knowledge as a directed graph GK whose edges require explicit validation, and the asserted knowledge state as a surface subgraph GK ̂ whose divergence from GK is measurable via Hausdorff distance. This structural variance, the Blaeu Rent, is shown to compound across the credentialing system, the civil service, corporate governance, and intergenerational knowledge transmission. A distributional analysis demonstrates that the gap falls hardest on communities of color, first-generation learners, and economically marginalized populations, whose differential exposure to high-stakes AI-mediated decisions amplifies the harm from biased surface expressions. The paper develops a public resource allocation model, a minimax decision framework for institutional reform, and a five-component social cost pricing function. It argues that the liberal arts corrective is not a moral or cultural argument but a strict optimization strategy: in a world where surface fluency has a marginal cost of zero, the capacity to verify GK is the only high-value signal the labor market will price. GPU-accelerated computation makes the cost of the knowledge gap formally expressible and measurable at population scale for the first time.

detail.abstract: This article extends current models of how consumers judge or perceive organizations as greedy using the theoretical framework of motivated moral reasoning. We show that inherent features of an organization (size and ‘black sheep’ status) and its behaviour (relative frequency) bias consumer perceptions of organizational greed. We use an experimental methodology, present subjects with vignettes describing different scenarios, validate our questionnaire using confirmatory factor analysis, and test our hypotheses using a general linear model with covariates. Our findings suggest that consumer perceptions of organizational greed are subject to three effects: the underdog effect (Study 1, n = 496), the black sheep effect (Study 2, n = 229) and the ‘common is moral’ heuristic (Study 3, n = 249). This is the first study to investigate greed under a motivated reasoning paradigm and to show that perceptions of organizational greed are subject to socio-psychological biases. This study also provides advice on branding and positioning strategies that appeal to the underdog status of an organization or its local origins.

title: The Limits of Freedom

detail.title: The Limits of Freedom
detail.abstract: At first glance, this World Bank dataset (World Bank, 2023) spanning India from 1991 to 2016 appears to tell a straightforward story of economic triumph. After all, 1991 was the year India famously opened its doors to the world (Ahluwalia, 2002), and the subsequent decades are often celebrated purely for their soaring GDP numbers. But the numbers reveal a more complicated, deeply human story. Looking at aggregate growth alone is like reading the cliff notes of a novel; you get the basic plot, but miss the character development, contradictions, and quiet tragedies. In accordance with the true definitions of holistic development not just as the accumulation of wealth, but as the expansion of human freedoms and capabilities, I decided to examine how shifts in employment structure, health outcomes, and income distribution across India's sectors from 1991 to 2016 actually changed the lives of ordinary people. How did the shifting economy change the daily lives, health, and options of ordinary Indians? And who got left behind?

title: What Drives Cadet Success? Predicting Academic and Athletic Performance
