detail.title: What Drives Cadet Success? Predicting Academic and Athletic Performance
detail.abstract: Military academies are high-demand training environments in which cadets must perform effectively across academic, physical, and organizational domains while adapting to discipline, hierarchy, and sustained pressure. In this context, success depends not only on cognitive ability, but also on psychological resilience, personality traits, emotional adjustment, and organizational behavior. This study examined the predictors of cadet success using a crosssectional dataset of 92 cadets from the Hellenic Air Force Academy. A multi-model machinelearning framework was applied, integrating stability selection, comparative model evaluation, cross-validated ROC-AUC, and SHAP-based explainability. Predictor variables included demographic characteristics, personality traits, psychological distress indicators, resilience, leadership, and organizational citizenship behavior measured across multiple time points. Results showed that cadet success is multidimensional and outcome specific. Academic performance was best classified by a Random Forest model (ROC-AUC = 0.805), with gender, baseline depression, neuroticism, openness, resilience, and selected organizational citizenship dimensions emerging as key predictors. Athletic performance proved more difficult to predict, with an SVM model showing the best performance (ROC-AUC = 0.729), primarily driven by resilience, agreeableness, anxiety, conscientiousness, and extraversion. A gender-neutral composite model of overall cadet success, combining academic, athletic, and leadership outcomes, achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.768 with CatBoost, with neuroticism, baseline anxiety, extraversion, and resilience identified as the strongest predictors. Across models, resilience emerged as the most consistent domain-general predictor of cadet success.

detail.abstract: This study explored the perceptual factors affecting consumers' advertising avoidance on social networking sites (SNSs) in the context of mobile YouTube by relying on the psychological theory of reversal theory. detail.abstract: The first four papers in this series established why the human layer matters, how to build it, how to measure it, and why capital nonetheless flows toward its elimination. Paper 4 closed on an unanswered question: if augmented systems are the durable bet, what exactly is the durable asset? This paper names it. The durable, non-substitutable layer of an AI-native organization is the memory it owns and the judgment it can prove, not the model it rents. Memory without accountable judgment is an archive; judgment without memory is amnesia. The two are the same asset seen from two sides, and the Sovereign Memory Layer is the architecture that binds them. The argument is that continuity is the strategic objective and memory the mechanism that delivers it; that the atomic unit of that mechanism is decision lineage, the ordered and append-only record of recommendation, action, delta, identity, and outcome, which is the genuinely novel category, distinct from the information storage, knowledge management, and audit logging it is routinely mistaken for; and that memory has crossed from feature to infrastructure by the only test that settles the matter, whether the firm and the systems built upon it can function without it. The case rests on three structural forces that predate any single event: model commoditization, the fragmentation crisis, and the concentration of dependence. It keeps the human central throughout: memory does not replace judgment, it makes judgment continuous and provable.

title: HDQS: A Conceptual Architecture for AI-Driven, Real-Time Healthcare Data Quality Enforcement Across Multi-Payer Clinical Environments

detail.title: HDQS: A Conceptual Architecture for AI-Driven, Real-Time Healthcare Data Quality Enforcement Across Multi-Payer Clinical Environments
detail.abstract: Background: Modern U.S. healthcare data environments span distributed multi-payer ecosystems, including Medicaid, Medicare, ACA Marketplace, and commercial payer systems, generating hundreds of millions of claims transactions annually. Ensuring data quality across these heterogeneous, high-velocity pipelines remains a critical unresolved challenge. Traditional rule-based EDI validation tools lack the semantic, temporal, and contextual intelligence required to govern data integrity at enterprise scale. Objective: This paper presents the Healthcare Data Quality System (HDQS), an original conceptual architecture for AI-driven, real-time healthcare data quality enforcement. HDQS introduces a six-layer architectural model integrating payer-aware metadata harmonization, ML-driven anomaly intelligence, multi-dimensional validation, temporal claims consistency assessment, and adaptive autonomous remediation. Methods: HDQS was designed through iterative applied research across multiple U.S. Federal and State healthcare data programs serving millions of patients. The architecture is described at a conceptual level, avoiding implementation-specific details, to support broad applicability and peer evaluation. Each architectural layer addresses a distinct class of healthcare data quality challenge identified through program-level operational experience. Results: Environments guided by HDQS architectural principles reported: 70-90% reduction in anomaly detection latency; 50-87% reduction in downstream pipeline incidents; 30-50% improvement in CMS regulatory audit preparation efficiency; and 20-40% improvement in healthcare AI model stability. Cross-payer reporting reconciliation cycles improved by 35-60%. Conclusion: HDQS provides a scalable, payer-aware, and temporally intelligent architectural blueprint for healthcare data quality governance. Its conceptual contributions advance the field beyond static EDI format validation toward dynamic, intelligence-driven clinical data integrity management, with direct applicability across Medicaid, Medicare, ACA Marketplace, pharmacy, and all-payer data environments.

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems into educational settings has transformed student engagement and learning processes. However, empirical evidence increasingly demonstrates that heavy reliance on these tools may foster problematic dependency patterns characterized by cognitive offloading, reduced critical thinking, and functional impairment. While validated measurement instruments exist for internet, social media, and smartphone addiction, these tools are inadequate for capturing the unique psychological mechanisms underlying generative AI dependency, particularly the novel dimensions of cognitive reliance and parasocial attachment. This study addresses this critical gap by developing and validating a multidimensional AI Addiction Scale specifically designed for university students. Grounded in established behavioral addiction frameworks (DSM-5-TR and ICD-11) and informed by three complementary theoretical perspectives-the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, Social Cognitive Theory, and Cognitive Load Theory-the study employed a rigorous three-stage psychometric development process: (1) expert review-guided item generation and content validation, (2) exploratory factor analysis (EFA) for dimensionality refinement, and (3) confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) for structural validation. Data were collected from 525 university students. The final 28-item scale demonstrates robust psychometric properties (CFI = 0.898, RMSEA = 0.062, SRMR = 0.047) across five theoretically coherent dimensions: Loss of Control, Cognitive Reliance, Socio-emotional Connection, Functional and Social Impairment, and Tolerance and Withdrawal. The scale provides a systematic, validated instrument for identifying and measuring problematic generative AI use among students, with important implications for educational institutions seeking to balance AI integration with the preservation of cognitive autonomy and critical thinking skills.

detail.abstract: World trade rests on one of the safest large asset classes in finance, yet US$2.5 trillion of annual demand for trade finance goes unmet, and the burden of the gap falls disproportionately on small and medium-sized enterprises and emerging-market firms. We argue that this is, in substantial part, a unit cost problem rather than a risk problem: the fixed cost of verifying, monitoring and documenting a shipment has historically exceeded the revenue available on small transactions, so rational lenders exclude the very borrowers whose marginal returns to capital are highest. We acknowledge that the headline loss data, being conditional on approval, cannot by themselves rule out the rival adverseselection explanation, and we specify the test that discriminates between the two. Three concurrent shifts now change the cost structure of safe origination: agentic AI that lowers the marginal cost of underwriting and compliance, legal reforms that make digital trade documents enforceable collateral, and the digitization of logistics data. Together they make it possible to finance, collateralize and distribute trade exposures at the level of the individual shipment, a state we describe as a liquid supply chain. We set out the mechanism by which automation converts unpriceable operational risk into investable credit risk, trace the consequences for firms, trade and capital markets, and examine the principal failure modes, including model monoculture, the screening incentive failures familiar from past securitization booms, and the lessons of the 2021 Greensill collapse. We close with a measurable research agenda and an invitation to externally funded research partnerships to design the evaluation of a new origination channel before its first transaction.

title: The Dynamic Aspects of Cognitive Load in Educational Videos
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University - H. John Heinz III School of Public Policy and Management, Carnegie Mellon University - H. John Heinz III School of Public Policy and Management, Carnegie Mellon University - H. John Heinz III School of Public Policy and Management ,  and

detail.title: The Dynamic Aspects of Cognitive Load in Educational Videos
detail.abstract:
In this paper, we study how intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load relate to learning outcomes throughout instructional videos. We conceptualize instructional videos as configurable digital instructional artifacts whose instructional dimensions are allocated throughout time and construct measures of realized instructional exposure by combining cognitive load representations with learner interaction histories. Using observational data from an existing educational platform together with a complementary randomized instructional experiment, we examine how instructional characteristics unfold throughout instruction and relate to educational outcomes across multiple levels of educational aggregation.

Across observational analyses, aggregate relationships between cognitive load and learning outcomes broadly align with established predictions from Cognitive Load Theory. However, these relationships vary systematically throughout instruction. Instructional experiences characterized by higher intrinsic load earlier in instruction tend to exhibit more positive relationships with learning outcomes than comparable instructional experiences in which intrinsic load occurs later. Measured extraneous load exhibits comparatively more positive relationships with learning outcomes during introductory instructional stages and less positive relationships later in instruction. Measured germane load exhibits increasingly positive relationships with learning outcomes later in instructional experiences.

To complement these observational findings and introduce experimentally assigned instructional variation, we conduct a randomized experiment comparing alternative instructional video implementations that preserve conceptual content and learning objectives while varying instructional sequencing and instructional support. Experimental results identify causal effects of instructional organization that vary across learners and exhibit temporal patterns broadly aligned with those observed in the observational setting. Additional instructional support appears particularly beneficial for learners with lower prior familiarity with chemistry content, whereas more condensed instructional implementations perform comparatively better for learners with greater prior familiarity with chemistry content.

Together, these findings suggest that instructional effectiveness depends not only on which instructional characteristics are present but also on when they occur throughout instruction. More broadly, the consistency of these temporal patterns across observational and experimental settings suggests that temporal allocation represents an important, measurable, and potentially optimizable design dimension of instructional videos and provides a foundation for adaptive educational systems that personalize not only what learners receive but also how instructional experiences unfold over time.

title: Source Verification as a First-Class Architectural Layer in Multi-Agent AI Deliberation Systems
affiliations: and Augle, Inc.

detail.title: Source Verification as a First-Class Architectural Layer in Multi-Agent AI Deliberation Systems
detail.abstract:
Citation hallucination—the generation of syntactically plausible but fictitious source references by large language models—represents a particularly damaging failure mode in multi-agent deliberation systems, where false citations propagate as evidence through downstream agents. We describe the Source Verification Service (SVS), an architectural component that addresses this failure mode by operating as an independent background service between the evidence extraction layer and the deliberation ensemble. The SVS performs identifierappropriate resolution across four citation types (URL, DOI, arXiv identifier, ISBN), applies content match verification to detect misattribution to real resources, and automatically applies tiered confidence downgrade rules to evidence nodes in a structured registry based on verification outcomes. Critically, the SVS preserves rather than removes failed citations, maintaining a complete audit trail while marking verification failures at the evidence node level. We describe the SVS design, its integration with the Augle seven-agent deliberation ensemble, and the design principle of preservation over removal that distinguishes this approach from prior citation filtering methods.

detail.abstract: Historical methodology has long recognized that archival silence is analytically significant, but the discipline has never developed a formal apparatus for what the archive structurally omits. Sensitivity to absence is not the same as a method for measuring it. This article argues that computational history, derived from first principles in combinatorial mathematics and algebraic topology, provides that apparatus. The discipline has perfected its instruments for the how, who, and when of historical events; the why has resisted, because structural explanation requires characterizing what was absent from the record rather than only what was present in it. Four claims are advanced. First, the historical record is fundamentally a complement problem: the analytically decisive object is not the archive's contents but the bounded, formally recoverable space of what the archive structurally excluded. Second, asymmetric knowledge has combinatorial structure: the epistemic horizon is characterizable from positive historical evidence about available instruments, trade routes, and institutional incentive structures. Third, the shape of a knowledge gap is topological rather than metric: a region surrounded by claimed knowledge without being penetrated by it constitutes a hole in the formal sense, recoverable through persistent homology. Fourth, Dutch cartographic distortion of the Darien isthmus between 1609 and 1714 serves as a bounded empirical existence proof for all three claims: the complement set is recoverable, its topological signature measurable, and its consequences historically lethal and verifiable. detail.abstract: Digital financial infrastructure has sharply expanded account ownership across low-and middleincome economies, and a celebrated literature links mobile money to households absorbing shocks. Yet whether expanding access is reliably associated with resilience across economies remains unsettled. Using the Global Findex 2025 microdata for 101,528 adults in 97 economies, a 2021-2024 country panel, and country-level configurational analysis, this paper asks when digital financial access is associated with household financial resilience-the ability to raise emergency funds without difficulty-and why. Three findings emerge. First, within countries, account ownership is associated with a modest, robust resilience premium (about 4.5 points, net of socioeconomic resources), but generic use is absorbed by socioeconomic and digital-access controls, and income and education dominate. Second, the conversion is profoundly uneven: the account-resilience association ranges from roughly-0.13 to +0.31 across economies, and standard moderators-connectivity, governance, income-do not explain the spread. Third, a withincountry panel shows that rising access tracks rising resilience over time (first-difference coefficient 0.26, p < 0.01)-evidence consistent with a conditional, not causal, relationship. Configurational analysis identifies one dominant sufficient configuration: access, active use, development, and connectivity jointly (consistency 0.81). No single condition is necessary, and several lowerdevelopment economies reach high resilience without high development. The access agenda's promise of resilience is therefore conditional: access is associated with resilience mainly where complementary use, development, and connectivity are jointly present. We argue for a conversion agenda that targets the whole bundle rather than accounts alone, and release open data and code for replication. Data availability: Derived data and code openly archived on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20932393; raw sources publicly available from their providers.

detail.abstract:
William Dampier's 1697 account of his voyage around the world is meticulous about what his charts recorded: the soundings, the headlands, the channels. What no chart of his era could record was what the act of surveying revealed about the surveyor: what the observer already knew, what they were looking for, and what category of the unknown they could not yet name. This paper takes that gap as its subject and proposes a formal system for closing it.

The Cognitive Universe System (CUS) is an observer-constituted knowledge space in which the user's authored universe — a directed graph of concepts, connections, and orientations of self — is continuously analyzed for the structure of what the user does not yet know. The central image is two mirrors facing each other: an infinite regress of reflections, each containing the full corridor including itself, converging toward a limit it never reaches. The paper argues that the CUS has precisely this structure, and that convergence is guaranteed by the Banach contraction mapping principle on a dynamic metric space equipped with a Wasserstein-1 distance over graph-topology distributions. The stable attractor of that contraction is not a fixed content state but a recognizable topological signature: the shape of the user's authored universe across time, stable even as its contents change.

The paper develops this argument across ten sections. The mathematical grounding (Section I) replaces Brouwer's fixed-point theorem — inapplicable to an expanding discrete graph — with Banach contraction on a Polish space. Section II introduces a four-level Zone epistemology: Terra Firma (the known and mapped), Terra Incognita (the partially structured), Hic Sunt Dracones (the known unknown, inferrable from graph topology), and Whisp (the unknown unknown, present only as a boundary condition). Section III develops the differential-geometric substrate: Ollivier-Ricci curvature for local bottleneck detection, the path-Laplacian spectral gap for integration health, and directed persistent homology as the basis for the Latent Yield metric. The system's AI presence, Nele, functions architecturally as a Topological Graph Neural Network whose persistence-diagram-augmented message-passing generates the purple helix proposals that constitute its Latent Yield signal. Section IV introduces observer-constitution of the knowledge space and five provisional orientation labels derived from Kuna spatial ontology, whose relational structure is an apt geometric analogue for a system in which placement is indexed to the observer's relationship to content rather than to a fixed taxonomy. Section V resolves the multi-user alignment problem through sheaf theory: user graphs are local sections; helix bridges are gluing maps; categorical pullbacks compute the maximal common structure between users' authored neighborhoods, collapsing asymmetry rather than reproducing it. Section VI frames Zone 4 boundary mechanics through Friston's free energy principle: the CUS functions as an externalized Markov Blanket for the user's epistemic state, with Nele's propose-not-execute principle mapping onto the active inference update cycle. Section IX surveys domain applications across six fields — large language models, parallel computing, healthcare administration, finance and systemic risk, education, and astrophysics — each stated as a structural correspondence, not a product claim. Section X traces the philosophical line from Kant through Mach to James, positioning the CUS as the computational version of James's stream of consciousness given external, navigable form.

The paper's central claim is epistemological and architectural. It borrows mathematical tools from differential geometry and network science without asserting physical identity with quantum mechanics or general relativity. The reflections are real. The corridor has a fixed point. The observer authors the space they navigate.
